News.title: Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests
News.content:
A clock tower spire has collapsed in a ball of flames in the French city of Limoges amid nationwide protests.

The local prefecture said the town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze started deliberately.

Fire crews were still battling the blaze late into the night, while eyewitnesses captured the dramatic moment the tower's turret fell.

News.title: More NHS staff sacked over attacks victims' records
News.content:
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.

Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "I am appalled, it's time to get a handle on these failures."

He added: "Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful."

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message â we will investigate and we will take action.

"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.

"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

News.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
News.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above; a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.

"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.

The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.

"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.

He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat; he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

News.title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
News.content:
This was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney.

His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.

Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".

A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.

Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.

News.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?
News.content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than Â£20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of Â£8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when Â£100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than Â£300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

News.title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
News.content:
Suspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.

But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.

Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.

As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.

Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning.

"I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).

Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach.

"They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."

News.title: The playground murder: Trauma, loss and a love that endured
News.content:
As we spoke, beside her on the sofa was her husband, Andy Thomson.

It took me a moment to take it in when they told me that Andy had been Alan's best friend.

That through all the tragedy and trauma, this couple found solace in each other and they've been married for 34 years.

Their little grandson is the light of their lives.

"We were kids and I got what she was going through because I was so close to Alan," says Andy.

"And then obviously when Alan passed away, it just drew the two of us even closer.

"And we're 34 years together, we're still going strong and always have been. And always will be."

"No one gives you a book on how to cope with trauma when you're a teenager," Pauline says.

"We were left to cope, and we helped each other. Our life hasn't been all trauma â not at all. But it has been a part of it.

"The most important thing for us was we wanted to talk about Diane and Alan, not just the names in the newspapers.

"For people to have a better understanding of them as kids â because that's what they were, they were kids. Just normal teenagers who should still be here."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

News.title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley Arena in one turbulent year
News.content:
A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.

As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.

The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya PÄ±nar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal YelekÃ§i and main dancer Esin Bahat.

But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions.

"After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal YelekÃ§i, playing on the group's name.

manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 TÃ¼rkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.

They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including GÃ¼lÃ§in ErgÃ¼l, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.

The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.

News.title: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says
News.content:
The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.

Lord Ricketts said more money should be spent on the defence budget, as well as improving the resilience of energy, transport and air traffic control.

He warned hybrid attacks were becoming "more reckless, more dangerous" and that people could end up being killed.

It comes after MI5 chief Sir Kevin McCallum said in his annual speech earlier this week that threats from foreign states, including Russia and Iran, had quadrupled in the last decade.

Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ministers had to warn British people about what might be coming.

"Not only is [Russian President Vladimir] Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he's also trying to undermine morale in European countries," he said.

He said there had been a stark warning from the head of MI5 that there could be worse to come in terms of hybrid attacks in the UK or on other Nato territory.

Responding to a question about the impact of disruption by Russia, Lord Ricketts said: "I'm not saying there's going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.

"But yes these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous...people are going to end up getting killed somewhere."

Hybrid attacks tend to use non-military methods, such as hacking, in an attempt to destabilise a country.

Moscow is suspected to be behind many such attacks in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, but it has always denied involvement.

As well as cyber-attacks, hybrid attacks can include attempts at sabotage and efforts to spread misinformation.

Lord Ricketts's warning comes after US President Donald Trump blocked sanctions on Russia. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the decision "only encourages him [Putin] to keep attacking" Ukraine.

The former national security adviser, who also previously ran the Foreign Office, said the UK's focus should be on putting more effort into the coalition of the willing, rather than attempting to act as a bridge between Zelensky and Trump.

"I don't think in Trump's current mood there is any influence Britain can have in the short term," he said.

A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Last month, Germany said Russia was responsible for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig, in which an explosive failed to detonate close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned in September that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France had intensified.

News.title: Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham
News.content:
John Swinney has taken aim at those who think Scotland "should be just like Manchester" as he vowed Scotland would soon be an independent nation.

In a closing speech at the SNP conference that did not mention Prime Minister Andy Burnham by name, Swinney issued a veiled retort to the former Greater Manchester mayor after he visited Scotland.

The first minister, speaking in Aberdeen, also announced that the country's bus network would be brought under public control by the end of the parliamentary term in 2031.

Swinney made further pledges to extend a Â£2 bus fare cap to the north east of Scotland, launch an independence campaign, fund anti-racism initiatives and tackle misogyny in schools.

News.title: Comedian Paul Whitehouse mugged at London cash machine
News.content:
Actor and comedian Paul Whitehouse has fought back against someone who tried to steal his card at an London cash machine, according to his wife.

Dr Mine Conkbayir posted on Instagram that her husband had gone out to get some medication on Friday, when he was mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington.

"He did fight back and retrieved his card, with the perp scuttling away empty-handed," she wrote, warning people to be "super vigilant" out there.

The Welsh comedian, 68, is known for his work on The Fast Show and BBC's Gone Fishing.

In her post, Conkbayir said Whitehouse was picking up medication for her after she had a bad reaction to some treatment.

"Well, a horrid start to the weekend, would be an understatement," she wrote, adding that she had been encouraged by her husband to make the post "in the hope that it might help folk to be more aware when out and about".

Friends and fans alike have flooded to the comments of Conkbayir's post, condemning the attack and wishing Whitehouse a speedy recovery.

Among them were fellow comedian Dawn French, who wrote that the incident in Islington was "utterly not okay", and Angela Barnes, who said it was a "horrible thing to happen" and she was "sending love to you both".

Whitehouse is best known for his work on Gone Fishing, which he presents alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer.

The BBC Two series began in 2018 and sees Whitehouse and Mortimer discuss life while fishing. It has been nominated six times for a Bafta TV award.

The comedian has also been cast as Hogwarts caretaker Argus Filch in HBO's upcoming Harry Potter television series.

News.title: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
News.content:
A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have died following a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash near the village of Drymen, in the Stirling Council area, at about 16:45 BST on Friday.

The boy and man were pronounced dead and their next of kin have been informed, police said.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) conducts its inquiries.

An AAIB spokesperson said: "A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation."

News.title: Man jailed for Starmer-linked arson attacks is deported
News.content:
A man who plotted to carry out arson attacks on property connected to Sir Keir Starmer has been deported, the Home Office says.

Stanislav Carpiuc, 28, was one of two men convicted over the attacks, which took place in May last year and targeted a car and two houses.

The Ukrainian-born Romanian national was sentenced to two years in prison in June. The Home Office said he had been removed from the UK, without specifying where he had been sent.

The BBC revealed the attacks were ordered on behalf of Russia, with an anonymous handler known as EL promising payment to Carpiuc's accomplice, Roman Lavrynovych.

Lavrynovych, a 22-year-old Ukrainian national, was sentenced to seven years imprisonment in June.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "This was an abhorrent attack and the conviction and imprisonment of these men should send a clear message to anyone blinded by the promise of money from strangers. You will be caught and face severe consequences.

"This individual has now been deported from the UK," it added, referring to Carpiuc.

News.title: Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements
News.content:
A nurse who stole Â£750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than Â£370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with Â£160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her Â£400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay Â£20,000 for a car and Â£9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days out.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

News.title: Why hasn't the UK had any named storms yet?
News.content:
With November already on the horizon the UK is yet to see its first named storm of the season.

Deep Atlantic lows responsible for more turbulent conditions have been steered away by dominant areas of high pressure.

This year the headlines have been about worsening drought rather than the impact of gales.

However, could this be the calm before the storms as the Met Office predict a growing chance that late autumn and early winter will turn wetter and windier as El NiÃ±o strengthens in the Pacific.

News.title: Husband calls for PM to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
News.content:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.

Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.

Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.

The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.

Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.

"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.

He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

News.title: Israel-Lebanon agreement shines light on long-lost Jewish community
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Rabbi Elie Abadie left his native Lebanon more than five decades ago and has not even visited since, but his Lebanese roots remain an integral part of his identity.

He has 3,000 Arabic songs on his smart phone. His wife, an American, learned from his mother how to cook the Lebanese dishes he loves. When he speaks with his siblings, he uses a mixture of Arabic and French, like many citizens of Lebanon, a former French protectorate.

The once-thriving Lebanese Jewish community has been largely forgotten in the decades since most of them left the country. But the latest Israel-Hezbollah war — which pushed Lebanon and Israel into direct negotiations — has brought them under the spotlight again.

Last month, Israel agreed to release five civilians detained by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon in exchange for Lebanon's help in searching for the bodies of Lebanese Jewish leaders abducted and killed in the 1980s, during Lebanon’s civil war.

The news stirred painful memories for Lebanese Jews like Abadie, 65, who was born and raised in Beirut to parents who moved to Lebanon from Syria. Abadie left his country of birth at 10 and settled for some years in Mexico. He is now based in Dubai, serving as the senior rabbi emeritus of the United Arab Emirates and the Gulf states.

He remembers the Lebanon of his childhood in the 1960s in its “best days” with “beautiful beaches and rivieras, mountain resorts, skiing resorts.”

His family, like many Lebanese Jews, left as anti-Jewish sentiment rose after the 1967 war between Israel and Arab countries. Security fears have kept him away since, but Abadie hopes to come back one day to reopen Beirut's long-shuttered central synagogue.

“It is unfortunately a sad reality that, since Lebanon and the Jews go back over 3,000 years from the time of King Solomon and King Hiram of Tyre and their peaceful and friendly relations, the situation in the last 50 years marked such a decline in Jewish population and life in Lebanon,” he said.

A once-thriving community has scattered

Nada Abdelsamad, a Lebanese journalist who wrote two books about Lebanon’s Jewish community, said the country once had between 18,000 and 20,000 Jews, many of them living in the central Beirut district of Wadi Abu Jmil, which was nicknamed the Valley of the Jews.

After the war surrounding the creation of Israel in 1948, many Jews fled other Arab countries like Syria and Iraq, where they faced increasing discrimination and sometimes violence, and came to Lebanon, a religiously diverse country where they felt safer. Some were then smuggled into Israel, but many stayed in Lebanon.

That changed after the 1967 war in which Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula from Egypt and the Golan Heights from Syria in addition to east Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. Lebanon was polarized between pro-West groups and others that supported Palestinian factions and Egyptian leader Gamal Abdul-Nasser.

In 1969, Lebanon and Palestinian factions signed the Cairo Agreement, allowing the Palestinian groups to operate freely in Lebanon.

“From that day on, the Jewish community in Lebanon felt very insecure and threatened,” recalls Abadie. “We started seeing marches and protests in the streets of Lebanon, chanting, ‘Death to Israel and to the Jews.’”

His family left.

The situation deteriorated further after the outbreak of the Lebanese civil war in 1975. With kidnappings by armed groups rampant, prominent figures from Lebanon’s dwindling Jewish community were taken by force from their homes, work or the streets. An organization calling itself the Organization of the Oppressed on Earth — believed to be linked to Hezbollah — was blamed.

Former Jewish leaders are among 17,000 missing since the civil war ended

At least seven Jews are among the 17,000 missing Lebanese people whose fate remains unknown decades after the 15-year war ended, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

The Jewish news agency says they include Isac Sasson, then-president of Lebanon’s Jewish community; doctor Elie Hallak, known for treating people from all religious sects at his Beirut clinic; and Salim Jamous, the Jewish community’s former secretary general. Several others were confirmed killed and their bodies recovered at the time.

Lebanese officials have not announced any breakthrough in discovering the fate of the missing Jews. It's not clear what will be done with their remains if they are found.

“In the end these are Lebanese citizens, and there is a legal process if they want to move them outside the country,” said Bassem El Hout, an attorney representing Lebanon's Jewish community.

Asked about Israel's interest in the disappeared Lebanese Jews, Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office, said, “Israel, as the nation-state of the Jewish people, has a profound and enduring responsibility to Jews throughout the world" which “does not end at Israel’s borders, nor does it end with death.”

A small community remains

Judaism is still one of Lebanon’s 18 officially-recognized religious sects, but only a handful of Jews remain. El Hout said no one knows the exact number. Abadie estimated that about 20 Jews are scattered across the country.

“Not all of them profess publicly about their Jewish religion, except for maybe to close friends and neighbors," he said.

On voting lists of Lebanese citizens, about 4,000 Jews are still listed in Beirut and about 1,000 in the southern port city of Sidon, but many are likely living abroad.

El Hout said there are five remaining synagogues in Lebanon, the oldest of which is in Sidon.

A sign reading “the Jewish quarter” still stands in the narrow alleyways of Sidon’s old quarter, where the synagogue and some Jewish-owned homes are shuttered.

Taleb Kara Ahmed, who wrote several books about the city's Jewish community, said many left to Latin America before Israel’s 1982 invasion of Lebanon. When Israeli troops withdrew from Sidon in 1985, the last Jews left with them, taking copies of the Torah from the city’s synagogue, he said.

The current head of Lebanon's Jewish community, Samo Behar, declined to be interviewed or to give The Associated Press permission to film inside the shuttered century-old Maghen Abraham Synagogue in Beirut, which was damaged during the civil war and renovated nearly two decades ago.

History left people with complicated identities

Dany Liniado left months after the outbreak of the civil war in 1975. She moved through several countries, including Israel, eventually settling in Mexico, which has a significant Lebanese Jewish diaspora. Many Lebanese Jews settled in the U.S., France and Brazil, as well as in Israel.

Two months after she left Lebanon, her father was detained in Beirut and beaten by gunmen who referred to him as “an Israeli agent,” before a prominent Lebanese politician secured his release and advised him to leave the country.

“When he reached me in Milan, he was not the same person,” Liniado said.

She has no plans to return, even to visit.

“For me, it's too late,” she said.

She cooks Lebanese dishes, listens to Lebanese songs and is proud of her “Lebanese DNA.” But now her identity is complicated. She lived in Israel for six years and also identifies as Israeli. Despite recent negotiations between their governments, the two countries remain officially at war.

“I am a Lebanese Jew but now I am everything. I can be Israeli, I can be French, I can be Mexican. You know what, I am a citizen of the world,” Liniado said by telephone from Mexico City. “I’m a Jewish citizen of the world."

___

Associated Press writer Natalie Melzer contributed to this report from Nahariya, Israel.

News.title: The no-go zones for Christians in India where families are being banished – even in death
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Simla Thappa didn’t go with the men who took her father’s body from the village. By then, she recalls, her family had spent most of the day resisting a crowd that kept making the same demand: "Exhume! Exhume! Exhume!"

Her father, Patiram Thappa, 50, a farmer, died in hospital on 10 August 2023. The family brought him home to Iradah in Kanker district of the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh, and buried him early the next day. They wanted to do it a little later, but their friends had urged them to be quick, Thappa says, because some villagers were conspiring to stop the burial.

It wasn’t long before villagers began arriving, to threaten them. “The entire village came, 200-250 people," she tells The Independent. They wanted the body exhumed and buried outside the village. Because the family had converted to Christianity.

“Burying the body was not an issue because everyone in our tribal community is buried,” Thappa says. “The real reason was our conversion.”

Inside the house, 20-25 people stood confronted the family of four, including Thappa’s minor sister and a brother serving in the Border Security Force paramilitary.

The villagers, she alleges, tried to hit her relatives and some women "misbehaved" with her mother. At about 5pm, after a day of resisting the stream of villagers thronging their house, the family gave in. Not because they were convinced, but because they feared for their safety.

They hired a vehicle and took the body to the nearest town of Kanker. "We were just afraid that the villagers would turn on us and beat or lynch us. So we just took out the body."

open image in gallery Patiram Thappa, 50, was refused burial in his own village in Chhattisgarh ( Supplied )

Thappa, 22, says her family converted to Christianity in 2016, drawn by how people in the local tribal Christian community lived. "It is not like we lived a violent life. But it felt more peaceful."

Her grandfather and other relatives lie in the Iradah graveyard. "It had never happened that a villager was forced to be buried outside the village premises."

She says that at least 19 of the village's 105-110 families are Christian. Two more converts have died since her father passed and both have been buried outside the village. Out of fear, she claims. The Independent hasn’t been able to verify these deaths.

The family went to police and found little help. "There was hardly any support. Otherwise we wouldn’t have had to bury him outside the village,” Thappa says. “He would be lying in peace alongside our other relatives."

Some local officials were present when the body was taken away. A statement by Thappa’s mother, Mangotin Thappa, filed in the Supreme Court, says police wouldn’t allow burial even in the Christian cemetery of Kanker town. So her husband’s body was instead buried on the Dudh river bank, some 15km away.

The Independent contacted the Kanker police for comment but did not receive a response.

open image in gallery In 2025, the body of Chaitibai, a Christian tribal woman, was exhumed from the Kurutola village graveyard where her had been buried for generations in Kanker district of Chhattisgarh ( Supplied )

The plight of the Thappa family is illustrative of the growing persecution of religious minorities under the rule of Narendra Modi’s BJP party, a critical component of a sprawling Hindu nationalist ecosystem. India Hate Lab, a project of the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, Washington, recorded more than 1,300 in-person hate speech events against religious minorities across India in 2025, almost all targeting Muslims but over 160 involving Christians as well.

Muslims make up 14.2 per cent of India’s population and Christians 2.3 per cent, according to the latest census conducted in 2011. Hindus form a dominant majority of about 80 per cent.

Thappa’s mother is one of the petitioners in a Supreme Court case brought by the Chhattisgarh Association for Justice and Equality, an advocacy group focused on human rights, civil liberties and environmental justice, that draws on the testimonies of over 140 families stopped by village councils and police from burying their dead in local graveyards. The petition includes references to a February 2024 village council resolution from Takraguda in Bastar that prohibited the burial of non-Hindus on village land.

The petitioners claim police are misusing a 2025 Supreme Court ruling in order to side with village councils and deny Christians dignified burials.

That case involved Ramesh Baghel, whose father, a pastor, died in January 2025 and the body lay in a mortuary for three weeks while the family fought to bury him in Chhindawada, Bastar. The two judges who heard the case differed. Justice BV Nagarathna would have allowed burial on the family's private land in their village. Justice Satish Chandra Sharma ruled that burials must occur in places designated by the village assembly. In the end, the court ordered the pastor laid to rest in a Christian cemetery in Karkapal, about 50 km away from his village.

The petitioners accuse the state of misleading the court in the Baghel case, which they say police cite even where nobody objects to a burial. The state's counsel claimed that Karkapal was 20-25km away from the village, according to the petitioners, even though it was at a distance of 60km and impossible to reach when the monsoon rains flooded the route.

The petitioners also rejected the contention that there was a designated burial ground for Christians outside the village. “There is no such thing" the petition says, citing responses received to freedom of information requests filed in 2025 seeking information on “all the public and private caste, religious and community based graveyard related documents, land, plot details in Bastar”.

The petitioners accuse police of playing a “communal role”, arresting and jailing some 50 pastors in the state for performing last rites.

The Independent contacted Chhattisgarh’s home ministry for comment but did not receive a response.

open image in gallery A crowd of villagers protests to prevent the burial of a Christian convert in Kanker district of Chhattisgarh in December 2025 ( Supplied )

Degree Prasad Chouhan, the association's convener, dates the ongoing pressure campaign against Christians to the 2012 social boycott of non-Hindu places of worship, and that the persecution goes beyond the denial of burials. "Even pastors are disallowed from entering the village.”

And there have been cases, he says, where “the skeletal remains of people buried years ago have been dug up by the villagers and thrown out of the village”, only because they had converted to Christianity.

He argues that the “root cause” of rising animosity against Christians in Chhattisgarh is the “cultural invasion of tribal culture” by Hinduism.

“When a person expresses his faith in any non-Hindu religion and method of worship, he is expelled from the village community by this traditional system,” he says.

“People are evicted from their sources of livelihood, markets, ancestral lands, residences. The dead bodies of their buried relatives are dug out from the graves and thrown outside the boundary of the village.”

On 18 February 2026, Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and NV Anjaria of the Supreme Court ordered that "no further exhumation of buried bodies shall be permitted" till the plea was resolved.

But the dispute isn’t going away.

In July, ETV Bharat reported that Hindu residents of Dhekuna village, in north Bastar, were demanding that the body of a Christian be exhumed and moved to a Christian cemetery elsewhere. This followed a protest over a Christian burial in neighbouring Hatkongera village.

"We are against the burial of a person who had converted to Christianity," village council head Kanchan Lata Salam said at the time after handing over a memorandum with their demand to local officials.

Another villager said people who didn’t follow the traditional faith wouldn’t be allowed burial on village land.

Officials confirmed receiving the memorandum and said they would examine the request and act within the rules.

Nearly three years since her father’s death, Thappa remembers feeling small. “There was a lot of pain and agony."

And all because her family wanted to bid her father goodbye “with due respect and dignity” and bury him “where he belonged”.

News.title: At least 19 dead as sudden downpour triggers stampede at Hindu festival in India
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

At least 19 people have died, and over two dozen are injured after a stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state, officials said on Sunday.

The stampede in the state capital of Kolkata happened on Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga. According to police, some worshippers fell on the road, triggering the stampede.

open image in gallery An injured woman lies inside an ambulance following the stampede ( AP )

Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment.

He said an investigation will be carried out by a special investigation team to be headed by a judge of the state’s High Court into what led to this stampede.

Police detained some pavilion organisers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.

open image in gallery An ambulance carrying Durga Puja Pandal stampede victims stops in front of the emergency building of Calcutta Medical College and Hospital in Kolkata ( AFP/Getty )

Indian prime minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.

Around 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions, known locally as pandals, have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.

Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures.

open image in gallery Police officers inspect the site of a stampede at a Durga Puja festival ( Reuters )

In January of 2025, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering. Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

In 2013, pilgrims attending a Hindu festival at a temple in the central state of Madhya Pradesh panicked amid fears that a bridge would collapse. At least 115 people were crushed to death or drowned in the river below.

Additional reporting by agencies.

News.title: Louise O’Neill: Why I went on 100 dates in a year – and what it taught me about turning 40
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When the writer Louise O’Neill was about to turn 38, her five-year relationship fell apart. A few months earlier, she’d been picking out pink tiles to renovate the bathroom of the home she and her partner had bought together in a coastal town in Wicklow, Ireland. Now she was moving back in with her parents, beset by a tidal wave of emotions that will be all too familiar to any woman in her thirties overwhelmed at the prospect of starting again.

“I instantly felt this panic, like ‘Oh my God, I have to get my eggs frozen, I have to get straight back on the dating apps, I should be engaged and pregnant by my 39th birthday if I rush,” O’Neill, now 41, tells me. And so she started planning out hypothetical timelines, ones that might fast track her life in the direction she’d always imagined: falling in love, getting married, having children.

Then she paused. “I just had this moment of going: ‘But is that what I actually want?’” she says. It might seem like a small question – but it’s one that many of us fail to ask ourselves before launching headfirst into our attempts to tick off the milestones of adulthood. If, she wondered, “I’m standing here and my life has fallen apart and I have to rebuild anyway”, then “surely this is the perfect time for me to take stock and put time and thought and consideration into what I actually want the next iteration of my life to look like”?

Her first realisation? That she “just wanted to have some fun”. That epiphany catalysed an odyssey of self-discovery, which would eventually form the basis of her eighth book, A Bigger Life. Her novels – including 2015’s Asking For It, which grappled with rape culture and victim-blaming – have been bestsellers, but this marks her first foray into writing memoir. “My first and my last memoir,” she laughs. “If you see me out in these streets with another memoir, I give you permission to be like, ‘no, what are you doing?’”

After a stint at a Thai wellness retreat, O’Neill travelled to Paris, London, New York and Rome, diving into the dating pool of each city by arranging near-nightly first dates – mainly using Hinge, sometimes the more exclusive Raya. All of this while working on a novel, too.

If you’re filled with app-induced ennui, such a scenario might seem like a unique form of hell. But O’Neill is an easy conversationalist with a knack for cutting through small talk – vital skills to have in the arsenal when embarking on more than 100 first dates in a year. “People would often say: did you ever get tired of dating? And I would say ‘no’, because firstly I was so curious about the person I was about to meet, but also I was really making time in my day for things that brought me joy. I went to the theatre, I went to museums, I went to galleries.”

open image in gallery After her break-up, O’Neill embarked on a dating odyssey that took her around the world ( Anna Groniecka )

She also set aside the criteria that past versions of herself might have become hung up on, instead going into each encounter with genuine curiosity, rather than any expectations. “I think if I was very much specifically looking for a husband, I would have had a very clear checklist,” she says. “Whereas I was dating men from 27 to 56. They had all sorts of jobs and came from all kinds of backgrounds.”

A Bigger Life chronicles all those dates. There’s the longevity-obsessed billionaire who offers to start looking for properties in West Cork immediately after their first rendezvous. The Irish guy who is disconcertingly open about his habit of wetting himself after a big night out. All the French men fixated upon showing her the best view of the Eiffel Tower. But it is also the story of O’Neill “reclaiming my power” and “prioritising my pleasure, my desires and what it was that I actually wanted”. If the conventional life milestones weren’t going to happen for her, she says, she “didn’t want to waste time waiting around and saying my life can only begin when I have met the right person or when I have ticked off those markers. I wanted my life to be fun. I wanted my life to feel fulfilling, so that if I met someone, it would be that they were adding to it rather than me being reliant on them”.

Essentially, A Bigger Life is “the book that I needed to read when I was in the depths of despair after my break-up”. It is frank, funny and a much-needed corrective to the pessimism that has permeated so much of modern dating discourse – no wonder it has been branded an Eat, Pray, Love for the Hinge generation. And O’Neill’s dedication to chasing and interrogating her own desires – “women have not traditionally been taught that it’s OK for us to want things”, she says – means some have likened it to a millennial version of All Fours, Miranda July’s bracing midlife novel.

Since A Bigger Life was released last month, she’s been inundated with responses from readers struck by its candour, or by the parallels with their own lives; I’m usually precious about keeping books unmarked, but my copy is already adorned by the fluorescent stripes of highlighter pens, dog-eared corners and tiny annotations. “To hear from women who are in a similar position, or even just feeling dissatisfied with their lives, if they’ve read it and it’s given them hope, that’s been really exciting,” O’Neill says.

open image in gallery ‘A Bigger Life’ is the book O’Neill ‘needed to read when I was in the depths of despair’ ( HQ )

The messages, she adds, tend to fall into one of two camps. “One is, ‘do you think I should leave my husband?’ I can’t make that decision. And the other one is, ‘I spent all of my therapy session today talking about this book.’ I’m like, that is just crazy.”

O’Neill has always kept diaries, and ended up consulting her reflections on each of these encounters when she started work on A Bigger Life. It was striking just how quickly she managed to shake off the sense of scarcity and panic that underpinned her initial worries about returning to dating in her late thirties. “I think it’s so easy for women to fall into that scarcity mindset – it’s a very clever trick that’s played on us,” she says.

We’re taught to believe, whether from pop culture narratives, snide comments or social media handwringing, “that once you hit 35 or 40, you may as well be dead, there’s no one on the apps, and you’ll just be ignored”. But this is just “scaring women into settling for less than they deserve and less than what they actually want”.

When her relationship was floundering, the fear of what might await her on the dating scene kept her frozen by inaction, she admits. “There were times in my relationship where I was like, ‘I just don’t feel happy and I don’t think this is the right thing.’ But I was too afraid to move or leave because I felt like there was going to be nothing else out there. Once I started dating, it was really interesting to see how it challenged the scarcity mindset that I had, because I kept meeting really nice, interesting, fun, sexy, decent men.”

I think it’s so easy for women to fall into that scarcity mindset – it’s a very clever trick that’s played on us Louise O’Neill

The “idea of time”, she reckons, “has really been used to browbeat [women] a bit. If you meet a man at 35, he does not feel panicked or under time pressure in the same way that a woman at the age of 35 will do”. Part of this is because we’ve “been subjected to a lot of fear-mongering, particularly around the idea of the biological clock”. Of course, a woman’s ability to have a child is significantly impacted by age, but it’s far more nuanced than chatter about how fertility supposedly “drops off a cliff” at 35 might suggest.

Her standards, she says, “have been raised throughout this dating process”, because the men she met “were not only able to meet my standards, but often would exceed them”. O’Neill sense of optimism feels particularly powerful against the prevailing wind of hetero-pessimism, and the almost performative despair about modern romance that infiltrates first our algorithms, then our own outlook.

“There are billions of people on this planet, and the fact that so many of us have come to believe that it is impossible for us to meet just one person that we could connect with, fall in love with and build a life with, I find that so sad,” she says, “and I think I really wanted to challenge that in myself.”

open image in gallery Her experiment, she says, ended up raising her dating standards ( Anna Groniecka )

This optimism, she reckons, doesn’t require being “blind to misogyny or sexism or rape culture”, topics she’s written about extensively, but the bleakness of the world, she says, makes it important to “hold on to hope and hold on to trust that people are inherently good – genuinely, once I started doing that, the way in which my dating life opened up was incredible”.

And if we become consumed by negativity when it comes to the state of romance, she argues in A Bigger Life, there’s a risk that we may go into each encounter “still bleeding from our old wounds”, and that we shrink from potential connection in the interests of self-preservation, or “protecting our peace”.

Towards the end of her book, O’Neill turns 40 and receives a letter from her cousin, who is 17 years her junior; in it, her cousin writes movingly about what she has learned from watching O’Neill deal with the ups and downs of the previous few years. It reminded the author that living life on her own terms hasn’t just been important for her own sake, but to show other, younger women that “there are other ways of living, of ageing, of thriving”.

“I look at her coming up behind me, and I want her to be excited to turn 40,” she says. “I want her to look at me and be like, ‘oh my God, 40 looks so cool, 40 looks fun. Forty looks like it’s full of adventure and hope.’ I want her to live the biggest life that she possibly can, and I can’t say that to her unless I’m doing the same thing.”

A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill (HQ, £20) is out now

News.title: Lesley Manville: ‘My first screen kiss was in a cowshed. I’ve had better since then’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When Lesley Manville was 23, she met Mike Leigh – and her future immediately came into focus. Just three years before, she’d been a soap star, appearing on Emmerdale as teenager Rosemary Kendall, but she decided to branch out to see what other roles she could find. “I wanted to be a character actor,” Manville tells me, ensconced in a cosy screening room at Chiswick Cinema. Well, mission very much accomplished. Through Leigh – a defining British filmmaker known for his realistic portrayals of working-class life – she was granted the chance to play roles she never dreamed possible. “Age 16 to 23 was fine, but it didn’t enter my head to play characters; I just played me and I was doing alright. But once I met Mike and we started working together, I loved it.”

Manville has worked with Leigh on eight films in total – more than any other actor – but this just scrapes the surface of a vibrant career that’s traversed stage and screen, big and small, with the actor always bringing a commanding, lived-in aura to her roles, be they icy, fragile, menacing or warm-hearted.

She is a prolific theatre star too: she originated Caryl Churchill and Andrea Dunbar roles in the 1980s, and starred in, among other productions, Ghosts, Long Day’s Journey Into Night and Oedipus. For the latter – her Broadway debut – she won a prestigious Tony Award. To mark the release of her new film, the thriller Winter of the Crow, we’re here to talk about all aspects of her career for interview series Life in Pictures – cutting her teeth on stage, through to her defining working relationships, being headhunted for Phantom Thread by Hollywood maestro Paul Thomas Anderson, her Oscars experience and the TV role she gets stopped for the most. You can watch the full interview here.

Lesley Manville on… starting out on Emmerdale in the 1980s

“It was Emmerdale Farm then. It was on twice-weekly at lunchtime. We shot the exteriors on the same kind of film that Paul Thomas Anderson would use to shoot Phantom Thread. I learnt so much about filming with a single camera. This was a great, great time for me. It was my first time living away from my home in Brighton – and I made some money! It allowed me, aged 19, to get my first flat, and that is not to be sniffed at. When I left, I remember they all said, ‘Why are you going? It’s so hard out there.’ But I knew I had to move on. I had lots more parts to play. It was a really good job. I had my first screen kiss… in a cowshed. I’ve had better screen kisses since then, obviously.”

open image in gallery Lesley Manville in 'Emmerdale' ( ITV )

On... her early theatre work

“My relationship with the Royal Court started from a Mike Leigh film for television that I made called Grown-ups when I was 23. It went out on the BBC and the next day, I was this new actress on the block, even though I’d been working since I was 16. I was at the Royal Court for a while. I did the original Top Girls. The original Rita Sue and Bob Too (both 1982). It was just an amazing time. It’s where I met Gary [Oldman, who she was married to from 1987 to 1989]. Everything was great at the Royal Court. You felt like you were at the cutting edge of things. Over about 12, 13 years, I did about 10 plays there, and now I think how lucky I was. Any young actor who would be able to mirror that situation now would be very lucky.”

open image in gallery Lesley Manville performing 'Serious Money' at Royal Court in 1987 ( Shutterstock )

On... working with Mike Leigh eight times

“I owe it all to him. Everything. I honestly don’t know where I’d be if I hadn’t met him. He liberated me to play characters that weren’t like me. You create a character one-to-one with him for months, then he’ll start to get you involved with other people, and then the improvisations start. You’ll do them in real time – for example, with the barbecue in Another Year (2010), we did a real-time improvisation of that at an afternoon party for five hours. And then it gets distilled into a scene. I’ve done big parts with him, small parts, as do all of his repertoire of actors. But he’s going to get you to play a character that you’ve never played before. I can’t express enough what I owe him.”

open image in gallery Mike Leigh has worked with Lesley Manville more than any other actor ( Getty )

On... working in Hollywood for the 2014 film Maleficent

“You get paid more and the catering’s better! Maleficent was the early days of motion capture. We had to wear what you’d wear for deep-sea diving, except it would have hundreds of cameras on it. You’d wear a helmet with two antennae cameras in your face, and cameras strapped to your body. Imelda Staunton, Juno Temple and I played pixies and we had the Cirque de Soleil people harnessing us up. We were quite literally flying around the studio at Pinewood! We had to do intensive pilates training to get ready for it. It was great fun. When we did Maleficent: Mistress of Evil, which was quite some years later, the technology had come on so far, we did it all with a grey T-shirt, no makeup and like 500 cameras in a semicircle all the way around us. We were on the first film for ages; the second film, I think we did in three afternoons. I wouldn’t like to do a whole big shoot that’s all green screen. I’m not that kind of girl.”

open image in gallery Imelda Staunton and Lesley Manville playing pixies in 2014 film 'Maleficent' ( Disney )

On... being chosen by Paul Thomas Anderson to star opposite Daniel Day-Lewis in Phantom Thread

“The big one. In 2016, my agent said, ‘Paul Thomas Anderson’s gonna call you tomorrow morning at 11am to talk about a film he’s got in his head.’ And I thought, ‘Well, OK. Wow. I bet he’ll forget.’ On the dot, he calls and says, ‘I've got this film. It’s you and Daniel Day-Lewis. You’d be brother and sister, and you run this fashion house, and it’s the Fifties.’ And in my heart, ‘I’m just going, ‘Please, please, please tell me this is mine!’ Because fashion has been a thing all my life.

“I’ll never forget, he said, ‘Give the script a read when you’ve got a minute.’ As if I wasn’t gonna tear through it. He called me back and said, ‘Look, Daniel and I are coming to London in a couple of months, so maybe we can meet up.’ I didn’t know if it was mine. Then I get an email from PTA over the weekend, and he went, ‘Oh sorry, I forgot to say – it’s yours.’ Little detail! So then we started shooting – it was 14 of the most heavenly work weeks of my life. The whole job was something else. I’m not superstitious but six has been a recurring number in my life, and the script that PTA first sent me was dated 6/6/2016. I’ve still got it. It’s gonna be archived by the V&A.”

open image in gallery Daniel Day-Lewis and Lesley Manville in Paul Thomas Anderson’s 'Phantom Thread' ( Universal Pictures )

On... attending the Oscars as a nominee for Phantom Thread

“I’d never been before. At the end of the ceremony, you’ve been there for five hours and you’re hungry, and it’s a lot of small talk, you know. Nice, but a lot of small talk. I said, ‘What are we gonna do? What’s the Vanity Fair party like?’ And PTA said, ‘It’ll be just like this, but with more models.’ So we did a great thing – me, him, Maya [Rudolph, PTA’s wife] and Jonny [Greenwood, of Radiohead] went to a quiet cocktail room in a hotel, and we had omelettes and cocktails. It was the best end to the night. And at midnight LA time – which is 8am the following morning in the UK – I had to go on the Today programme, so I had to be sober. I thought, ‘I absolutely can’t be drunk as a skunk on live radio!’”

On... BBC series Mum, which ran from 2016 to 2019

“What a beautiful job that was – and it’s the thing I get stopped for the most. If I’m at the National Theatre or the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, it’ll be a play, but on the street, on the train, it’s Mum. It was so sublime. Obviously, I get to meet and work with so many different people, and you can’t keep all of them in your contacts list, but very unusually, there were eight principal actors in Mum, and we are all close. I mean, Peter Mullan! I don’t think he’ll mind me saying this, but I think he was nervous doing Mum because he usually plays characters who’re going to, you know, scoop your eyes out. But Peter is the most gentle, warm, loving human being. It was nice to see that natural side of him come out in this. Everyone asks if we’re gonna do any more and I say no because [creator] Stefan Golaszewski intended it as three seasons. That’s what I always saw in my head. It’s beautifully timed – of course you wouldn’t do it again!”

open image in gallery Lesley Manville and Peter Mullan in the BBC series 'Mum' ( BBC )

On… playing Princess Margaret in The Crown

“This was an amazing job. Imelda [Staunton] and I were cast two years before, so I used to wake up every morning thinking ‘I’m gonna play Princess Margaret!’, which was so exciting. And for two years, I could research really leisurely. And working with Imelda – we’d been pixies together! Maleficent was our research, really. I knew it wasn’t gonna be 20 episodes about Princess Margaret, but boy oh boy did Peter Morgan write me two amazing episodes. Astonishing. I felt for Margaret deeply. I felt the pain of somebody trapped in a circumstance and wanting to be something, but not quite having the freedom to be that person. I loved playing her – I had a cigarette holder, a silk dressing gown and a fabulous wig. It was win-win.”

open image in gallery Lesley Manville played Princess Margaret in the final two seasons of 'The Crown' ( Netflix )

On… how she chooses roles

“All I want is to play a cleaning lady in Mrs Harris Goes to Paris [2022] and then Princess Margaret – two ends of the social spectrum. You couldn’t get further away. That’s what gets me up in the morning. I don’t want people to think, ‘Oh, that’s alright for you to say, Lesley. You get those opportunities.’ I’m grateful and humble about that. But that’s my modus operandi.”

On… remaining in the UK

“I never considered moving to America. I didn’t think I would do it as a goal. Why would I do that when I was doing the best work that was on offer to anybody, anywhere? I do think we do the best theatre in the world – and I was doing it at the Royal Shakespeare Company, the National Theatre, the Royal Court, occasionally the West End, working with Mike Leigh, Max Stafford-Clark, Richard Eyre, Nick Hytner, Sam Mendes, Marianne Elliott. I mean, the list goes on and on and on. Why would I go to America?”

On… going viral for saying people shouldn’t take photos in theatres

“Lots of other actresses are doing it now. The thing is, I’m not saying it wouldn’t be all right at the end of any production, but it felt particularly wrong or inappropriate at the end of Oedipus [Robert Icke’s 2024 West End production that she starred in]. You know how it ends! It’s pretty devastating. And most of the audience were sitting there just going, ‘I don’t know what I’ve just watched.’ And then you get these other people who just think, ‘I've gotta capture this on camera.’ Cate Blanchett was going on about it recently because somebody was filming her in Electra/Persona and at the end of the show, she quite rightly said, ‘Look, you’re spoiling it for people who haven’t seen the show yet.’ I feel I’m fighting a losing battle, but I don’t feel I can’t say anything.”

open image in gallery Lesley Manville in new film 'Winter of the Crow' ( Signature Entertainment )

On… being a national treasure

“It’s not for me to say. All I want is for people to like my work, see what I’m trying to do – not just in each individual performance – but acknowledge that I’m trying to do characters that are different and keep it alive for myself, apart from anything. I think I’m just Lesley Manville!”

‘Winter of the Crow’ is in cinemas now

News.title: Japan to launch spacecraft on a mission to get samples from a Martian moon
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Japan is set to launch a spacecraft on the world's first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars.

Scientists hope the mission, which is expected to take five years, will provide clues to how Phobos and its smaller sibling Deimos formed, and hopefully even shed light on the origins of life in the solar system.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s launch of the spacecraft Tuesday on a new Japanese mainstay H-3 rocket comes as the United States, China and others consider sending astronauts to Mars.

Samples from Phobos will provide useful data for scientists to consider using a Martian moon as a base for a future manned mission to the planet, said MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu.

“Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated," Kawakatsu said. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system."

Japan leads the international mission that includes equipment and communications support from NASA and other national space agencies.

JAXA aims to study how Mars' moons formed

Since the 1960s, dozens of missions have been sent to Mars, but its moons largely remain a mystery. Phobos and Deimos take their names from the Greek mythological personifications of fear and terror, sons of the war god Ares, whose Roman counterpart is Mars.

Multiple Russian attempts to land on Phobos, including one in 2011, have failed.

A key question will be how they formed and what they are made of. Some scientists think the two irregular crater-pocked bodies could be remnants of debris formed after a large celestial object crashed into Mars. Others say the moons could be asteroids that have come from elsewhere.

JAXA officials think samples from Phobos will provide answers.

“We can almost certainly come to a conclusion by analyzing (Phobos) soil samples," MMX principal investigator Kiyoshi Kuramoto said.

Scientists chose to collect samples from Phobos mainly because the moon is closer to Mars than Deimos and therefore may have more information about the planet. Material from Mars is expected to make up about 0.1% of the material collected from Phobos, JAXA officials say.

Phobos, about 20 to 30 kilometers (10 to 20 miles) in diameter, orbits Mars at a distance of about 6,000 kilometers (3,700 miles) three times a day.

Samples from Phobos could also shed light on the origin of Deimos as the two moons are believed to have similar roots, Kuramoto said. The mission also includes plans to fly by Deimos and collect observations.

MMX will spend 3 years studying Phobos

It will be a long journey to reach the red planet, 55 million kilometers (34 million miles) away from Earth at their closest point.

After launching on the H3 rocket, the spacecraft will arrive at the Mars region a year later. Then it will fly near and around Phobos for three years to collect data and gather samples from the moon before returning home in 2031.

MMX is made up of three modules — for propulsion, exploration and return — and weighs about 5 tons. Only the third module will return home, with the samples stored in a capsule.

The spacecraft will carry 13 instruments, including a rover jointly developed by France and Germany that will land on the moon, as well as a NASA sampling device and instrument to measure gamma rays, and the European Space Agency's deep space communication device. A Japanese radiation monitor will collect data that can help a future manned Mars exploration.

The mission will collect moon samples from Phobos

The French-German rover Idefix lands on Phobos first. During a 100-day mission in around 2029, it will explore the surface of the moon to help the subsequent Japanese soil-sampling.

Once the MMX lands some time later, JAXA scientists aim to collect at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of soil from the moon from two sampling attempts using U.S. and Japanese methods.

NASA's sampling device uses pressurized gas to lift surface dust into a container, and JAXA's coring method will collect samples from a depth of about 2 centimeters (less than 1 inch).

In the first attempt, the MMX will collect surface and underground samples using both devices, and take additional underground samples in the second landing.

Scientists say collecting samples from multiple locations increases the chances of obtaining any potential traces of past microbial life from Mars.

The samples will be stored in a heat-protected capsule designed to survive reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. It’s expected to land in Australia before being sent back to Japan.

Japan’s two Hayabusa missions returned asteroid samples, the first in 2010 and again in 2020.

The moon's extremely low gravity is a challenge

The spacecraft has to choose a relatively smooth and level site for its landing based on topographical data provided by the rover, and then collect samples within two hours.

Landing on the pockmarked moon, which has just one two-thousandth of Earth's gravity, is a challenge.

To minimize bouncing at touchdown, the MMX's exploration module is equipped with four-legged landing gear with shock absorption features.

The rover has wheels that can get traction in low gravity, right itself if it tips over, and move “at a snail's pace," JAXA said.

News.title: Truck drives through soccer field during game in Kansas, killing 2 and hospitalizing 11
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A woman drove a truck through a soccer field during a youth game in Kansas on Saturday, killing two people and sending 11 other victims to the hospital, authorities said.

A 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man were killed, Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said. The ages of the injured people ranged from 5 to 68.

Moses said the driver, a 34-year-old, was in custody. He did not say whether authorities believe it was intentional.

“We are still working to determine how this happened and why this happened,” he said.

Two children were also in the truck, Moses said.

Police Chief Joe Sullivan said that immediately after the incident, and before first responders arrived at the scene, people “sprang into action” to provide lifesaving assistance to the victims.

“It was truly amazing,” Sullivan said. “But I think it's indicative of the Wichita community.”

Authorities said there was no further public threat.

Mayor Lily Wu advised people to avoid the area during the investigation and said the news was heartbreaking.

“My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved,” she said via Facebook.

News.title: Ruthless Daniel Dubois dispatches Fabio Wardley in just two rounds
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley.

When Wardley dragged himself out of the ring at Manchester’s Co-Op LIVE Arena, the physical damage was obvious, but the psychological sting was far deeper. Wardley had Dubois severely hurt early on, flooring the Londoner twice and teetering on the verge of a career-defining stoppage. Instead, he let the knockout slip away, allowed Dubois to find his rhythm, and was ultimately broken down and halted in the 11th round - surrendering his WBO heavyweight belt in a dramatic comeback victory.

Now, just five months after that gruelling night, the two heavyweights meet again at London’s O2 Arena in an immediate rematch that carries potentially massive implications for the entire division.

For Wardley (20-1-1, 19 KOs), the decision to trigger his rematch clause was instant. Dismissing concerns over the severe punishment he absorbed down the stretch, the Ipswich man is motivated entirely by redemption and the belief that his early success proved Dubois is beatable.

Dubois (23-3, 22 KOs), however, views things very differently. Entering as The Ring’s No. 1 heavyweight contender and a proven two-time world champion, Dubois has brushed off Wardley’s power, claiming his rival “punches like a baby” and insists Wardley threw away his one and only chance at glory in Manchester.

With Oleksandr Usyk approaching the final chapter of his career and the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury blockbuster looming just eight weeks away, this London clash is far more than a personal grudge match. The winner won’t just walk away with the WBO strap; they will stake an undeniable claim as the torch-bearer for the heavyweight division’s next era if they can land another title fight in short order.

News.title: Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working
News.content:
Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

News.title: Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card
News.content:
Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

News.title: Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury
News.content:
This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

News.title: Wallabies humiliated in ‘unacceptable’ thrashing by New Zealand
News.content:
New Zealand blew Australia off the field in an extraordinary first-half display in Sydney as they claimed a 13th successive win against the Wallabies and completed a 2-0 Bledisloe Cup clean sweep.

The annual series had already gone New Zealand’s way for a 24th successive year at Eden Park last weekend, but Australia did enough in a highly competitive first half in Auckland to suggest they could give the All Blacks a game on their home turf. And in a breathless opening six minutes in Sydney, it looked as if they might.

The ball-in-play time during that opening spell was incredible as both teams committed to fast, attacking rugby, offloading from everywhere. Like two heavyweights going toe-to-toe in the opening round of a boxing contest, throwing haymakers to see who would get knocked out first.

Ryan Lonergan produced an excellent turnover for the Wallabies to trigger an Australia counter, and the irrepressible Peter Lakai responded with one for the visitors, as the ball travelled from one end of the pitch to the other in one long unbroken spell.

But after New Zealand wing Josh Moorby finally crossed the whitewash, it was Australia who found themselves out on their feet, punch drunk.

News.title: England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes in tatters after Tonga defeat
News.content:
McDermott was full of credit. “They’re a big team, a strong team,” he said. “They’ve got some tremendous players in there, and I thought we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game.

“They scored some tries through kicks, which are always hard to defend, and then towards the back-end of the game we made some errors chasing the scoreboard.”

It should be factored in that this was McDermott’s first match in charge and strides have clearly been made since England were woeful in losing the Ashes 3-0 last year.

“I thought we opened up Tonga in that first 20,” McDermott added. “Whether we went through the middle or the edge, we found ourselves in a good ball position, but we had some scrappy finishes to the good ball sets. It was too erratic. We wanted to put a load of fatigue into Tonga, but credit to them. I thought they were terrific defensively.”

Having been beaten by Samoa in the World Cup four years ago, England must face up to the burgeoning conviction that they are no longer among the top three countries in international rugby league. There was the palpable sense of the old order being changed in a stadium packed with the red shirts of Tonga.

As Williams said in the build-up, this is a “mad” format, with only the top two from the combined six-team group of Pool B and C going through to the semi-finals, but now it is very simple as far as England are concerned. They must beat France and Papua New Guinea in their remaining two matches, and do so heavily, then pray that Tonga can beat Samoa in the last match of the pool stage. However, Samoa thumped France 78-4 on Friday, so even that potential avenue appears blocked. McDermott has no other option but to look ahead.

“We know what’s in front of us now, we’ve got to win the next two games and improve on the things we need to improve on,” he said. “But I’ve seen enough tonight that is telling me we’re heading in the right direction.

“It would be tremendously disrespectful to either France or PNG to suggest we’re going to rack up points. I can start looking at points difference and start working out our strategies, but the road will lead us back to winning those two games, and winning them in a strong way.”
