Andrews' No 5 jersey was laid on the pitch as his full name, Hyron Diego Andrews, appeared on the stadium's big screen. Several Lions players were visibly tearful, with team-mates embracing one another and others standing with their heads tilted back and eyes closed during the emotional tribute.

La Rochelle went on to claim a 31-14 victory, with tries from Tevita Ofa (17), Oscar Jegou (30), Davit Niniashvili (39), Tolu Latu (61) and Avakuki Niusalelekitoga (76).

Sports.title: Kiltie double helps Kilmarnock beat fellow-strugglers Motherwell
Sports.content:
Greg Kiltie scored twice to lift Kilmarnock off the bottom of the Scottish Premiership with a 3-2 victory over Motherwell.

Kiltie struck first and last as Neil McCann's side inflicted a fifth consecutive defeat on the Steelmen, who join Killie in the bottom three, one point off bottom-placed Hibernian.

Motherwell had a dominant spell after recovering from Kiltie's second-minute opener and goals from Alex Lowry and Seb Palmer-Houlden turned the game on its head.

But Tyreece John-Jules soon equalised and Motherwell were cut open before Kiltie knocked home a 69th-minute winner.

Given their run, Motherwell fans would have feared the worst when their team gifted Kilmarnock a goal with little over 60 seconds on the clock.

Goalkeeper Alex Paulsen misplaced a short pass into central midfield and Kiltie ultimately converted after some desperate defending.

Worse almost followed several moments later when Well centre-back Martin Moorman lost possession midway inside his own half, but Joe Hugill dragged his shot wide.

But the visitors levelled in the 17th minute when Lukas Fadinger sent Emmanual Longelo down the left wing. Calum Ferrie made a great stop after Palmer-Houlden got on the end of the left-back's low cross but Lowry kept his composure to fire the rebound into the bottom corner.

Motherwell took control as Killie struggled to keep possession inside their own half. Maswanshise hit the post from 25 yards and scuffed a decent chance wide, and Ibrahim Said forced a good save from Ferrie.

Neil McCann brought on Jamie Brandon for on-loan Hearts right-back MJ Kamson-Kamara in the 33rd minute in a bid to deal with the twin threat of Longelo and Said. He was forced into another change two minutes later when the injured Bailey Rice went off for Aaron Tshibola.

The hosts improved towards the end of the half. Paulsen got down well to stop a John-Jules drive after Motherwell failed to deal with a long ball and the unmarked Tom Lowery volleyed well over.

Killie were grateful for a VAR intervention after referee Calum Scott sent George Stanger off for a high boot on Lowry. The punishment was downgraded to a yellow card after a trip to the monitor.

Motherwell were soon in front in the 56th minute after a low cross from Said. Palmer-Houlden was denied at close range by Ferrie but the ball ricocheted in off the centre-forward.

The visitors' lead only lasted two minutes. Two Motherwell defenders were barged off the ball as Brandon headed the ball back into the box after a half-cleared corner and John-Jules produced an emphatic finish.

Brandon delivered another assist when his crossfield pass played in Kiltie, who again slotted into the far corner.

Paulsen made saves from substitute Ieuan Owen and Hugill to keep Motherwell in it.

Alfred Johansson's side struggled to create chances though, and Ferrie saved from Johnny Koutroumbis deep in stoppage time when the substitute found himself in a good position.

Johansson bemoans 'low-level' defending

Motherwell manager Alfred Johansson:

"I'm very, very disappointed and frustrated with how we end this game. It's extremely difficult to accept the fact that we lost this game.

"Obviously we make it difficult for ourselves right at the start as well, but that can happen in football, you make a mistake and get punished in that way.

"But we reacted fantastically and the rest of the first half is very, very good. We're pressing together, we're aggressive, we catch them on the break, we create chances.

"They start going long into the strikers with one touch and we just don't defend those long balls well enough.

"I don't think we're winning enough second balls and also, prior to the second goal, for instance, we have the ball under control, but we give it away way too easy.

"We have chances to score more than two goals but we can't rely on scoring three goals away from home. We need to be much more solid. It's just way too low a level, how we defend."

McCann: We showed spirit and character

Kilmarnock boss Neil McCann:

"I talk about the spirit that I've got in that dressing room now.

"I talk about the character, with a group of boys that have taken a wee bit of time to come together, and I thought second half we were absolutely brilliant.

"We had a couple of wee things that we tinkered with, in terms of where we wanted to get at Motherwell.

But, tactics aside, that was just about them saying, 'no, we're going to get ourselves back in that game, and we look to go and try and win it'."

What the result means and next fixtures...

Sports.title: Hits & Misses: Liverpool clicking and Chelsea get serious
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Brentford and Liverpool.

Liverpool spent close to £400m on Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. Against Brentford, there was evidence that expensively-assembled attack might finally be clicking.

Isak was on the fringes of the game for long periods, limited to only 16 touches by the dogged hosts. But his brilliantly-taken goal, controlled and rifled home with dizzying speed in the second half, was a reminder of just how deadly he can be at his best.

It took him to five goals for the season. Only Erling Haaland has scored more in the Premier League. He is putting a difficult first season behind him and Andoni Iraola will be encouraged that it was Barcola who provided the assist.

The France international came into the game off the back of scoring a hat-trick against LASK in midweek and while he couldn't find the net against Brentford, missing a golden opportunity in the first half and hitting the bar in the second, Iraola liked what he saw.

"I love that he's having so many chances and being in those situations," said the Liverpool boss.

Then there was Wirtz, who provided the assist for Victor Munoz with a perfectly-weighted through-ball.

It was one of nine chances created - the joint-most by any Liverpool player in a single game since Opta started taking records in 2003/04.

Nick Wright

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Everton and Chelsea.

Chelsea have the best front three in the Premier League but attack being the best form of defence for Xabi Alonso was never going to be sustainable. No team had conceded more goals than Chelsea's 13 after six Premier League matches.

But, in Saturday's 2-0 victory at Everton, they showed a different side to their game. Remarkably, this was not only Alonso's first clean sheet in the league since his appointment but also Chelsea's first clean sheet in the league for nine months.

Defensively, Chelsea have been a liability for some time. Alonso must fix that if his team are to take the leap and challenge again. The win at Everton was a step in the right direction. In the manager's words, Chelsea produced a "serious" and "mature" performance.

These are the characteristics that will differentiate Chelsea from most of the chasing pack in a Premier League season where seriousness is sorely lacking among some of the so-called 'Big Six'. Alonso, clearly, is a serious manager.

Zinny Boswell

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Manchester City and Ipswich Town.

Lauding Erling Haaland's goalscoring prowess is clearly not a hot take. It's barely even news. But he is outdoing even his own outlandish standards so far this season.

Twelve goals across all competitions; four just this week, including two in Man City's most recent victory over Ipswich.

Haaland is a symbol of City's immense wealth in a myriad of ways. He's a wealth of talent, leadership and obviously goals.

But he also represents the riches of a club transformed beyond recognition since its Abu Dhabi takeover. The very thing under intense investigation by the Premier League.

Haaland too hot to handle Erling Haaland has now netted 100 non-penalty goals in the Premier League, reaching this milestone in fewer appearances than any other player (139).

Haaland is indeed a complete luxury. A high-end sports car with all the optional extras. Everything about him is premium. There is every chance he will go on to be the most ruthless striker the Premier League has ever seen.

And yet, many will still come to view this era of Manchester City through a different lens - no matter the outcome of the club's ongoing appeal process. Too much has already been aired.

It's a shame Haaland's immense gift cannot be celebrated for what it is in its truest form. Perhaps in the future it will be again. Because he really is a different breed of scorer.

Laura Hunter

In patches, Newcastle's performance against Aston Villa epitomised the heavy-metal, high-pressing football that defines Mattihas Jaissle's school of Red Bull philosophy. When executed well, it's high-octane and overwhelming for an opponent.

But Newcastle's approach at times seemed to be all-out chaos, planned or otherwise. The Premier League is defined by its physicality, but two yellow cards at the same time for Joelinton and Sven Botman tackles is not something we see often. The latter should also have been sent off.

The Magpies were continuously exposed by Aston Villa's transition and counter, especially in the first half, and the chaos only continued when Dan Burn came on late on as a No 9. You are only using a centre-back up front when you are desperate for a goal or rotating because you have too many. This fell into the former camp.

Amid all this, Newcastle had just one shot on target in the whole game and set a new record for goals conceded in consecutive matches at home in all competitions (16). There were bright moments, but no sense of real cohesion.

The stats this season show that whatever Jaissle is attempting is not working. A change in system coupled with a new, young squad is only exacerbating things and if the German wants to continue the gung-ho approach, it needs to be harnessed in a far better and more productive way.

Charlotte Marsh

A headline taken from Sky Sports commentator Gary Weaver, who so eloquently epitomised Aston Villa's last few seasons.

It took them seven matches to win a game last term and while it did not take as long this time around, questions were being asked about whether Unai Emery's glorious revolution at Aston Villa was finally beginning to falter.

A summer exodus coupled with an intense season in which they won the Europa League - had it all come to a head?

No such luck.

Emery is a demanding manager. He's known to hold hours-long meetings and high-intensity training sessions to get the best out of his players. That takes time to adapt to, as Tyrone Mings noted in his post-match interview with Sky Sports.

Rebuilding a team is never easy but Emery is starting to find the solutions, as he always does. Aston Villa are now unbeaten in five games and have kept back-to-back clean sheets.

The clocks go back next Sunday - as Weaver predicted, right on time for Aston Villa to start their charge up the Premier League table.

Charlotte Marsh

An ominous stat was provided by Opta during the build-up to Brentford's clash with Liverpool at the Gtech.

"Since their promotion to the top flight in 2021, the Bees have dropped more points from winning positions than any other side in the Premier League (102)."

A surprise, perhaps, given the Bees have taken to the top flight so well and finished in the top half in three of their first five seasons. And one that poses the question: what could have been?

For Brentford fans, that will not bear thinking about.

But that figure increased to 105 on Saturday, as they took the lead against the Reds before falling to a 2-1 defeat in a game they ended with nine men on the pitch.

Without the first of those reds - shown to Yehor Yarmoliuk before half-time, it might have been different. The reality? It's 11 points dropped for the season now, more than any other team in the division.

It has become a horrible habit - and one that needs kicking in to touch by Keith Andrews' men if those European ambitions are to materialise.

Dan Long

Could this be the turning point in Alvaro Arbeloa's Fulham reign?

It is certainly a start. With reports suggesting the Spaniard had two games to save his job, he needed a response and his players delivered one.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Fulham and Hull City.

Fulham played with an intensity and attacking fluency that had been missing during their winless start to the Premier League season.

They registered 10 first-half shots, moved the ball quickly and repeatedly exposed a Hull side who struggled to impose themselves. Alex Iwobi's goal was deserved, but the hosts could easily have won by a greater margin.

There were encouraging signs of an identity taking shape, with the performance even prompting thoughts of 'Arbeloa-ball' at Craven Cottage.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alvaro Arbeloa feels the support from the Fulham owners and believes Joshua King has everything and can become a top, top player.

Yet one result cannot erase the concerns of the opening weeks, and Fulham made the closing stages unnecessarily nervy before Ryan Sessegnon's stoppage-time red card.

The win lifts them out of the relegation zone and gives Arbeloa breathing space.

Whether it proves a turning point depends on what follows. For now, he has bought himself time and shown what his Fulham side can be.

William Bitibiri

Sports.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free.

Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.”

This was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was even an injury-time winner from, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki.

Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.

View image in fullscreen Sunderland fans enjoyed a trip they will remember for ever when they played Torreense Photograph: Paulo Cunha/EPA

The four Premier League clubs involved in the lesser two European competitions play each other on Sunday. Brighton are thriving; the other three are not. Palace were 12th before the weekend fixtures but not playing well. Bournemouth against Sunderland is a battle of third- and fourth-bottom. Whether the Europa League football can yet be blamed is debatable. Brighton surely can’t be bucking the trend just because of the lesser demands of the Conference League. Thursday’s was only the second round of Europa League league games, and the clubs involved bypassed a round of the Carabao Cup; fatigue may come but it shouldn’t be an issue yet.

There are other factors at play. Sunderland have already played Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford, the top four going into this weekend. They could easily have been a couple of goals up by half-time at Brentford. They missed a penalty to go ahead against Arsenal. They registered an xG of 2.72 in losing 5-3 at Manchester City. Only in the defeat to Brighton last weekend have they really disappointed. In the equivalent six games last season (substituting Ipswich for Burnley), Sunderland took only one point; in that sense, they are actually three points better off this campaign.

But that can’t alter the fact that four points from six games leaves them beginning to fret. There is pressure on this next run of fixtures: after Bournemouth, they are home to Leeds, then away to Coventry. Sunderland’s transfer business left a major question on the right of the forward line that has yet to be resolved. A lack of depth in certain areas has been exposed by injuries to Brian Brobbey and Habib Diarra, although both players were on the bench on Thursday.

Bournemouth have also lost key players to injury. Eli Junior Kroupi, who scored 13 league goals last season, has not played this campaign. Neither has Amine Adli, although he came off the bench on Thursday, as did Justin Kluivert, who had been out for a month. Most damagingly of all, perhaps, after impressing for England against Croatia, Alex Scott has been ruled out with a thigh injury.

The transition away from Andoni Iraola was always likely to be disruptive and, while Saturday’s 5-1 defeat at Chelsea was a jolt, their other losses this season were to Manchester City and Liverpool. There has been a sense of margins going against them, of draws that might have been wins. The concern, as with Sunderland, comes if that affects morale, and decent displays that have yielded disappointing results curdle into disappointing performances.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Álvaro Rodríguez scores Bournemouth’s third goal against Sturm Graz, but they have found domestic assignments tougher. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

Palace are in a slightly different position. Other than City, their fixture list has been relatively kind. Seven points from six games would constitute comfortable survival if extrapolated over the season as a whole, but Opta’s expected points table, which has Bournemouth ninth and Sunderland 10th, has them 18th. A new manager is settling in, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Múñoz were sold over the summer, while Jean-Philippe Mateta hasn’t played since the opening weekend.

For none of those three sides can unsettled starts be blamed entirely or even primarily on Europe. That said, the evidence is clear: over the past five years, teams who did not play in Europe the previous season see their league position fall when they do play in Europe: Palace dropped from 12th to 15th, Nottingham Forest from seventh to 16th, Newcastle from fifth to 12th, Brighton from sixth to 11th, West Ham from sixth to seventh. Of those examples, only Forest even came vaguely close to relegation, but the fear nags away.

Although winning the Europa League would bring the vast rewards of Champions League football, losing in the final would probably bring in not much more than £20m for a Premier League club, plus gate receipts and whatever intangible benefits there might be from increased exposure. To put that in context, that’s roughly the difference between finishing ninth and 14th in the Premier League.

Which is to say that while fans revel in trips to Milan, Prague or Lyon, for club executives a few nice mini-breaks do not balance out the potential financial headaches.

Sports.title: Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich
Sports.content:
There have been few winners in Manchester City’s guilty verdict, except highly paid lawyers and the inflatable fruit industry. The fans have suffered, being forced to question everything they have been told, while being labelled “cheats”, but they were able to forget the cacophony of noise around the club as Enzo Maresca became the first Premier League manager to win his first seven games.

Ipswich were the latest victims, but they put up a fight in City’s first home Premier League game since being found to have breached financial rules. Defiance has fortified most of the City fanbase, who were able to see local boy Phil Foden instigate the triumph with a kiss of the badge, before an emblem of their wealth, Erling Haaland, secured the points to move six clear, albeit with a few scares between, courtesy of Daizen Maeda and Zian Flemming.

“I didn’t expect to win seven out of seven, but we are working well,” Maresca said. “This is the most important thing.”

Victory came at a cost as Haaland and Antoine Semenyo limped off at full-time, in addition to Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O’Reilly suffering injuries, although Maresca was left unsure of the severity as City prepare to host AEK Athens on Tuesday.

If City have felt like it has been their backs against the wall for the past few weeks, it was Ipswich’s turn. Gary O’Neil put 11 men behind the ball whenever the hosts ventured over the halfway line as City enjoyed 90% possession in the opening quarter-hour, but without truly threatening as they struggled to find space in the lowest of blocks, expertly organised and fully disciplined.

Maresca had made six changes to refresh the side and it took time to understand one another’s rhythm, with Ayyoub Bouaddi creating it from defensive midfield in another mature performance from the teenager making his first Premier League start.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca has guided Manchester City a record seven-match winning start in the Premier League. Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty Images

It was inevitable what was coming as there was irrefutable evidence that City were dominant. As at Anfield, Jérémy Doku was a key instigator, showing mesmeric skill on the left of the area before finding Foden to sweep home for his first goal since mid-December.

“I know him from years ago, for me he’s one of the best Premier League players,” Maresca said. “Since day one, it’s my duty to help him to be again one of the best players. I’m very happy for his goal and hopefully it can be just the beginning of many goals and many good performances.”

There was an element of pantomime around the ground from the booing of the Premier League anthem, the singalongs and inflatables. It was fitting Marc Guéhi did not know Maeda was behind him, allowing the Ipswich man to latch on to a sublime curved through ball from Abdoul Ouattara and equalise two minutes after the opener.

Quick Guide Manchester City 3-2 Ipswich key facts Show • With Manchester City maintaining their 100% record, Enzo Maresca is the first manager to win his first seven Premier League games in charge of a team. • Manchester City are the third team to win their opening seven games of a Premier League season, after Liverpool in 2019-20 (first 8) and Chelsea in 2005-06 (first 9). • Erling Haaland (pictured) has now scored 100 non-penalty goals in the Premier League, reaching this milestone in fewer appearances than any other player (139). The previous fewest was 150 appearances, by Alan Shearer in 1996. Opta Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

After a missed chance, Haaland showed it is possible to get a better result second time around, making the most of Kovacic becoming an auxiliary winger. The header lacked power, but Christian Walton could not keep it out, palming the ball from one hand to the other and into the net before Haaland was serenaded with the clap of bananas.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City found themselves stuck in a lull, unable to prise open Ipswich, instead having to bide their time. It was a test of patience and a sweeping move upfield concluded with a precision pass from Iliman Ndiaye and an aggressive finish from Haaland, who was later denied a hat-trick by the video assistant referee.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City fans have gone back to more innocent times with their inflatable bananas. Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty Images

Farai Hallam reviewed footage of Guéhi taking out Abdul Fatawu in the area and Flemming did the rest in the 90th minute, as reward for an impressive team performance, leaving O’Neil upset Ipswich departed with nothing.

“They’re an incredible group,” he said. “Players giving everything. It’s a privilege to stand there and represent them because they’re an incredible group.”

City were left to complain about a Premier League official’s decision when 12 minutes was added on, with few knowing why, but this result will not be questioned.

Maresca called on his team to make their own noise while a cacophony swirls around them, but on-pitch success will not speak louder while what is happening off it is unresolved. The fans sang about relegation and trips to Stockport, embracing a dark situation with humour to match.

Sports.title: Manzambi maintains Aston Villa progress with win to seal dismal week for Newcastle
Sports.content:
There is a reason why Aston Villa were so desperate to hijack Johan Manzambi’s proposed summer move from Freiburg to Newcastle. The tall, quick, tricky, clever and perfectly balanced 21-year-old Switzerland attacking midfielder looked worth every penny of the record £50m plus fee Villa ended up paying and he duly delighted in showing Tynesiders what they missed.

For Newcastle and their disconsolate manager, Matthias Jaissle, there was a cruel irony that Manzambi ended up heading the winner on a day when the Premier League’s CEO, Richard Masters, was in the directors’ box to watch arguably the two teams most affected by the spending rules imposed during his tenure.

Those regulations have turned Unai Emery into a master of reinvention at Aston Villa but, in the league at least, the Spaniard’s latest rebuild has been slow to click cleanly into place. On the evidence of their fourth win in five games in all competitions, that just might be changing.

While Villa kicked off having won only once in the league this season, Newcastle sought redemption after last Monday night’s chastening 4-1 defeat at Coventry.

Emery, who changed his mind about taking charge of Newcastle before Eddie Howe took the job, said: “It was a tough match but it was very important to win after our poor start. But we set a high standard.”

Jaissle, whose team are level on points with Villa but faces an appreciably tougher reconstruction project, was left to reflect on his “frustration” and blamed his young team’s decision making. But Newcastle’s manager was also sanguine. “Big names left the club in the summer so for sure, we knew it would be challenging,” he said. “That’s not an excuse, we have to learn fast.”

View image in fullscreen Johan Manzambi strikes a pose after scoring the winner. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

There has always been a certain edge between these teams and Jarred Gillett issued two first-half yellow cards in quick succession. First Joelinton lunged in, two-footed, on Manzambi and then Sven Botman was guilty of another reckless challenge, two-footed and over the ball, on the dangerous Nicolas Jackson.

A video assistant referee check ensued but, after lengthy deliberation, it was decided the original decision was correct and Botman’s yellow did not require upgrading to a red. The Newcastle centre-half was probably a little fortunate. “It was so high it nearly broke my leg,” said Jackson. “But I’m OK; it’s part of football.”

Joelinton, meanwhile, has now been booked in each of the two games he has been involved in since returning from injury as a substitute at Coventry. Plus ça change.

The elegantly impressive Manzambi, seemingly electrically powered, exerted the best sort of revenge on the Brazilian when he gave Emery’s side the lead. That goal arrived in the 36th minute and involved an unmarked Manzambi – a creator brilliant at drifting into space – ghosting away from Malick Thiaw before meeting João Gomes’s splendid cross with a tremendous header.

Newcastle suddenly looked extremely vulnerable but they were reprieved when Emiliano Buendía’s shot rebounded off the inside of a post and deflected off Lukas Hornicek’s back before eventually being cleared by Lewis Hall. Once again, Hall was Jaissle’s best player.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery secured his 100th Premier League victory but it was another game to forget for Matthias Jaissle. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

It was all too easy to see why Newcastle have now gone 13 Premier League home games without a clean sheet, equalling an unwanted record set in 1998-99.

Jaissle’s frustration surfaced itself as he exchanged words with Emery after an altercation involving Alysson and Hornicek and subsequently looked suitably downcast as his side were booed off at half-time.

Those home fans were not relishing the sight of Villa’s forward repeatedly accelerating behind the sometimes dangerously high home backline.

Quick Guide Newcastle 0-1 Aston Villa key facts Show • Newcastle United are now without a home clean sheet in each of their last 16 games in all competitions; it's the longest run in their history. • Yoane Wissa’s seven shots on goal with none on target is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Newcastle teammate Harvey Barnes against Brentford in April 2025 (also 7). • Unai Emery (pictured) has earned his 100th Premier League win as a manager, doing so in his 197th game in the competition (D44 L53), only eight managers have done so in fewer games in the competition’s history. Opta Photograph: Ed Sykes/REUTERS Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Zion Suzuki had been rather underemployed but a goalkeeper briefly courted by Newcastle in the summer opened the second half by making a superlative flying save to keep Botman’s high velocity strike out. It was Newcastle’s sole shot on target.

The Villa substitute Ross Barkley almost showed Jaissle’s players how to do it when he would have scored with his first touch had Hornicek not dived smartly to turn his blistering shot around a post.

Although Newcastle’s manager sent Dan Burn on for the closing minutes – as a striker – nothing was going to come between Emery and his 100th Premier League win.

Sports.title: Pressure on Arbeloa lifted after Alex Iwobi sinks Hull for Fulham’s first win
Sports.content:
It was not until his post-match lap of the pitch that Álvaro Arbeloa allowed himself a smile. After an uncomfortable week when his future was being called into question, the former Real Madrid manager has a Premier League win under his belt at the seventh attempt, lifting his side off the foot of the table. But it is not a win without caveats.

Alex Iwobi’s goal in the first half should have been one of many, with the Nigeria winger among those guilty of missing gilt-edge chances. Gonzalo García, who has not scored in the league since the opening weekend of the season, headed against the crossbar from close range in the second half.

Fulham ended with 10 men after Ryan Sessegnon’s red card in stoppage time, but it did not matter against a toothless Hull side, who are now winless in five.

With Fulham also a goal up against Ipswich last Saturday and Manchester United here before the international break before dropping vital points, you could forgive Arbeloa for the stern expression he wore as his team continued to pass up opportunities.

“I saw this movie before,” he said. “I didn’t have the feeling we were in danger, but in football you never know. In one second, any team can score.

“It is so important to get the chances [converted] because you want to play the last minutes with a little more calm. It’s better to win 2-0 than 1-0, even in a game like that where we were a much better team.”

This was a sentiment shared by Hull, whose lack of quality at either end of the pitch was another caveat. “That was the worst performance since I’m here,” said their head coach, Sergej Jakirovic, who is in danger of a promising start fizzling out. “You see in every challenge, they were stronger. Every challenge, they ate us alive.”

View image in fullscreen Referee Chris Kavanagh shows a red card to Ryan Sessegnon (left) of Fulham after his foul on Robinio Vaz. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

This was the type of performance Fulham would have expected when it appointed Arbeloa as Marco Silva’s successor in the summer. It was a move designed to bring a more entertaining style to Craven Cottage after four years of Premier League stability in midtable – the Spaniard brought five members of staff with him from Real Madrid and three players.

There was plenty of creativity on show against Hull, especially from the wingers Iwobi and Oscar Bobb. They started fast, with Iwobi sending a curling shot on to the roof of the net from the left and Bobb a constant threat on the right.

It was from an attack down the right that Fulham produced their winner. Hull’s left wing-back, Brooke Norton-Cuffy, held off Josh King, but failed to clear and Sander Berge poked the ball into Iwobi’s path. His first-time shot should not have troubled the goalkeeper, Konstantinos Tzolakis, but it squirmed under his rolling dive at the near post after coming through a crowd of bodies.
