View image in fullscreen Fulham’s Alex Iwobi (centre) scores the only goal of the game. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

Jakirovic needed to find answers at half-time and he replaced the centre-back Lucas Herrington, who had been booked for one of his fouls on the elusive King, with the midfielder Tim Iroegbunam. After a bright breakthrough season in the first team, the 19-year-old King is expected to push on. He was allowed to roam against Hull’s low block and after neatly combining with Shea Charles should have doubled their lead, but his low shot was too close to Tzolakis.

A smart turn from King away from Semi Ajayi preceded a chance that Iwobi, with time and the whole goal to aim at, should have buried, but he telegraphed his low effort for Tzolakis to read and smother. García was unmarked at the back post when he headed Iwobi’s cross against the bar, but Hull provided such little threat that what could have been a nervy ending, especially after Sessegnon’s stoppage-time dismissal for leaving his studs on Robinio Vaz’s achilles, was anything but.

With the pressure now relieved a little and his ideas evidently translating to his players, will the often stoney-faced Arbeloa feel more relaxed at training? “I always try to smile,” he said. “Even when you are losing, it’s even more important that you try to smile.”

Sports.title: Isak completes Liverpool’s comeback win as Brentford finish with nine
Sports.content:
If Liverpool’s spluttering forwards end up remembering this as the day when their luck turned then they will owe a big debt of gratitude to Yehor Yarmolyuk. This was a game with a very clear before and after.

Andoni Iraola will hope surviving one of the toughest tests the Premier League has to offer is a sign his methods are starting to work, but Liverpool’s manager will not forget it was a very different contest after Yarmolyuk’s red card for a butt on Jérémy Jacquet left Brentford trying to defend a 1-0 lead with 10 men for the entire second half.

Brentford, who later lost Vitaly Janelt to a second yellow card, could not hold out. They raged at John Brooks’s officiating after their unbeaten start ended, but they had only themselves to blame after tumbling out of the top four. Brentford pressed the self-destruct button when they had Liverpool on the ropes. Yarmolyuk was never going to get away it in the video assistant referee era and Liverpool made the midfielder pay.

Iraola was delighted with how an attack worth close to £400m made the numerical advantage count after half-time. Most important was a telling contribution from Florian Wirtz. The £100m signing has struggled with the responsibility of playing as Liverpool’s No 10 since joining from Bayer Leverkusen, but this time he was decisive. The clever pass to release Victor Muñoz for a sharp equaliser was his second assist of the season and was followed by Bradley Barcola creating a goal for the first time since his move for an initial £106m from Paris Saint-Germain, the French winger’s header teeing up Alexander Isak to complete the turnaround in the 70th minute and lift Liverpool into fifth place.

The challenge is to push on. Isak’s Liverpool career has been stop-start since his £125m move from Newcastle, injuries holding the forward back. The Spaniard was critical of some sloppy finishing from Barcola, but was readier to dish out the praise for Wirtz’s intelligence in tight spaces in the second half. It feels significant that both of Wirtz’s assists have come for Muñoz.

“A good battle today,” Iraola said before switching focus to Barcola and Wirtz. “Both had a lot of influence. Bradley and Flo, they are players that against 10 men are lovely to have.”

There was not much between the sides before Yarmolyuk’s rush of blood to the head. Isak returned after missing last week’s defeat to Manchester City and Liverpool shaded the early openings. Barcola almost punished an error from Janelt, only to miss a chance to build on his midweek hat-trick against LASK. Isak nodded over from a good position.

Brentford responded with a series of fast breaks and Liverpool had to be strong. They looked readier for the threat posed by Brentford than when they folded in this fixture under Arne Slot 12 months ago. Jacquet, quietly impressive in central defence, made a crucial tackle to deny Igor Thiago. The initial problem for Liverpool was more their expensive attack was yet to gel.

Michael Kayode was keeping Barcola in check and Keane Lewis-Potter was edging his battle with Muñoz. Wirtz was timid and Liverpool’s worries grew when they lost Dominik Szoboszlai to injury.

With Ryan Gravenberch suspended, Liverpool were light on midfield options. Trey Nyoni replaced Szoboszali and the 19-year-old’s introduction was followed by a whirlwind spell. Iraola was unhappy when Liverpool had a penalty overturned as replays showed Dango Outtara got a clear touch on the ball before colliding with Alexis Mac Allister.

View image in fullscreen Yehor Yarmolyuk leaves the pitch after being shown the red card. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Brentford were pumped up after the VAR intervention and soon made Liverpool rue a failure to clear their lines. The ball came back too easily, Mac Allister backed off Thiago, who crossed for Lewis-Potter to run in from left-back and head into the top corner.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We were edging it,” Keith Andrews said. Brentford’s manager wants his team “to play on the edge”, but felt too many decisions went Liverpool’s way. However, he had no complaints about the first red. He said Liverpool were “cute and clever” during the incident, but promised that Yarmolyuk would learn from his mistake.

They were into six added minutes at the end of the first half when the midfielder clashed with Jacquet before a Liverpool corner. It was more of a jut than a proper blow, but it was enough to justify the sending off. Brooks checked the pitchside monitor and his decision was not a surprise.

Liverpool took a while to adjust in the second half. They encountered further complications when injury forced Jeremie Frimpong off seven minutes after replacing Ronald Araújo at right-back. Mac Allister let fly from distance, but Caoimhín Kelleher saved and Rio Ngumoha, on for Frimpong, crossed for Virgil van Dijk to volley wide.

Quick Guide Brentford 1-2 Liverpool key facts Show • Florian Wirtz is the first player to create nine or more chances from open play in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané against Burnley in January 2021 (9), also for Liverpool, and first in an away match since Samir Nasri for Manchester City v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Victor Muñoz (pictured centre, with Wirtz and Trey Nyoni) scored from one of them. • Liverpool’s Alexander Isak has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford (5 goals); only Erling Haaland v Crystal Palace (6) has a better 100% rate in the competition. • Brentford received two red cards in the same league game for the first time since April 2013 against Sheffield United in League One. Opta Photograph: Peter Cziborra/REUTERS Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Brentford began to wobble and they were caught on the counterattack in the 62nd minute. Wirtz dropped back and played a clever pass inside Lewis-Potter. Muñoz raced clear, cut back and drilled a low shot into the far corner with his left foot.

The change in mood was dramatic. Barcola sliced a volley just wide, but the winner was coming. Mac Allister took a pass from Wirtz and crossed. Barcola headed down and Isak finished from close range.

Iraola was not happy with Liverpool’s play once they led. Brentford threatened an equaliser through Thiago and Liverpool were too rushed. There are flaws to iron out, but this was a positive week for Iraola.

Sports.title: Boos for Arsenal as draw with Birmingham extends winless WSL run
Sports.content:
An equaliser from Olivia Smith averted defeat for Arsenal, but a home draw with Birmingham did little to calm fears for Renée Slegers’s future as Gunners coach. Boos accompanied the final whistle at the Emirates Stadium, as the result left Arsenal on six points from six matches and without a win in five Women’s Super League matches, the club’s longest winless run in WSL history. They are eighth in the table, nine points behind the leaders, Manchester City, who have played one game fewer.

Birmingham opened the scoring at the start of the second half when Océane Hurtré coolly tapped in after her run from the halfway line went unchecked. Alessia Russo had hit the woodwork in the first half with a diving header, among a slew of Arsenal chances as Sophie Baggaley was kept the busier of the goalkeepers.

“I don’t think we created enough in the first half,” said Slegers. “Second half is different. There was one player we needed to stop and that was Hurtré. But she came through in a fast break and a counter, we don’t defend that well enough.”

After Smith’s spectacular strike, in the 66th minute, curled from outside the area, Arsenal would not find the winning goal that might ease pressure on Slegers. Baggaley’s goalkeeping and slack finishing meant Birmingham secured their point. “We are in a scenario we’ve had too many times season,” said Slegers.

Next week for Arsenal is a north London derby with Tottenham, who kick off at Chelsea in fourth on Sunday. Slegers said: “The next game is always the next opportunity. [It’s good] we always keep going and we rise after setbacks.

“We just need to put ourselves in better positions earlier so that’s not necessary every time because it takes energy from the team having to play those scenarios. But yes, the team has been brilliant. The urgency, the willingness, the desire in the second half was really good.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Despite those boos at the final whistle, Smith said of the home fans: “They always bring out great support, [we’re] so happy to have them here. Again, disappointed not to get the result, must be frustrating for them, but they stay with us and support us.”

Sports.title: Championship roundup: West Ham go second; Norwich beaten again
Sports.content:
Nuno Espírito Santo was delighted West Ham finished a “demanding week” by toppling Championship leaders Swansea.

Divine Mukasa’s first-half strike in front of a record Swansea.com Stadium crowd of 20,973 gave the Hammers a 1-0 win and took them into second place and within a point of the league leaders. It was their second success in four days after a 6-0 romp at Lincoln, and ended a week that began with a 1-1 home draw against QPR following Jarrod Bowen’s last-gasp penalty miss.

“We wanted not only to keep the momentum, but to build on it,” said Nuno. “It was a very demanding week in terms of the opponents we had to face, but it finished really well due to the hard work of the boys. The commitment, the unity and the way they played was really good against a very good Swansea side. It was a very intense.”

Kim Hellberg defended his decision to rest Will Lankshear against Cardiff after the division’s top scorer came off the bench to rescue a point for Middlesbrough. Lankshear, who took his tally to 10 for the season in all competitions midweek, was rested him for the visit of the Bluebirds. That selection backfired as Cardiff stunned Boro with two first-half goals from Jack Moylan and Ollie Tanner. Lankshear was then introduced at half-time and inspired a fightback, levelling for Boro with his 11th goal of the campaign after Tommy Conway had halved the deficit.

View image in fullscreen Will Lankshear’s goal saved a point for Middlesbrough. Photograph: Richard Sellers/PA

“You need to manage your players in this league and look into numbers,” said Hellberg. “We have a lot of players that have no pre-season. Will is one of those who came late and has been doing a lot of good things. He’s been absolutely brilliant and sometimes you need to also protect him.”

Liam Millar scored twice as Birmingham beat QPR 3-0 at St Andrew’s. Millar swung the game Birmingham’s way in the 27th minute and then doubled their advantage just after the break. On both occasions he was assisted by Tomoki Iwata while Demarai Gray added the gloss in the first minute of stoppage time by hammering a pull-back by fellow substitute Luis Vázquez into the top corner.

Quick Guide League One roundup: Bradford go top; Plymouth lose Show Bradford moved top of League One with their first home win under Michael Duff, as Plymouth slipped up against Huddersfield. The Bantams, who appointed Duff as manager earlier this month following the departure of Graham Alexander, claimed a 2-0 home win over Stevenage thanks to goals inside the last 11 minutes from Antoni Sarcevic and substitute Will Swan. That proved enough to put them a point clear at the top, with previous front-runners Plymouth going down 2-0 at home to Huddersfield and dropping to fourth in the process. The Terriers climbed above their opponents into third after strikes from Derensili Sanches Fernandez and Bojan Radulovic. Stockport climbed to second, edging out Bromley 1-0 with Kyle Wootton on target, while Robbie Savage’s first home league game in charge of Peterborough ended in a 2-2 draw with Burton. It looked as if Gbemi Arubi’s 89th-minute wonderstrike had earned Albion their first win in three, but Matt Garbett responded with a 96th minute leveller to snatch his side a point. Savage started his time at London Road with a 3-1 win at Leicester last Saturday. Aaron Collins scored the winner as MK Dons beat Luton 2-1 to claim a first league victory of the season. Alex Gilbey fired the Dons ahead with a fine strike before Jordan Clark equalised for the visitors. But Collins’s penalty won the match to condemn Luton to a third defeat in their past four games. Under-pressure Leicester manager Russell Martin celebrated a badly needed win, seeing off visiting Doncaster 2-1 – with Warren O’Hara’s 84th-minute own-goal causing some late tension. Cambridge kept pace with the promotion hopefuls after Shayne Lavery grabbed the winner in added time to leave Barnsley with a 2-1 win, while Sheffield Wednesday eased to a 5-0 win over AFC Wimbledon – Davis Keillor-Dunn with a double. Bottom club Wigan registered a first league win since 2 September, Scott Hogan with the only goal against Reading. Notts County lost 2-0 at Wycombe and Leyton Orient beat Blackpool 2-0. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Luke Graham scored his first goal for Stoke as they won 1-0 at Pride Park to pile more pressure on struggling Derby. The Scotland defender headed in a free-kick early in the second half and that was enough to settle a scrappy contest. Derby, who are missing a number of key players, battled away and nearly snatched a point when David Ozoh’s shot was superbly saved by goalkeeper Viktor Johansson.

West Brom completed a stunning comeback after conceding two early goals as they beat Blackburn 3-2. Andri Gudjohnsen had Rovers two up before the break, before Barney Stewart pulled a goal back for Albion. Isaac Price’s penalty levelled it up before the substitute Felix Horn Myhre netted a dramatic winner for the home side a minute from time.

James Bree, Lewis Dobbin and Léo Scienza all squandered chances as Southampton dropped points at home for the first time this season with a 0-0 draw against Bolton. The trio all wasted tap-ins, while Saints were also left bereft by a penalty not being given for a Rúben Rodrigues handball.

View image in fullscreen Luca Kjerrumgaard enjoys his crucial opener for Watford against Charlton. Photograph: Ben Peters/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

Watford lifted the pressure on Alessio Dionisi and quelled their supporters’ rebellion against the owner, Gino Pozzo, with a deserved 2-0 win against a sluggish Charlton. After shipping nine goals in defeats by Burnley and Cardiff, Watford had slumped into the bottom three and the fans had turned their anger on Pozzo. But goals from Luca Kjerrumgaard and the substitute Jordan Zemura extended Charlton’s worrying run to eight games without a win as they were booed off at Vicarage Road.

Dionisi said later his team was “not yet strong enough for the Championship but it’s possible to improve. I’ve been a coach for 14 years and I know when my team stays near my idea. This result is important and tonight I will drink a glass of red wine.”

Portsmouth piled on the misery for struggling Norwich as they made it back-to-back Championships victories with a 1-0 win at Carrow Road. Pompey followed up their midweek victory against Sheffield United with a hard-fought success in East Anglia, with a 51st-minute penalty from striker Marezi settling the issue.

It was a sixth successive league defeat for the hosts and there were calls for the sporting director Ben Knapper to go from frustrated supporters at the final whistle.

Norwich’s head coach, Philippe Clement, had no complaints with his side’s effort – but felt they sometimes failed to see the bigger picture on the pitch.

“I am very disappointed, very frustrated,” he said. “I saw a lot of passion out there, a lot of effort, but not enough overview. It’s about getting the balance right between their hearts and their brains. I understand the frustration of our fans and all I can say is that I will work even harder than I did last season to turn it around.”

View image in fullscreen Portsmouth’s Marezi celebrates on another bleak day for Norwich. Photograph: Stephen Pond/Getty Images

Jake Cooper’s scrambled equaliser rescued a point for Millwall as they came from two goals down to draw 2-2 with Lincoln. The visitors looked on course to put Wednesday’s 6-0 home thrashing against West Ham behind them in style when goals from Andrei Coubiș and Rob Street put them in a strong position after 33 minutes at the Den. But Millwall were able to prevent back-to-back home defeats with a much-improved second-half performance, and the visitors were hanging on for a share of the spoils after having Deji Elerewe sent off soon after Cooper’s leveller. Kyrell Lisbie had scored Millwall’s first.

Quick Guide League Two roundup: Salford make it five in a row Show League Two pacesetters Salford made it five wins in a row in the fourth tier as Macaulay Langstaff scored twice in a 2-1 success over bottom side Crawley. Barnet and Crewe remain close by just a point further back. Barnet came from behind to beat Tranmere 2-1, Kabongo Tshimanga scoring both, and Crewe defeated Rochdale 3-2. York were held to a 1-1 draw at Newport after going down to 10 men but Shrewsbury held on 1-0 against Bristol Rovers despite two red cards in the last 10 minutes. Ian Holloway’s Swindon are now eight games without a win in all competitions after a 1-1 draw with Walsall, Oldham eased to a 4-1 result against Cheltenham and Port Vale edged Chesterfield 1-0. Ten-man Grimsby went down 2-0 to Northampton, Accrington took a 3-1 win over Gillingham, strugglers Rotherham lost 2-0 at Fleetwood and there was a goalless draw between Colchester and Exeter. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Oliver Arblaster’s early strike and a strong defensive display saw Sheffield United take all three points from a 1-0 victory over Bristol City at Ashton Gate. The visitors took a fifth-minute lead when a headed clearance fell to Arblaster, who connected with a sweet right-footed volley from just outside the box which gave the City goalkeeper Sam Tickle no chance. It proved enough to settle a contest high on endeavour but low on entertainment from which the Blades emerged worthy winners.

Wrexham eased the pressure on Phil Parkinson with a 4-1 win over rock-bottom Preston. Joe Worrall scored his first goal in more than two years and, after Alfie Devine briefly brought Preston level, the former Lilywhites midfielder Ben Whiteman struck next to score his first goal in Wrexham colours. Sam Smith gave the hosts breathing space just before the hour and Kieffer Moore killed it off moments later.

In a week that had seen former Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard linked with the manager’s job, Wrexham’s third league win of the season was a vital one as they moved up to 14th. But Preston remain stuck on four points from 11 games, with Graham Alexander having lost his first three games in charge.

Sports.title: Scottish Premiership: Rangers miss chance to go top after pulsating draw with Dundee
Sports.content:
Rangers passed up the chance to go top of the Premiership in a pulsating 2-2 draw against Dundee at Dens Park. The home side took a deserved lead in the 38th minute through the striker Bradley Fink but the returning Gers attacker Badredine Bouanani fired in a stunning equaliser three minutes later with his first goal for the club.

Derek McInnes’s side came out re-energised for the second half and took the lead on the hour with the midfielder Nico Raskin’s long-range drive but in the 68th minute the midfielder Callum Jones took advantage of Gers slackness to level. Dundee were well worth a point, with Rangers moving one point behind Celtic, who can increase their lead at home to Hearts on Sunday.

Greg Kiltie scored twice to lift Kilmarnock off the bottom with a 3-2 home victory over Motherwell. Kiltie struck first and last as Neil McCann’s side inflicted a fifth consecutive defeat on the Steelmen, who join Killie in the bottom three, one point above bottom-placed Hibernian.

Motherwell had a dominant spell after recovering from Kiltie’s second-minute opener and goals from Alex Lowry and Seb Palmer-Houlden turned the game on its head. But Tyreece John-Jules soon equalised and Motherwell were cut open before Kiltie knocked home a 69th-minute winner.

View image in fullscreen Greg Kiltie celebrates scoring his second goal against Motherwell, which proved to be Kilmarnock’s winner. Photograph: Mark Runnacles/Shutterstock

Motherwell’s manager, Alfred Johansson, bemoaned his side’s defending, saying: “I’m very, very disappointed and frustrated with how we end this game. It’s extremely difficult to accept the fact that we lost this game. We have chances to score more than two goals but we can’t rely on scoring three goals away from home. We need to be much more solid. It’s just way too low a level, how we defend.”

Falkirk secured an entertaining 2-1 win at Hibernian. Their only other league victory this term was at home to Hearts in September.

In a game that went from end to end, Jacob Murrell put Falkirk 2-0 ahead inside 37 minutes, before Hibs struck back with an Owen Elding goal. The home side dominated the second half, but could not bag an equaliser.

Aberdeen returned to winning ways as a 3-1 victory over St Mirren moved them above their opponents, who have now lost five straight matches. Brad Lyons gave the hosts the lead in spectacular fashion after two minutes, but the Buddies went on to dominate the first half and levelled through Eseosa Sule. In a much-improved second-half display strikes from Kevin Nisbet and Ayoub Mouloua gave the Dons three points. Aberdeen are seventh.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Lyall Cameron’s 79th-minute strike earned Dundee United a 1-1 draw at St Johnstone. United trailed at half-time to a Josh Fowler goal, the striker’s sixth of the Premiership campaign. The league’s top scorer did not make it out for the second half due to illness and Simo Valakari’s side were unable to repeat the trick of last Sunday in Aberdeen when they successfully defended a 1-0 lead.

Jim Goodwin had too many creative and attacking options to throw at their hosts and despite a decent defensive stand from the hosts, Cameron struck the second goal of his impressive loan spell from Rangers. The clubs are locked together on 12 points in the top half of the table after encouraging starts to the campaign, with the Saints in fifth on goal difference.

Sports.title: The untold story of Jason Wilcox at Man United: A 'no bulls*** approach, what agents and executives REALLY think about 'interfering' director - and how he is hamstrung by Sir Jim Ratcliffe at Old Trafford
Sports.content:
The untold story of Jason Wilcox at Man United: A 'no bulls*** approach, what agents and executives REALLY think about 'interfering' director - and how he is hamstrung by Sir Jim Ratcliffe at Old Trafford

There is a picture of Sir Jim Ratcliffe with his Manchester United executives that offers a fascinating glimpse into the dynamic of the Old Trafford boardroom.

A furious-looking Ratcliffe is pointing his forefinger at director of football Jason Wilcox, who raises a bent finger of his own in cautious defence, while chief executive Omar Berrada shields between the two men.

It was taken during the half-time interval at Molineux last December after United conceded an equaliser against Wolves before going on to secure their last away win under Ruben Amorim.

A month later, Amorim self-destructed at Leeds in a post-match rant aimed at Wilcox and club bosses, two days after an angry bust-up between the two men at Carrington, and was sacked.

United return to Elland Road on Sunday with former Leeds winger Wilcox once again in the crosshairs following Lisandro Martinez’s criticism of him in a television interview after Tuesday’s defeat by Atletico Madrid, in which the Argentine said he ‘expected more from our technical director’ in the summer transfer market.

Martinez accepted a fine and apologised for the timing of his comments in a statement referencing Wilcox when he said ‘everyone at the club is doing everything they can to make the team successful’, but has not said sorry to Wilcox himself.

Jason Wilcox (right) has felt the wrath of a number of those associated with Manchester United - including Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left)

Wilcox still has Ratcliffe's backing but has come under criticism again this week - this time from Lisandro Martinez

Ratcliffe has quoted Manchester City’s former director of football Txiki Begiristain as saying Wilcox has the ‘best set of eyes’ in the game, but the 55-year-old knows that counts for little.

The photo at Molineux was taken almost a year to the day after Ratcliffe sacked his predecessor Dan Ashworth on the spot after a game at Old Trafford and then promoted Wilcox from technical director.

It’s understood that he still has the backing of the Ineos billionaire but there has to be a degree of sympathy for any executive working on a limited budget, which made signing top targets like Elliot Anderson in the summer impossible, with Ratcliffe looking over their shoulder.

As one agent explained to Daily Mail Sport: ‘Jason is in an incredibly difficult position. Everybody would think he’s the decision-maker at the club, but he absolutely isn’t. Manchester United is run by the owners, Sir Jim and the Glazers. If you sack Wilcox, nothing will change. It’s a mess.’

Another adds: ‘We had a deal agreed with Jason and then Jim got involved and tried to change it. He ended up killing it.’

A year after United were praised for signing Senne Lammens, Benjamin Sesko, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha, Wilcox has been criticised for focusing on a midfield recruitment drive that brought in Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans.

United faced Atletico in the Metropolitano in midweek without a recognised striker or left-back due to wholly foreseeable injuries to Sesko and Luke Shaw.

It’s understandable that Wilcox is facing questions about his suitability for such a big job after six years as City’s academy head and nine months as Southampton’s director of football. If United cannot turn their season around, should he be held just as accountable as head coach Michael Carrick?

One agent said the situation at United is 'a mess' - with Ratcliffe making a lot of decisions

Erik ten Hag was never a fan and Wilcox’s relationship soured with Amorim who hinted that he was too sensitive to criticism from TV pundits like Gary Neville.

Others have a different view. ‘Straight to the point, no bulls***,’ said a source. ‘An absolute gentleman and man of his word,’ added another.

One Premier League executive who didn’t wish to be named said: ‘Wilcox is ultra-professional, or at least he has been in my experience. Is he as hard-faced as some of them out there? Maybe not and maybe that may put him on the back foot on occasion.

‘He works for Man United, though, and I think there needs to be a certain standard of behaviour that comes with that. I feel Wilcox understands it. He has a pretty good reputation in the league.’

Wilcox chatted briefly with reporters before United played Paris-Saint Germain in Gothenburg in the summer, but has maintained a relatively low profile since succeeding Ashworth who – like John Murtough before him – was more open with the media.

Wilcox spoke with United’s in-house station MUTV in October last year, coincidentally after a run of three straight wins, a month after he appeared on stage at a gala dinner for the Association of Manchester United Players when he admitted that his coaching background means ‘I always want to interfere with what the managers are doing’.

That might not be what Carrick wants to hear but the two men are said to have a good working relationship, and the United boss said he has no problem with Wilcox keeping his head below the parapet when he spoke before the Leeds game on Friday.

‘I don't think that's for me to say whether he should or not,’ said Carrick. ‘I've got absolutely no problem sitting here and talking to you guys and leading the football club from this position.’

Michael Carrick (left) is under pressure - and Wilcox is keen to involve himself in his area

When Blackburn Rovers’ squad of 1995 gathered together last year to celebrate the 30th anniversary of beating United to the Premier League title, Wilcox took some stick from his old teammates.

‘He took it really well,’ said one. ‘He’s very self-effacing. There’s no airs and graces. He was always a conscientious lad with a great sense of humour who worked really hard – although you wouldn’t necessarily have had him down as the future director of football at Manchester United.’

Raised in Bolton, the boyhood Liverpool fan represented England at judo after achieving his black belt at the age of 14.

Wilcox joined Blackburn two years later after he was rejected by City and his father sent off 30 letters to clubs in the north-west asking them to give him a chance.

He built a reputation as a dressing-room joker as Kenny Dalglish forged a title-winning team under millionaire owner Jack Walker, and his better impersonations were said to include Bruce Forsyth and Norman Wisdom.

When Rovers edged out United by one point on the final day of the season, Wilcox was on crutches at Anfield following knee surgery – just as he had missed out on the club’s promotion to the Premier League via the Play-off Final at Wembley in 1992 because of injury, his misery complete when a bird defecated on his club suit before the game.

Wilcox did make three appearances at Wembley for England – against Hungary, France and Argentina – in a career that included spells at Leeds, Leicester and Blackpool.

In retirement, he continued to follow Blackburn as part of the commentary team on BBC Radio Lancashire, and he also wrote a regular column for the Lancashire Telegraph.

A former Blackburn title winner, it's now Wilcox's turn to feel the pressure with Ratcliffe breathing down his neck

He always felt destined to go down the coaching path, though, and joined City where he led the Under-18s to two FA Youth Cup finals before making his name as the club’s academy head.

Wilcox oversaw the progression of a number of young stars to the first-team including Phil Foden, Cole Palmer, Rico Lewis and Liam Delap – notably sticking by Palmer when others considered letting him go at 16.

He also helped City make a big profit from selling their surplus academy talent, something United are now trying to emulate.

‘Jason was always very fair at City,’ says one agent. ‘If he said your player would get a new contract if he played well, he was usually true to his word. He is very black and white. He doesn’t pussyfoot around on decisions like some.’

It was no surprise that Berrada took Wilcox from Southampton as part of the influx of ex-City staff into Old Trafford, even if the overlap with Ashworth never looked like working out for long.

Now it’s his turn to feel the heat with Ratcliffe breathing down his neck.

Sports.title: How Chelsea turned nasty and ditched 'soft' mentality in Everton victory: The nuisance who led the charge and Xabi Alonso's key role as Blues finally show mean streak, writes KIERAN GILL
Sports.content:
The game was goalless when Thierno Barry was on the ground injured and Levi Colwill had the ball by the halfway line. Chelsea’s defender kicked it out of play so Everton’s striker could pick himself up.

Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro did not like that one bit. They both yelled at Colwill for his generosity, taking turns telling their team-mate it would have been better to try to take advantage.

Colwill was too nice in that moment. But this was a game won in the second half by Chelsea by dominating in duels, by battling for balls, and by being a little nasty.

Xabi Alonso made a point of praising his players for that edge they carried afterwards, saying: ‘Sometimes it is not about playing nice. It is about playing well. We needed a result like this. We needed to show that we can win in this way.’

Chelsea have been accused of being soft before. That has contributed to their poor record when playing up north, usually allowing themselves to be bullied at places like the Hill Dickinson Stadium. They had lost 19 of their last 41 matches north of Luton. That included being beaten 3-0 here during Liam Rosenior's five-match winless and goalless run which got him sacked.

This was Chelsea’s first game outside of London this season, and Palmer led that nastiness which so pleased Alonso. The playmaker talked himself into a caution from Paul Tierney and yet continued to be a nuisance.

Cole Palmer was a nuisance throughout as he demonstrated Chelsea's new nasty approach

Xabi Alonso praised his side's edge as his Chelsea team won 2-0 at Everton on Saturday

Even as the clock ticked over into 100 minutes after Emiliano Martinez’s injury, he pulled back Tyrique George and slid in on Jarrad Branthwaite. Palmer escaped the second yellow which would have seen him suspended for the visit of Tottenham Hotspur next weekend.

The same went for Morgan Rogers. He squared up to James Tarkowski. He crunched into James Garner. He added to the 15 fouls committed by Chelsea in this match. He too avoided a second yellow despite being constantly combative.

Even as Chelsea were preparing to take the free-kick from which they scored their second, Joao Pedro was there, winding up Jordan Pickford while Everton’s goalkeeper was trying to organise his wall.

As they told Colwill, they were not here to make friends, but to win.

Palmer did not score. Rogers did not score. Joao Pedro did not score. But Chelsea’s front three contributed in their own ways as Pedro Neto got the two goals which won them this match.

It felt like a new side to Chelsea. There was a resilient feel to the visitors, who have benefitted from the addition of Jordan Henderson to their line-up as he fights their corner with the referees. Chelsea have added players who do not want to be considered pushovers.

After full-time, the celebrations in front of the away end were more energetic than that of a regular win. Palmer pushed Alonso in front of the supporters, and Joao Pedro did the same with Neto.

There was extra appreciation from the travelling contingent for what they had seen, and Chelsea are likely to need to show more of this side to them when Tottenham visit next weekend.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois announced himself as the undisputed champion-elect with an explosive win over Fabio Wardley - the next generation of heavyweights has arrived, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
To hell with the romance. Stuff the slow starts. Never mind most of the O2 shouting against him.

Daniel Dynamite Dubois exploded into the ring with such power and brutality that he might have sent a tsunami along the Thames.

What he did beyond doubt last night, and what cannot be contested by Fabio Wardley or the three other world heavyweight belt wearers, was announce himself as the undisputed champion-elect.

White-collar Wardley was disabused of any notion he might regain the WBO title he lost to Dubois five months ago.

He was stunned in 17 seconds by Dubois's first booming right-hander of a red-hot night. And so the pain continued unabated.

'Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time, and my era,' said Dubois. 'I had my intentions, bad intentions, from the beginning.'

Daniel Dubois brutalised Fabio Wardley in their rematch as he wrapped things up in two rounds

This time there was no delay in Wardley's corner throwing in the towel. No point in the referee delaying the inevitable.

Dubois's sledgehammer blows rained down like missiles, with none travelling in the opposite direction.

One of the rival world champions was here to see the ferocity in person. Filip Hrgovic, who had disposed of Moses Itauma recently, sounded somewhat shell-shocked.

Agit Kabayel may be in no rush to meet Dubois. Nor, perhaps, will the winner of December's WBA clash between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.

This was an enormous statement by a man whose courage had been questioned but who will now be favourite to hunt them all down in his quest for the succession to Oleksandr Usyk as the undisputed champion.

'I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in,' said Dubois. 'At this stage in my career, big money, big fights.'

The next generation of heavyweights has arrived.

So the irresistible force and the immovable object came to blows again at the O2. Dubois had risen from the canvas twice in the spring to claim his second world heavyweight title. Wardley, who neglected to finish him off, paid such a bloodied price that he left us wondering how he had stayed on his feet.

After being dropped in the opening seconds in their first fight, Dubois delivered revenge this time around

Their mutual hammering in Manchester had left us greedily wanting more at the O2.

Both pledged to put the savagery on after-burner second time around. Forget the concerns for their health.

In the parlance of the first promotion, Don't Blink was the warning to all those in attendance. These two had spent their careers knocking people out for fun or sometimes being stopped themselves.

No one expected this fight to go the distance. Not the fighters themselves. 'Me early,' predicted Dubois. 'Me earlier,' said Wardley.

'Twelve rounds?' opined promoter Frank Warren. 'No chance.'

The majority of the crowd were with the underdog, roaring Wardley into the ring. Partly from their feeling for romance, with a white-collar boxer breaking into the highest echelons of the heavyweights.

Dynamite Daniel's reception was more subdued. Even a hint hostile. Wardley hoped for a first-round knockdown, but that went to Dubois.

The first right of the night had Fabio reeling on the ropes for an eight count. More hell followed.

Dubois may have found greatness and is the undisputed champion-elect in the next generation of heavyweights

It was all over in round two. Wardley was brave as always, but his corner could not let him keep taking sledgehammer blows without reply.

'I just came in and I didn't execute the game plan properly,' Wardley admitted. 'I hold my hands up to that; that is entirely down to me.'

'A little white-collar boy like me could never have dreamed like this,' he added, reflecting on a sold-out O2 despite defeat.

Dubois may have found greatness with this mammoth performance.

Sports.title: Aston Villa had better players and a better plan than lumbering Newcastle - this was a harsh indication of the Magpies' current situation, writes CRAIG HOPE
Sports.content:
Aston Villa had better players and a better plan than lumbering Newcastle - this was a harsh indication of the Magpies' current situation, writes CRAIG HOPE

On the day Newcastle United revealed a slower version of their Blaydon Races anthem, the team on the pitch responded with a performance every bit as lumbering.

When the match ball burst in stoppage-time, it was a signpost for the deflating mood that would soon descend on St James’ Park. At least, that was, after the home masses had let their feelings be known with a chorus of boos.

It was just as well that this game also marked the unveiling of the club’s new pour-your-own beer pumps, for the locals needed something to numb the pain of a second defeat in a week. On this evidence, there will be plenty more.

The sight of head coach Matthias Jaissle breaking the glass on the emergency option and throwing Dan Burn up front in the closing stages told of Newcastle’s desperation, as well as the absence of a workable Plan A. Come full-time, there had been just one shot on target — and that was from a defender. The club have spent £175million trying to replace Alexander Isak, and Burn is where they have ended up.

Unai Emery’s Villa, by contrast, had a plan. They also had better players, including match-winner Johan Manzambi. Remarkably, the visitors are still below Newcastle in the table, not that they will be for too much longer. Villa are unbeaten in five in all competitions and this was Emery’s 100th win in the Premier League.

‘I hope there are 100 more,’ said the Spaniard. ‘This was very tough and for us it was very important after our poor start [to the season] that we needed to try to come back feeling confident, feeling comfortable in how we are building our structure.’

Aston Villa had better players than Newcastle, including match-winner Johan Manzambi, as they beat the Magpies 1-0

The midfielder, who nearly joined Newcastle in the summer, was the game’s star man and scorer of its only goal

Matthias Jaissle's side are heading towards the bottom three after a second defeat in a week

Much of that structure centres on the athleticism and ingenuity of Manzambi. Newcastle missing out on the signing of the Switzerland World Cup star was a sliding-doors moment in their summer, and it was among the reasons why Eddie Howe headed for the one marked ‘exit’.

Had Manzambi and Victor Munoz — the Spaniard who defected to Liverpool — signed, Howe would likely have still been in charge. Sliding doors and, now, a team sliding towards the bottom three. That is the reality of their current plight.

‘Johan has skills and intelligence,’ said Emery. ‘His physicality is also very important to help us defensively. He decided he wanted to be with us [and not Newcastle]. We have Champions League. He has had a very good impact with his qualities.’

It is easy to see why Manzambi was so desired by Newcastle, who thought he was ready to join. The midfielder, 21, was the game’s star man and scorer of its only goal. Not that he had to be so great to convert a free header from six yards — for that he had the pinpoint cross of Joao Gomes to thank and, more so, the failure of defenders Sven Botman and Lewis Miley to react to his presence in the goalmouth.

The moments that followed exposed the fragility of Newcastle’s confidence. Manzambi netted in the 36th minute and the hosts were fortunate not to enter the break at 2-0 down or worse. They lost shape, energy and ideas. It was like watching a boxer lose his legs after the first punch. Emiliano Buendia hit the post after a back-to-front offensive that was devastatingly simple in its execution — pass, pass, chance. It infuriated Jaissle, who yelled at Joe Willock for not stopping the move at source on the edge of Villa’s own area. The midfielder protested his innocence, in a manner to suggest he believed the job of closing Gomes belonged to someone else.

That is never a good sign and was reminiscent of his team-mates’ abdication of responsibility for the goal moments earlier.

MATCH FACTS Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek; Miley, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Joelinton (Burn 90), Gonzalez; Fernandez-Pardo (Toure 56), Willock (Osula 56), Barnes; Wissa Subs not used: Pope, Schar, Dedic, A Murphy, Steur, Bamba Booked: Thiaw, Botman, Gonzalez, Joelinton, Wissa, Osula Manager: Matthias Jaissle Aston Villa (4-2-3-1): Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Mings, Wan-Bissaka (Torres 77); Kamara, Gomes (Barkley 72); Alysson (McGinn 46), Manzambi (Mbiaye 72), Buendia (Goretzka 72); Jackson Subs not used: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Bogarde, Madjo Booked: Alysson, Gomes Goal: Manzambi 36 Manager: Unai Emery

Jaissle had demanded his team come out swinging in response to Monday’s 4-1 defeat at Coventry, and they did, albeit with a little too much fight. The ferocity of Botman’s tackle on Nicolas Jackson needed 60 seconds of attention from Stockley Park, who eventually deemed the on-field yellow sufficient. It was a borderline red.

Jackson later said: ‘I know the referee said yellow card but it was so high and hopefully maybe next time a red card. I nearly broke my leg. The most important thing is that we won, so I’m OK.’

Joelinton was also booked during the same passage for a typically robust challenge on Manzambi, requiring Villa’s medical team to divide their attention.

Still, here was proof of a team ready to scrap for each other, and that resolve did at least extend until the very end, when they threatened to nick what would have been a barely-deserved equaliser amid the chaos of Burn. What was missing throughout, however, was quality and control. Marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo remains without a goal and was hooked on 57 minutes after another subdued outing. The others in attack repeatedly ran down blind alleys.

These two clubs have long been kindred spirits in their attempts to storm the Premier League’s elite. But whenever they have lowered the drawbridge, the following season has invariably seen them thrown back in the moat.

Newcastle, you suspect, are set to sink even deeper this season.

Sports.title: Revealed: Marcus Rashford has been undergoing regular treatment all season in bid to beat injury that has affected performances for Man United
Sports.content:
Marcus Rashford is having running repairs to be available for Manchester United this season as the England star continues to struggle with the hip injury that has dogged him since the World Cup. Rashford has started six of United's nine games this season having returned to Old Trafford in the summer following loan spells at Barcelona and Aston Villa. The 28-year-old has yet to score or make an assist, and failed to convert a volley in front of goal during Tuesday's Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid. However, sources say that Rashford has been undergoing regular treatment all season to be available for head coach Michael Carrick, and it is inevitable that the problem has impacted his performances. It remains to be seen if Rashford – who withdrew from England's recent Nations League games – starts against Leeds at Elland Road on Sunday with Matheus Cunha able to revert to the left flank after Amad Diallo's return from injury on the right freed up Bryan Mbeumo to play through the middle. 'Marcus has done a lot of good things,' said Carrick. 'He obviously had a slight injury where he pulled out with England, and he's had to manage that a little bit. Marcus Rashford has started six of Man United's nine games so far this season despite a hip injury 'He's not quite getting that little bit of a break, putting himself in good positions and having some opportunities. He had one the other night maybe that he felt he probably could have done better with, but he's in there to make a difference. 'He keeps doing the right things, and you get the rewards in the end. So as long as he keeps doing that, he'll be okay.' Bruno Fernandes has also been carrying an injury that forced him to sit out one of Portugal's games during the international break and appears to have affected his recent performances for United, although Carrick said that was not the reason his captain came off in the 80th minute in Madrid. 'He's been carrying some sort of issue, but he's pretty much over that now, to be honest, and he'll be back to his best,' added the United boss. 'A lot of players do carry them and it goes under the radar. People just think everyone's 100 per cent fully fit and it's probably not very often the case. 'We've got to share the load in all sorts of different ways: that's working, quality-wise, performing, being available. 'It's not an individual thing. When it's all good, it's not always just Bruno. Certainly if it's not so good, it's not all Bruno. He's a fantastic footballer, and he has a big impact on our group. 'Just because he may not be hitting the headlines or the highlights like he did last year doesn't mean that he can't, and that he won't, and I'm sure he'll do that pretty quickly.'
