Sports.title: Michael Carrick responds to Nicky Butt's 'management's not for me' claim before landing the Man United job - as defiant boss insists he does not fear the sack ahead of crunch Leeds clash
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick responds to Nicky Butt's 'management's not for me' claim before landing the Man United job - as defiant boss insists he does not fear the sack ahead of crunch Leeds clash

Michael Carrick has laughed off former Manchester United midfielder Nicky Butt's claim this week that the Old Trafford boss had told him he was no longer interested in football management before landing the job.

Butt told The Good, The Bad & The Football podcast sponsored by Midnite this week, that Carrick had revealed in a private conversation before replacing Ruben Amorim: 'no it's not for me, it's too much, my head's all over the show, I'd only do it for the big job. The big job is Man United.'

Carrick returned to Old Trafford in January as Ruben Amorim's replacement seven months after he was sacked from his first managerial job at Middlesbrough, and led United to a third-placed finish in the Premier League.

Carrick insists though, ahead of this weekend's trip to Leeds: 'I definitely wouldn't be here if that was the case, would I?' At this stage, it's the best job and the best role I could possibly have.

'I feel a real privilege of being in this position and a real responsibility, but equally a drive of wanting to make a difference and having success here.

'I'm loving it. I love the situation when actually you get some sort of struggle and you've got to find a way out of it. I actually enjoy that because that's part of what drives you to have success.

Michael Carrick was given the permanent role as Manchester United manager in the summer but has experienced a challenging start to the new season

Nicky Butt took to his podcast to suggest that Michael Carrick had no desire to go into management before landing the United job

'If you're not ready for that and you can't do anything that's difficult, then you're never going to be great. So we've got to work our way through it, and I'm enjoying it as we go.'

Carrick will take United to Elland Road – the scene of Amorim's last stand as head coach in January – adamant that he does not fear for his job.

United face old foes Leeds with Carrick under increasing pressure after a run of four defeats and two wins in nine games this season.

His predecessor Amorim was sacked over a post-match meltdown at Elland Road in which he took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox but Carrick isn't worried about his future.

He said: 'I don't think about: 'How am I going to get through this? How am I going to survive this? What do I need to do to look after myself?'.

'It's not important. I really don't take it about me. It's about this football club and winning football matches.

'I don't think (Leeds) is the last game I need right now. I'm really looking forward to the game. I generally feel the drive for myself to want to push this club forward more than anything.

'There's always negativity if you want to look for it or want to feel it. But I don't go looking for it, and I don't want to feel it.

'I understand the reality. I accept where we are, but I don't feel that. I'm totally focused on what's best for this football club and what it's going to take to win games: get the boys playing how we know we're capable of, and we still don't think we're that far away.

'We can turn a few things in our favour, and we can move forward pretty quickly.'

Sports.title: NFL analyst slammed for 'outrageous' Jalen Hurts theory after Eagles star is ruled out with scary blood clot
Sports.content:
NFL analyst slammed for 'outrageous' Jalen Hurts theory after Eagles star is ruled out with scary blood clot

NFL Network analyst Michael Robinson has come under fire after appearing to question the scary blood clot that has seen Jalen Hurts put on injured reserve.

'To me, it looked like Jalen is kind of getting himself out of the fray so that this lost season... doesn’t look like it's on [him],' the ex-NFL star said in a clip that has sparked outrage.

Philadelphia announced on Thursday that star quarterback Hurts has a superficial blood clot and on Sunday it was confirmed that he will miss at least four games. A superficial blood clot develops in a vein close to the surface of the skin.

The issue was discovered before Sunday's loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London, where Hurts was deemed healthy enough to play and finished the game without incident.

Since then, the Eagles said, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the blood clot, forcing the team to rule him out indefinitely.

But Robinson, a Super Bowl champion with the Seattle Seahawks, has now implied that there is more to the injury than meets the eye.

Michael Robinson appeared to question the blood clot suffered by Eagles star Jalen Hurts

Philadelphia quarterback Hurts will now miss Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers

'If I'm Jalen Hurts... I’m saying: "Well if everybody's hurt, I'm hurt, too,"' Robinson said

'It looked like they were trying to pin the outcome of this season on Jalen Hurts, just so that they can have an excuse later on to move on from Jalen Hurts,' he said on NFL GameDay Kickoff before suggesting the quarterback is choosing to sit on the sideline.

'If I'm just playing devil's advocate... if I'm Jalen Hurts, or anybody in Jalen Hurts' camp, I’m saying: "Well if everybody's hurt, I'm hurt, too."'

He continued: 'Guys, I've been cleated before. And I'm not saying a superficial blood clot isn't serious. I’m not saying that. But I would advise all of our viewers to Google "superficial blood clot" rather than a real blood clot.'

Among those to criticize Robinson was former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, who called his comments 'ridiculous' and 'outrageous.'

He wrote on social media: 'WHAT ARE WE DOING MAN? I would never expect this from a former player. I wouldn’t expect this from ANYBODY. Jalen Hurts can’t even have a serious medical condition in peace.'

Robinson floated his theory despite the Eagles releasing a lengthy statement explaining the timeline of Hurts' injury.

'On Thursday, October 8th, Jalen visited the training room after practice requesting treatment for his calf,' the team wrote. 'He informed the medical staff he had been cleated during the Rams game on October 4th.

'This was his first treatment session for the calf injury following the game, after having practiced in full both Wednesday and Thursday. On Friday, Jalen received treatment, practiced in full, and was added to the practice report.

THIS IS RIDICULOUS.



The negative narratives around Jalen Hurts have to stop.



Michael Robinson is accusing Jalen Hurts of saying, 'Well if everybody's hurt, I'm hurt, too.” And that Jalen Hurts is “pulling himself out so that this doesn't look like it's on me." when Jalen Hurts… pic.twitter.com/vdqU6Qb3YB — Robert Griffin III (@RGIII) October 17, 2026

Hurts' issue was discovered before Sunday's loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London

'Out of an abundance of caution, an ultrasound was performed on Saturday following the team's flight to London and walkthrough,' the statement continued.

'The ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play. Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia.

'Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday, received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report. Throughout our time in London and this week, we have remained in communication with the league office regarding the matter.

'On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment. His health and safety are our highest priority.'

The Eagles are 2-3 this season and have lost three straight amid injuries to running back Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith and guard Landon Dickerson, while center Cam Jurgens was traded to the Baltimore Ravens and right tackle Lane Johnson abruptly retired.

Sports.title: Top NFL draft prospect Colin Simmons carted off field after suffering worrying injury in Texas' clash with Florida
Sports.content:
Texas star Colin Simmons had to be carted off the field after suffering a worrying injury during the Longhorns' clash with Florida on Saturday.

Simmons is one of the best defensive players in college football, with the 20-year-old edge rusher expected to be a top-five pick in the 2027 NFL draft.

Early in the fourth quarter of Saturday's game in Austin, however, he appeared to hurt his lower leg after being thrown to the ground.

Trainers rushed on to treat Simmons, who was helped toward the sideline before he was put on a cart and driven from the field.

The injury occurred after the edge rusher was blocked by Florida tight end Lacota Dippre and offensive tackle Bryce Lovett with the two teams tied at 17-17.

'[A] scary sight for Colin Simmons - and if you're a Texas fan. Not just of the best defensive players in the country, but one of the best football players period,' ESPN’s Jordan Rodgers said on the live broadcast.

Texas' Colin Simmons took a cart to the locker room against Florida. pic.twitter.com/gSvB3y6nOv — ESPN College Football (@ESPNCFB) October 17, 2026

Texas star Colin Simmons had to be carted off the field after suffering a worrying injury

Simmons, one of college football's best defensive players, is expected to be a top draft pick

Simmons gave fans the Longhorns' customary 'Hook 'em' gesture before the cart left the field. But he cut a devastated figure as he headed toward the locker room.

Before the injury, no one in Texas burnt orange had amassed more tackles (eight) than Simmons, who had also recorded a sack.

The edge rusher has been one of the most devastating players in college football this season. Over the past three games alone, the 20-year-old has 8.5 sacks to his name.

Without Simmons, Texas fell to a stunning 27-24 loss to the Gators that could prove pivotal in the Longhorns' hopes of making the playoffs.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

YouTube YouTube , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: Following decades of US domination, British heavyweight boxing is on top - after Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley and Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua, there are Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
In the small hours of May 16, 1955 my father woke me in the darkness, lit a candle in the scullery, plugged in his old crystal radio set and told me to listen to a world heavyweight title fight taking place in San Francisco.

Don Cockell of Balham, south London, was challenging Rocky Marciano of Brockton, Massachusetts, for the world heavyweight championship. Most of the sound which came whistling through the static was that of Marciano’s eight-ounce gloves thudding into Cockell’s head and body.

Marciano kept knocking down Cockell, who kept getting up. Until the ninth round, when Rocky nailed him to the canvas for good with a booming right which seemingly connected while he was on his knees.

When the BBC radio commentator put that question to the champ, Marciano replied: ‘Britain can be proud of her boy Don Cockell.’

Jack Powell, whose toughness had carried him through the landings and trenches of the Second World War as well as countless fights inside and outside the ring, slammed his fist on the kitchen table and said: ‘As if keeping beating us ain’t enough, they have to bloody patronise us.’

I was 13. Not until I was 50 – and Marciano had long since become the only heavyweight champ to retire undefeated – would Lennox Lewis end our century-long wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons.

Lennox Lewis (pictured) ended Great Britain's wait for a successor to Bob Fitzsimmons as the United States dominated the heavyweight scene

American stars such as George Foreman (left) and Muhammad Ali (right) dominated the previous era

That eternity was flooded with such revered Americans as Jack Johnson, Jack Dempsey, Joe Louis, Floyd Patterson, Sonny Liston, Muhammad Ali, Joe Frazier, George Foreman, Mike Tyson, Larry Holmes and Evander Holyfield.

The golden age of heavyweight boxing gave us the Fight of the Century and the Thrilla in Manila – both between Ali and Frazier – the Rumble in the Jungle with Ali and Foreman, the Upset of the Century by Buster Douglas over Tyson, Dempsey v Gene Tunney, Louis v both Max Schmeling and Jersey Joe Walcott and Ali’s slaying of the Liston monster. That was the time when the Star Spangled Banner flew over America’s mocking of ‘Britain’s Horizontal Heavyweights.’

Henry Cooper remained perpendicular against The Greatest of them all but there was scant recognition over the water of how he knocked Ali down and almost out with the left hook renowned as ‘Enery’s ‘Ammer’ in the first of two stadium fights he lost to his propensity to suffer cuts.

So, oh, how we gloated when we watched Riddick Bowe dump his WBC belt in a London dustbin rather than fight Lewis, who was thereby elevated to his first title by decree. Rejoiced when Lennox validated his title by beating Oliver McCall in September 1995. Acclaimed Lenny the Lion when he became our only three-time world heavyweight champion.

We breathed a huge sigh of relief when Frank Bruno beat McCall at an emotional Wembley, finally to become world champion. Just as we fretted for him when he genuflected umpteen times on his way to the Las Vegas ring for a second crushing by Tyson and the loss of his crown.

Even so, British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast. The US can boast 53 champions all time in the prize-ring’s marquee division. All the way back to the immortal John L Sullivan in the late 1880s. But the UK has accelerated from one active heavyweight champion in 2003 – Lewis when he bloodied and defeated Vitali Kliltschko – to a running total of 11 today if you delete the asterisks against Michael Bent, Herbie Hide and Henry Akinwande who wore the WBO belt before that organisation was fully recognised.

David Haye built on the Lewis legacy when he bamboozled Russia’s 7ft giant Nikolai Valuev and thereby emulated Holyfield’s feat of an undisputed cruiserweight king becoming world heavyweight champion.

The Russo-Ukraine brothers Klitschko broke the US domination but then both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua followed that Lewis victory over Vitali by vanquishing Wladimir.

British heavyweight boxing was transitioning from famine to feast, which has included the likes of Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua (right)

Britannia’s Rule was stunningly interrupted by Oleksandr Usyk’s revival of the Kyiv Conspiracy with two dazzling victories apiece over the Gypsy King and AJ, followed by another double over their heir apparent Daniel Dubois.

Oleksandr The Great’s abrupt relinquishing of all the belts opened the gateway to an immediate UK renaissance. One in which it is not Americans but Brits fighting each other for the glittering prizes.

This Saturday at the O2, Dubois and the amazingly reconstructed white-collar boxer Fabio Wardley reprise their blood and thunder war for the now-respected WBO title. This time with Dynamite Daniel as the champion.

The winner is likely to go on to meet in the not-too-distant future whoever prevails in the over-long awaited settlement between Fury and Joshua - which, belatedly though it comes in December, is so full of fascination that it has sold ticket at prices higher than the gross national product of some third-world countries.

By then Moses Itauma should have recovered from the drastic loss of stamina – and a blown IBF title shot against Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic – to resume leadership of the next generation. German WBC champion Agit Kabayel will soon be in all those crosshairs.

With all the above except Joshua in Frank Warren’s stable there are more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made. With only one big guy of promise, Jared Anderson, to be seen on the western horizon.

And to think Americans used to belittle their last heavyweight champion of note Deontay Wilder as ‘just a puncher’.

The biggest puncher since Iron Mike, as it happens. How they must be wishing over there that Fury had not ended the Bronze Bomber’s five-year run of knockouts in the murderous final act of their epic trilogy.

Daniel Dubois (left) and Fabio Wardley (right) will face off this weekend with more Brit-bashes galore waiting to be made

Throughout America’s glorious boxing history the world heavyweight champion was the symbol of their national manhood. Today they lay no claim to any of the alphabelts.

There are extraneous factors at work. The majority of strapping young American athletes - be they graduating from college or seeking ways out of the projects - are taking to basketball, their version of football and baseball, rather than take a headbashing in the ring on the off-chance of making their fortunes.

US boxing is down to pinning its hopes on a brash young Mexican-American welterweight Ryan Garcia - on the back of his destruction of a humiliated Conor Benn. All while the Blue Riband of the ring is hoisted this side of the pond.

Not so Yankee-Doodle-Dandy now, gentlemen.

Sports.title: 'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that': Daniel Dubois' trainer warns Fabio Wardley is risking his boxing future - and says team put his health at risk by letting him battle on in first bout
Sports.content:
'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that': Daniel Dubois' trainer warns Fabio Wardley is risking his boxing future - and says team put his health at risk by letting him battle on in first bout

Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter, as he suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long.

Wardley and Dubois produced a gruelling contest in Manchester last May, with the fight eventually stopped in the 11th round after the former world champion had subjected his opponent to a sustained assault in the latter rounds.

Wardley's remarkable resilience was a defining feature of the contest, but Charles believes the damage he endured could already be catching up with him ahead of their highly anticipated rematch this Saturday.

The veteran trainer also questioned whether Wardley's team should have intervened sooner, suggesting that their hope of seeing the champion produce another fight-changing punch may have come at a cost to his health.

'They let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health,' Charles said.

'Being the champion, being a guy who has done it previously and is able to pull out a shot at any point during the fight, whether early or late, he has got that in him.

Daniel Dubois' trainer Don Charles believes Fabio Wardley is already feeling the effects of the punishment he absorbed in their brutal first encounter

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

'So perhaps the team were thinking, 'Maybe he just needs that one punch', because he has done it in the past. But there comes a point where you have to do the sensible thing.

'A couple of days after the fight, I relaxed and watched it back. Oh my God, it was really bad, in my opinion.

'Again, it is their decision. There is the referee there and there are the doctors. But I think they let Fabio down a little bit, in my opinion, for his health.'

Charles stressed that his focus during the fight had been entirely on Dubois, meaning he had not fully appreciated the extent of Wardley's punishment until he watched the contest back afterwards.

His comments come amid renewed scrutiny of the first fight and the decision to allow Wardley to continue into the championship rounds, although the man from Ipswich has defended his corner against suggestions they got it wrong.

Wardley regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night in the ring, arguing that the damage accumulated in such gruelling contests can gradually take its toll.

'I think he is already noticing the wear and tear, from an observational point of view,' Charles said.

Charles suggested the former heavyweight champion's corner did him a 'disservice' by allowing their fight to continue for so long

Dubois has just signed a six-figure deal brokered by NVA SEG Talent Group to become the global ambassador for British performance and lifestyle brand Resonance Energy Wear

'It is entertaining for the public, granted, but you cannot have a very long career fighting like that. It catches up with you. It really does, and it chips away at you.

'You cannot keep fighting gung-ho like that. It is very entertaining, like I said, but you really have to look at the bigger picture.'

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early despite preparing for the possibility of another prolonged battle.

'What you are going to see is a more disciplined display and more alertness,' he said.

'Obviously, we got caught off guard last time, so we have rectified that. This time, it is going to be a more disciplined, more dynamic and more technical performance.

'We have trained as if this were the olden days, when you boxed up to 15 rounds. If this fight has to go 15 rounds to get a victory, 15 rounds it is.

'This fight could end in round one, or it could end in round 12 or 15. It needs to be.'

One of Charles's biggest questions ahead of the rematch concerns how Wardley will respond when Dubois lands cleanly, particularly if DDD can recreate some of the punishing moments from their first encounter.

Charles believes Dubois will approach the return bout with greater discipline after being caught off guard in their initial meeting and warns the rematch could end early

Charles believes the physical demands of Wardley's all-action style could have consequences beyond a single night, arguing that the damage accumulated can gradually take its toll

The expert trainer suggested that the memories of that night could return once Wardley begins absorbing shots again, although he acknowledged the 31-year-old's extraordinary toughness.

'Fabio is made of something else. He is made of steel, that man, the amount of punishment he took and kept taking,' Charles said.

'But it is our duty to recall those entries, to remind him of the pain he felt last May in Manchester.

'As soon as that bell rings, our duty is to recall that pain. If he has forgotten it, Daniel will remind him in that ring: 'This is what you were feeling.'

'He is a human being like you and I. Once he starts feeling that unbearable pain, the rest is up to him and his team, and what they do under the referee's supervision.'

Sports.title: Floyd Mayweather gushes over Donald Trump after President praises boxer's 'good looks' at Republican rally
Sports.content:
Floyd Mayweather gushed over Donald Trump on stage in Arizona - after the President praised the boxer's good looks.

Mayweather flew on Air Force One to Bullhead City, Arizona for a campaign rally held to support Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The undefeated fighter was the latest sports star to join Trump on the campaign trail and drew high praise as he was introduced.

'One of the greatest fighters in boxing history,' Trump said, calling Mayweather an 'unbelievable defensive fighter.'

'That's why he looks so good,' Trump continued, before adding as he walked up to the stage: 'Look at this guy, he looks so good. Who would believe he's a fighter? He looks so good! He doesn't have a mark!'

And the high praise was reciprocated, as Mayweather declared: 'We couldn't have chosen a better president twice than Donald Trump.'

Donald Trump welcomed boxer Floyd Mayweather to the stage in Bullhead City, Arizona

Trump praised Mayweather's good looks as he welcomed him to the stage at the rally

Mayweather delivered praise of Trump as he called America the 'greatest country in the world'

Mayweather had started his address by telling the crowd: 'America is the greatest country in the world. If I died and came back a million times, I would always choose America.

'It was great to represent this country in the 1996 Olympic Games,' Mayweather said. 'To go out there and represent the red, white, and blue.'

He then turned his praise to Trump before adding: 'So it's all about keeping this country strong, sticking together, and believing in one another. America is the greatest country in the world. Thank you.'

Mayweather, 49, a Vegas native, happens to have strong business ties in Arizona.

Dennis Rodman, Mike Tyson, Jake Paul, Roger Clemens and Jon Gruden have all made appearances at recent rallies in support of Trump.

Mayweather has long been an outspoken supporter of Trump, hailing him the 'best president in US history' last year.

He attended Trump's first inauguration as president and supported him throughout his first term in the Oval Office.

Policy-wise, Mayweather and Trump have been aligned on a few issues, including in the Middle East. Mayweather is a staunch supporter of Israel and donated $1million to the United Hatzalah of Israel in 2024.

Mayweather flew to the event on Air Force One earlier in the day to travel to the event

Mayweather has been aligned with Trump on several issues and been a public supporter

Mayweather is the latest sports star to be brought in by Trump on the midterms campaign trail

Join the discussion What do you think motivates celebrities like Mayweather to publicly align themselves with political figures?

'We had Trump before, we didn't appreciate him,' Mayweather told Fox Business in February of last year. 'I think Trump is a great president, actually he's the best president in my eyes, he's the best president we've ever had. Great business man and that's what it's about.'

'Trump has done an amazing job and a lot of people around America are upset. But no matter who goes into the White House, we're always upset. And I think Trump is the man for the job, he's the best president in my eyes.'

Mayweather's fellow boxing icon Tyson also joined Trump on the Presidential aircraft last week, making the journey from the White House to Syracuse, New York.

During his speech at the rally, Trump spotted Tyson in the crowd and invited the former boxing champion on stage.

'I think we have to call him up, Mike Tyson, will you get up here?' Trump said.

As the President's athletic guest of the day, Tyson praised Trump in front of the Syracuse crowd, thanking him during a brief moment on stage.

'Thank you, thank you very much. I'm just happy to be up here with my president, President Trump. There's no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn't for a president like Donald Trump,' Tyson said.

Trump was also joined by NBA icon Rodman in Durant, Oklahoma, and former NFL coach Gruden and influencer-turned-boxer Paul in Youngstown, Ohio.

He announced his intention to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom to MLB legend Clemens when the former pitcher joined him at a rally in San Antonio, Texas.

Sports.title: Former world champion boxer dies, aged 59, after heart attack at a bingo hall: Jorge 'Locomotora' Castro's daughter talks of dad's 'quick' death
Sports.content:
Former boxing world champion Jorge 'Locomotora' Castro has tragically passed away at the age of 59.

Castro, an Argentine great who won 130 of his 144 fights across a 20-year career, died on Wednesday after suffering a heart attack at a bingo hall.

Castro's daughter, Quimely, confirmed the cause of death and gave a heartbreaking account of his final moments in an interview with the Argentine media.

'My dad’s passing was natural,' she said. 'He had a heart attack. His chest started to hurt and he couldn’t take it.

'It was just a matter of 15 minutes, nothing more. The Scientific Police already took care of proving it was totally natural.
