World.title: Search continues for 11 missing after boat sank off Mexico’s Baja coast
World.content:
Some of 16 survivors treated for suspected shark bites, US coastguard says.

The search continues for 11 people still missing after a boat capsized off Mexico’s Baja California coast on Friday, as multiple survivors have been treated for suspected shark bites, according to the US coastguard.

“Several of the individuals rescued were suffering from severe injuries consistent with shark bites, and the Coast Guard provided life-saving first aid while en route [to] San Diego,” the coastguard said in a statement on Saturday.

Sixteen Mexican nationals were rescued on Friday. Survivors told officials there were 27 people on board.

The coastguard and US Navy used multiple aircraft and boats, along with assistance from the Mexican Navy, to search the area for the remaining passengers. An additional helicopter will be deployed later on Saturday, according to the coastguard.

A Mayday call was transmitted from someone on the boat at about 1am on Friday, coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini said on the day.

A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours later. It took about 90 minutes for the crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, he added.

The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico, an area popular with fishing and leisure boats, but that is also frequented by smugglers.

Although the incident did not happen in US waters, coastguard official Charlie Valor said on Saturday they “were able to help, and that’s why we launched our assets”.



Fatal attempts to transport refugees and migrants from Mexico to the US have occurred in the past.

In May 2025, at least three people died when a boat flipped off the coast about 56km (35 miles) north of the US-Mexico border.

In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the US coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog, and one capsized in the surf.

World.title: Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion
World.content:
Kabila’s move raises fresh questions about the war in eastern Congo and prospects for peace.

Goma, DR Congo – Hopes for peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have suffered another setback after former President Joseph Kabila joined a new political-military coalition challenging President Felix Tshisekedi.

Announced in Goma on Monday evening, the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), or Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, is led by Kabila and replaces the existing alliance between the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and the March 23 Movement (M23). The new coalition brings together figures and forces associated with the two movements, accuses Tshisekedi of tyranny and calls for resistance by all means, including force.

Goma, the main city in eastern Congo’s North Kivu province, has been under M23-AFC control since January last year. Kabila’s move brings a former head of state directly into the leadership of the rebellion.

The conflict has displaced millions and drawn in neighbouring countries. Its roots stretch back decades, shaped by regional rivalries, unresolved security concerns and competition for territory and mineral resources. The aftermath of Rwanda’s 1994 genocide helped fuel wars across the region, while tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali continue to shape the fighting.

M23 says it took up arms because the Congolese government failed to honour earlier commitments. The Congolese government and international actors have accused Rwanda of supporting the group, an allegation Kigali denies, citing security threats from armed groups operating in eastern Congo.



Whether Kabila’s leadership will reshape the rebellion or further complicate efforts to end the war remains unclear. In Goma, residents fear the latest realignment will push peace further out of reach.

Why do residents fear the war is far from over?

For Basa Juhudi, Kabila’s decision has revived fears that the conflict will drag on.

“As a resident of Goma, I believed the war might end in the very near future, hoping that the Congolese government would liberate us. And we are greatly surprised that even our former president has joined the fray,” he told Al Jazeera.

Juhudi said Kabila’s political experience makes his involvement particularly troubling.

“The fact that Joseph Kabila has joined the rebellion, bearing in mind that he is our former president and knows this country inside out, means the war is far from over. I am not happy about this frightening situation.”

He also fears for the country’s democratic future, recalling the peaceful transfer of power in 2019, when Tshisekedi succeeded Kabila.

“Today, I am very afraid. I don’t know if I will be lucky enough to experience a proper democracy in the DRC. I was delighted by the country’s very first peaceful transfer of power,” Juhudi said.

How does Kabila’s past shape his return to the conflict?

Kabila came to power in 2001 following the assassination of his father, Laurent-Desire Kabila. He was elected president in 2006 and re-elected in 2011.

His second constitutional term was due to end in 2016, but elections were delayed. Critics accused him of seeking to remain in power beyond the constitutionally permitted two terms. Protests against the delays were met with deadly violence before a political compromise paved the way for elections in December 2018.

Tshisekedi was declared the winner and took office in January 2019, marking the DRC’s first peaceful transfer of presidential power through elections. Kabila defended the election delays, arguing that the Congolese people had ultimately resolved their problems through dialogue.

His alignment with the FRN marks a new phase in his confrontation with Tshisekedi. The coalition presents itself as a political alternative to the government while maintaining an armed challenge to its authority. Whether Kabila can translate his political experience and networks into wider support remains uncertain.

Can dialogue still avert a wider confrontation?

Kabila’s move has drawn criticism from within the Congolese political establishment.

Vital Kamerhe, a former speaker of the National Assembly and leader of the Union for the Congolese Nation (UNC), urged the movement to abandon armed struggle.

“You cannot erase your own record by accusing your successor,” Kamerhe declared in a speech on Wednesday.



“I call on the leaders of this movement to abandon their plans and prioritise the path of dialogue. Whatever our frustrations, our differences or our ambitions, nothing, absolutely nothing, can justify us taking up weapons against our own country, at the risk of sacrificing our own Congolese lives,” he said.

His appeal highlights the central challenge facing peace efforts: political grievances remain unresolved, while renewed fighting threatens a population already battered by conflict.

What does Kabila’s move mean for peace initiatives?

The United States and Qatar have pursued separate diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the conflict.

In Doha, representatives of the Congolese government and AFC-M23 have discussed a ceasefire, the return of refugees, the release of detainees and measures to counter rhetoric that stigmatises ethnic minorities.

Washington has pursued an agreement between the DRC and Rwanda, including commitments relating to the neutralisation of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the withdrawal of Rwandan troops from Congolese territory.

The initiatives address different but connected dimensions of the crisis. Kabila’s emergence as leader of the FRN raises questions about who will represent the armed opposition and whether existing commitments will be respected.

However, the new coalition has said it intends to honour commitments made during the Doha negotiations.

In a communique released on Wednesday, Freddy Kaniki, one of the FRN’s leaders, said the signing of the coalition’s memorandum of association and its official launch marked the dissolution of the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), which the FRN succeeds by right.

The communique said the FRN would assume the AFC’s “rights, obligations and commitments, in particular those entered into as part of the Doha negotiations”.

The statement suggests that the coalition intends to maintain the commitments made by its predecessor. It remains to be seen, however, how this pledge will translate into progress towards a ceasefire and a lasting settlement.

For Josue Akuzwe Walayi, a Congolese human rights activist, the development threatens to undermine hopes raised by the negotiations.

“My greatest fear is for the future of the Doha and Washington peace initiatives; it is not just that they will be a diplomatic failure, but that they will become yet more agreements without any real peace for the Congolese people,” he tells Al Jazeera.

Walayi argues that agreements without effective accountability mechanisms risk becoming empty promises. Lasting peace, he says, requires parties to honour their commitments and violations to be documented, investigated and punished in accordance with the law.

“What would the Doha and Washington agreements be worth if, despite the negotiations, Congolese people continue to die, families remain forced into exile and communities live in fear? The danger would be to normalise the war whilst the people pay the price,” he warns.



Could Kabila’s return pose a broader challenge to Kinshasa?

Kabila’s return to the centre of the conflict comes amid his legal confrontation with the Congolese state. Last year, a Congolese military court sentenced him to death in his absence on charges, including treason and war crimes, linking him to the M23 rebellion. His relatives described the conviction as “unjust” and “politically motivated”.

Goma resident Willo Riziki says Kabila’s involvement should prompt the government to reassess the challenge it faces.

“The Congolese authorities must now take this war very seriously. If Kinshasa thought it was dealing with puppets, that is no longer the case. There are people all over the country who remain loyal to Kabila,” Riziki told Al Jazeera.

How far that loyalty extends, and whether it can translate into organised political or military support, remains uncertain.

There has been no official government reaction to the coalition’s announcement. Last week, after Kabila warned that the country was in peril and needed to be saved, government spokesman Patrick Muyaya said the former president had “nothing to offer but chaos”. In a post on X, Muyaya described Kabila as a “man of the past, nostalgic for anti-democratic methods”.

The confrontation between Kabila and Tshisekedi reflects a wider struggle over the country’s political future. But for civilians in the east, the immediate question is whether the latest realignment will bring more fighting and further delay a negotiated settlement.

“We don’t know if the war will end here,” said Juhudi.

World.title: Iran says two tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The vessels, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, used an unauthorised route, the IRGC says.

Share Iran says two tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Strait of Hormuz on social media

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said two oil tankers, each carrying about two million barrels of crude oil, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

The first tanker hit a mine, triggering an explosion and a “fierce fire”, the IRGC said on Saturday, while the second tanker hit a mine that engulfed it “in a massive blaze”, Iran’s official IRNA news agency reported.

Information about the ships’ names or the origin of their cargo was not immediately available.

IRNA said the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route not authorised by Iran.

The IRGC also claimed that while one tanker tried to cross the waterway “with US support”, the second vessel was left immobilised.

Iran seized control of the Strait of Hormuz after the US-Israeli war on the country began in late February. Tehran has since demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. About one-fifth of global oil consumption transited the waterway before the war.

This week, IRGC naval commander Rear Admiral Ali Azmaei warned that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile”.

The United States has imposed its own naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Iran’s army earlier said that two tankers caught fire on Thursday and Friday in Tehran’s “prohibited zone” in the Gulf of Oman.

Maritime monitors also reported two tankers struck in Gulf waters off Saudi Arabia on Friday.

Last Sunday, six vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, the most in a single day since the war began, according to security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization and the UK maritime agency UKMTO.

Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past two weeks, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month.



Nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through on October 8, but only 2.9 million on October 11, according to Kpler data.

The disruption has pushed up global energy prices and inflation.

US President Donald Trump has explicitly ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran. “I wouldn’t use nuclear,” he told the Newsmax news site in an interview on Thursday.

Trump said that he was also not considering putting troops on the ground in Iran. “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it,” he said, adding he believes a deal to end the war will be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.

World.title: Buildings burn as French protests go into the night
World.content:
Buildings burn as French protests go into the night

NewsFeed Buildings burn as French protests go into the night

Witnesses say masked protesters set fire to Limoges town hall, which officials say is now ‘largely lost’. In Paris, fires, looting and tear gas marked a night of unrest as cost-of-living protests raged on throughout the country.

World.title: Saudi-led forces try to break Houthi siege of Taiz with airstrikes
World.content:
Saudi-led forces try to break Houthi siege of Taiz with airstrikes

NewsFeed Saudi-led forces try to break Houthi siege of Taiz with airstrikes

Saudi-led forces say they’ve struck multiple positions around the Yemeni city of Taiz to break the Houthi siege. The city has emerged as the new frontline in the war between the internationally recognised government and Houthi fighters.

World.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
World.content:
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.

At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.

In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.

Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.

Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.

World.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
World.content:
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.

But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".

The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".

It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".

World.title: Deaths confirmed in major fire at Canada military base
World.content:
A large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta has killed and injured some people, the defence minister said, without confirming the number of casualties.

The Canadian Armed Forces were working with local authorities to manage the fire and were looking into what caused it, David McGuinty said, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate".

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said on X that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation describes it as "the principal base for live fire training exercises". About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a regular day, according to the CBC.

Saturday's blaze "spread rapidly due to high winds" and had torn through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said.

McGuinty told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory".

Alberta's premier Danielle Smith says the "significant and tragic fire" is "affecting many of [the province's] brave military personnel". Provincial authorities are in touch with the central government in managing and investigating the situation, she added.

It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT).

Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way.

Neighbouring provinces have offered their support.

Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe says he has deployed resources to Alberta and is "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia premier David Eby says his government has "reached out to Alberta to offer all possible assistance".

World.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
World.content:
US President Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the president in September.

But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the suspension would consist of a 60-day pause intended to analyse the impact on the global economy.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

Rubio said Trump wanted to use the 60 days to analyse "what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy".

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Since then, Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The sanctions suspension seemed to add further fuel to the fire, while Russia welcomed it.

World.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
World.content:
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.

Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.

The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.

Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.

Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.

The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.

During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.

Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.

Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.

Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.

World.title: At least 17 dead in crush at Hindu festival event in India
World.content:
At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.

The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.

West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.

Six of the dead have been identified, Adhikari said.

A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.".

Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions.

Two years ago, 121 people were killed in Uttar Pradesh during a Hindu religious gathering.

World.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
World.content:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

World.title: Teacher fought US school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
World.content:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.

The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.

The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.

He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.

Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.

He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".

"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.

Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.

"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".

The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.

Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.

World.title: Court remands man who killed girlfriend over alleged HIV infection
World.content:
A magistrate’s court in Enugu State has remanded Chibuike Okpara, the 30-year-old man who allegedly killed his girlfriend and concealed her body in a toilet in the state.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the police in the state arrested the suspect for killing the victim on 19 September in his apartment at Olympic Layout, One-Day Area of Enugu State.

The victim has been identified as Chinyere Ugwu, a 27-year-old graduate of Medical Laboratory Science.

The victim recently concluded her mandatory one-year National Youth Service Corps in Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

Arraignment and remand

Mr Okpara was arraigned before the magistrate’s court on Friday, Daniel Ndukwe, the police spokesperson in Enugu State said in a statement on Saturday.

Mr Ndukwe, a superintendent of police, said the arraignment of the defendant followed the conclusion of investigations into his offences.

The spokesperson said the defendant said the court subsequently remanded the defendant in the correctional facility.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The court also ordered the transmission of the case file to the attorney-general of Enugu State through the Directorate of Public Prosecutions (DPP) for review and legal advice,” he said.

He did not mention the particular court where the defendant was arraigned and remanded.

Mr Ndukwe did not respond to a PREMIUM TIMES enquiry sent to him on Saturday night seeking to know the exact court where the arraignment took place.

The spokesperson said the Commissioner of Police in Enugu State, Bitrus Giwa, has reaffirmed the command’s commitment to combating violent crime and ensuring the prompt prosecution of offenders.

Mr Giwa also urged young people, particularly women, to exercise caution in their relationships and remain alert to potential signs of violence.

Background

Mr Okpara was arrested on 19 September for killing the victim and concealing her body in his apartment at Olympic Layout, One-Day Area of Enugu State.

The suspect later confessed that he killed the victim over an argument that he infected her with HIV.

The suspect claimed he dumped the body of the deceased in the toilet because he did not know what to do at the time.

He said neighbours who later perceived offensive odour oozing from the victim’s corpse forced their way into the apartment and saw the body.

Mr Okpara further confessed that, to prevent her family from calling her phone, he damaged her mobile phone and her SIM card too.

The suspect recalled that he met the girl friend on Facebook in 2023 before he decided to relocate from Owerri in Imo State to Enugu in December 2025.

He later claimed that he killed the victim because he was under the influence of drugs at the time.

World.title: Transition from dinosaurs to the streets of USA, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
I try to understand countries by pounding their streets. This was partly why early morning Monday, 5 October, I hit the streets of New York. How early do people wake up in a city that never sleeps? The rush hour, how is it like?

This day, what attracted me most were children going to school. A man appears with a child sitting with the feet round his neck and clutching his head. I thought this was dangerous. Another approaches, singing loudly with a child running by his side. Then, a lady dashes across the road with two children following closely to catch a bus. Also, there is the kindergarten weeping as the mother dragged him to school. Yes, education is the key to the future, but these children don’t know that yet.

Three days later, a piece of news I dread in ‘God’s own country’ began to circulate. There has been a shooting. This time, in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of New York City. No, not by a disturbed individual or the police. The shooters were the new kids on the block; the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents. They had surrounded the car of 28-year old Dominican migrant, Oscar Belgal, who had his five-year old son with him. ICE agents fired at least seven shots into the car. Belgal was hit in the neck and, seized. But the boy was unhurt.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani called President Donald Trump and, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to negotiate Belgal’s release. Unsuccessful, he called a press conference demanding ICE stops its enforcement activities in the city because they are making it less safe. He then made a poetic demand: “This city wants ICE out. We want ICE out of our city, ICE out of our schools, ICE out of our hospitals, ICE out of our ​streets, ICE away from our kids.”

The Department of Homeland Security said it was a targeted enforcement operation during which, “the criminal illegal alien was injured.”

The city erupted in anger and two days of rallies followed. The anger was not only directed at the Trump administration, but also at Mamdani because protesters suspect the New York Police Department (NYPD), which he controls, might have aided ICE in the operation. Mamdani had wisely ordered a probe into possible NYPD co-operation.

I thought a lot, not just about American life, but humanity. Where are we coming from, where are we headed? I turned to the American Museum of Natural History. Perhaps it contains some answers. The museum itself is not allergic to controversy. One case was over the bronze statue of former President Theodore Roosevelt. It depicted him on horseback flanked by a walking indigenous American-Indian and an African-American. Some argued that it placed a Whiteman in a position of dominance and the Indigenous and the African as assistants or servants. To these activists, this was a depiction of internal colonialism. The controversy and protests which spread nationwide were so much that in June, 2021 the city Public Design Commission, voted to remove the statute, which had been unveiled in 1940.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

My primary attraction in the museum were the dinosaurs. The creatures had lived 245 million years on earth. There is a 65-million gap between their extinction and the arrival of human beings. It means, before we were, they were; before Adam was created and the subsequent genetic engineering that produced Eve, the dinosaurs had lived.

They seem better adapted to the earth than us. For instance their digestive system enabled them to eat and chew various things including pebbles. While we have two sets of teeth; the baby and adult teeth, the dinosaur with an average 65-teeth, had multiple teeth sets, always replacing its teeth when one is broken or worn down. The Duck-billed dinosaurs for instance, used up to 10,000 teeth in a lifetime. So what do we learn from these creatures that were one to forty metres in length? It is the explosions that led to the dinosaurs extinction. They covered the earth, shading it from the sun for months or years, making living practically impossible. The good news is that we have a similar capacity to cause explosions that can make human life go extinct.

I went through the section on origins of humanity. The Neanderthals, archaic humans who have gone extinct.

In our post-dinosaur world, the largest land animals are the elephants. I went to their section in the museum; giant creatures. The biggest known, was 3.96 metres tall weighing 12.24 tonnes found on 7 November, 1974 in Angola. I looked at them and other animals like gorillas, bears and lions and thought, our predatory inclinations may make these animals go extinct like dinosaurs. The creative displays depicted these animals in their natural environment.

Then, I stepped into another controversy; the North West Coast Hall dedicated to indigenous Indian life and culture. These included regalia for chiefs and spirits and, forms of government in which hierarchy depended not on wealth but how much a person gave out. The hall was filled with works of art and samples of Ocean-going canoes. The carvings, some over seven metres high, were carved from huge trees as were canoes that could carry dozens of persons.

The controversy is the indigenous people who did not see any reason why they should be located in a museum of natural history when they are not animals. But a scholar, Morgan Guerin defended the exhibition. He wrote in a part of the hall: “There is a lot of the ancestors’ souls within these pieces.”

There wasn’t much on Europe and I was advised to go to ‘The Met’ on 1000 Fifth Avenue which had over 5,000 years of art from various parts of the world. Next day, I was there, combing through Roman and Greek arts and African sections which showed that humanity began in Africa as did history.

Outside ‘The Met’ were crowds, some, sitting on steps built from the lower steps of the road, into the doors of the museum.

As usual, when in New York, I visit Harlem. There was the huge statue of Fredrick Douglas, the African American fighter who escaped from slavery to become one of the greatest abolitionists and orators. He once said: “It is easier to build strong children than to repair broken men.” There was that of Harriet Tubman who helped to free slaves. For her, it was “liberty or death.” On, to an African restaurant almost opposite the Malcolm X Mosque, beside the boulevard named after him. Brother Malcolm used to say, we must be liberated: “By Any Means Necessary.”

Similarly, we must protect human beings from predators and, save humanity from possible dinosaur-like extinction by any means necessary.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Obasanjo’s “My Watch”: A rare and generous act of witnessing (1), By Zayd Ibn Isah
World.content:
To understand the living legend and national icon that is Olusegun Obasanjo, one must first read and appreciate his unforgettable autobiography.

“During his watch, a watchman has no sleep and no respite.” — Olusegun Obasanjo, My Watch

There is a famous line in Chinua Achebe’s classic, Things Fall Apart: “Looking at the king’s mouth, one would think he never sucked at his mother’s breast.” It came to mind as I read Baba Obasanjo’s account of his early life, because few memoirs by men of such stature begin so humbly.

The book opens with his birth, as his mother narrated it to him: “You were born on Ifo Market day. I had put my wares together for the market when I suddenly went into labour. It meant that I could not go to the market that day. But before those who went to the market returned to the village, you were already born.”

With no birth certificates in those days, an event had to stand in for a date, and it was left to Baba to work out which Ifo Market day his mother meant. He settled on 5 March 1937. What could have been a dry footnote becomes, in his hands, a window into a world that measured time by markets rather than calendars.

His brief account of the Owu lineage works the same way: it gives just enough history to explain the audacity for which he is known, and never so much that it delays the story. This is among the book’s real strengths. Baba writes as a historian, digging as deeply into the wars of Ogun State and the founding of Kaduna as into his own memories, and the personal vantage point restores what school textbooks flatten. There are stories behind the stories, and it takes someone who has studied and documented them to show their depth. His account also reveals how connected Nigerians are: beneath our different tribes and tongues lie striking similarities in language, culture and tradition.

Just as impressive is the voice. Obasanjo writes plainly, without ornament, and the plainness is a form of authority: he narrates a long life in the idiom of a man speaking to a younger relative, mixing humour, history and blunt self-assessment. The structure serves him too. Chapters move from private memory to public history and back, so that national events are always anchored in a human being, and the reader sees the soldier, the farmer, the prisoner and the statesman as one continuous person rather than four public masks.

The epigraph frames the whole book. A watchman has no sleep and no respite, and the memoir reads as the testimony of a man who has kept watch through coups, a civil war, prison and the presidency. The image is apt: it casts Obasanjo not as a spectator of Nigeria’s history but as a sentry in it, answerable for what he saw and did.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

His upbringing is rendered with warmth and restraint. One of only two surviving children out of his mother’s nine and his father’s twelve, he was a boy and still was not pampered; his parents were disciplinarians. Yet his mother, firm as she was, would beg him to eat whenever he went on hunger strike over what he saw as unfair treatment. It is a small detail, but it shows the quality that makes the memoir work: Baba’s gratitude to his parents never hardens into sentimentality, because he is willing to be seen as a stubborn child. The same ease marks his portrait of his father’s liberal attitude to religion, which let him attend Islamic school until the flogging drove him away, and which reflects the Yoruba habit of letting Christians and Muslims live peacefully under one roof.

Olusegun Obasanjo’s My Watch is a story of grass to grace. He was not born with a silver spoon; his father was a farmer, and when his father’s fortunes declined he took menial jobs while his mother took centre stage in his education. The finest chapters here are those at the crossroads in Ibadan, where an entrance examination to the University of Ibadan, a United Nations scholarship to study in the United States and a cadetship examination into the Nigerian Army all lay before him.

“The lure of the adventure of the military was strong,” he writes, and he chose the barracks. Obasanjo is most persuasive in these pages because he presents the choice not as destiny but as a decision made under constraint, by a young man who refused to let other people’s opinions decide for him.

His early army years carry a quiet nostalgia that gives the book moral weight. Having excelled in the rigorous training in Ghana and been sent to the United Kingdom, he began his career in Kaduna, where he met officers who would later rewrite Nigerian history. He mourns the Kaduna that lost its lustre to ethno-religious conflict, and he praises the cooperation, discipline and dedication of Nigerian troops in the Congo, wishing that politicisation had not destroyed those qualities. The elegy is more than regret; it is an argument about what institutions lose when they are bent to politics.

Baba also has a gift for the telling anecdote. While on a survey course in Newbury, he invited his girlfriend, Oluremi Akinlawon, to join him in the UK, but only after her dowry was paid and the rites performed. At their simple registry wedding in London, her brother, who was to be her witness, was nowhere to be found. Baba excused himself, went out onto the street, and invited a West Indian stranger passing by to stand in. I laughed my heart out. The scene captures a free soul who improvises, and it shows a rare willingness in an autobiographer to let the reader laugh with him.

On the coups, he writes with notable restraint. A close friend of Chukwuma Kaduna Nzeogwu, he was out of the country during the first coup, yet was investigated, and he credits the objectivity of the panel that later exonerated him. In the retaliatory coup, his Squadron Sergeant Major knocked on his door at night asking permission to kill Igbo officers in the unit; Baba refused. His reflection on the episode is the book’s moral centre: “We all have different identities, but I use the identity of tribe or language only when it is absolutely necessary. The commonest and most important identity for me is Nigerian.”

It is the sort of passage that justifies reading an autobiography at all: we watch a principle tested at midnight, at his door, with lives hanging on the answer.

His treatment of the civil war, in which he commanded troops, is equally instructive. The war is a conflict any true lover of this country would wish had never happened, and the country has yet to fully heal from it; Obasanjo treats it accordingly, offering not trophies but twelve lessons, with peace, security and stability first among them. Because he has already captured the war’s graphic horrors in My Command, he wisely does not repeat himself, and the restraint keeps this memoir focused on its own task.

His satirical eye is sharpest in his time as commissioner for works. When he told the permanent secretary he had no need for a tea girl, he was asked to put it in writing, and a committee was formed. Its report recommended keeping the post because, even if Baba did not need a tea girl, his successor might. No treatise on bureaucratic waste says it better, and the anecdote shows our problems did not begin today.

After his stint as military Head of State, he retired to farming, and Ota Farm became an operational base. There he founded the African Leadership Forum to connect serving African leaders with the next generation. His appointment to the Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group on South Africa cemented his Pan-Africanist credentials, and the memoir lets us see conviction turned into gesture: using a whites-only toilet and walking a whites-only beach to send a message, and writing to Margaret Thatcher to urge sanctions. Even his failed bid to become UN Secretary-General is told with candour. The continent could not agree on a consensus candidate, and the lesson he draws, that Africa can achieve whatever it wants only if it is united in its goals and processes, lingers longer than the defeat. These episodes show a pattern the book documents consistently: Obasanjo’s politics are most convincing when they take the form of personal risk rather than public speech.

The most gripping chapters concern the Abacha years. After elder statesmen came to his farm in 1994, the formation of the National Unity Organization of Nigeria began his troubles, and his lecture at Arewa House in Kaduna was the last straw. What astonished me was his defiance. Warned in Copenhagen that Abacha had decided to arrest him, and offered political asylum by the American ambassador, Walter Carrington, he returned home, reasoning that he had committed no offence and need not become a fugitive.

He wrote: “Death comes by only once. At some point in life, decisions have to be taken that, if they turn out right, may prove heroic and if they turn out wrong may be regarded as foolish and foolhardy. Whichever way it would turn out, I took the decision to return home” (p. 416).

It turned out well for him, though not for his friend Shehu Yar’Adua, who did not live to tell the story. The prison chapters are sobering, yet they reveal his humanity: at Jos he asked to be shown the facility and stopped to speak with condemned prisoners. Most remarkable are the condolence letters he wrote to Abacha when his son died, and to Abacha’s family when the general himself died. When I asked him why, he gave me four lessons for life, three of which I remember: forgiveness, gratitude and relationships. The memoir earns its authority in moments like these, because they cost its author the comfortable role of victim.

Yet for all its candour and charm, My Watch is not without faults: at 1,572 pages across three volumes it demands a stamina few readers can spare and might have gained from firmer editorial pruning.

Still, whatever its faults, My Watch remains an indispensable work: a rare and generous act of witnessing by a man who has stood at nearly every crossroads of modern Nigerian history, who writes with humour where he could have written with bitterness, who treats forgiveness as a discipline rather than a weakness, and who offers the nation twelve hard lessons from its worst war and a lifetime of evidence that patriotism is a daily practice and not a slogan.

This book is at once a soldier’s testimony, a statesman’s ledger, a farmer’s reflection and a father’s inheritance to a country he refused to abandon even when asylum was offered, and it will be read, argued over and learned from long after the quarrels it provoked have faded.

To follow Baba from the market day of his birth to the cell in Yola and the seat of power in Abuja is to understand that Nigeria’s story can hardly be told without him, and that the story is richer, and more honest about our contradictions, because he took the trouble to tell it. Beyond its pages, its greatest gift is an invitation to every Nigerian reader, whatever their tribe or faith, to see themselves in one shared national story.

I am grateful for the sleepless watchman’s account, and eager to continue with Not My Will. To understand the living legend and national icon that is Olusegun Obasanjo, one must first read and appreciate his unforgettable autobiography.

Zayd Ibn Isah. Email: [email protected]

World.title: FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup: Flamingos Fall to Poland in Rabat
World.content:
Nigeria’s U17 girls, the Flamingos, began their FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup campaign on Saturday with a 1-2 defeat to Poland in Rabat.

Poland took the lead in the 33rd minute after the referee awarded a penalty following a Video Support review of an incident involving a Nigerian defender and a Polish attacker. Wiktoria Skrzypczak converted from the spot.

The European side thought they had doubled their lead in the 63rd minute, but the goal was ruled out for offside. Natalia Skrok made it 2-0 two minutes later, capitalising on a poor clearance by the Nigerian defence.

Flamingos coach Akeem Busari responded with a double substitution in the 68th minute, bringing on Oluebube Umejiaku and Awawu Bashiru for Harmony Chidi and Mary Dunstan. Kanyinsola Yusuf and Precious Oscar replaced Queen Joseph and Adesuyi ten minutes later.

The changes paid off in the 79th minute when Yusuf pulled a goal back shortly after coming on, giving Nigeria hope of a comeback. The Flamingos sought a late equaliser and appealed for a penalty in the 86th minute following an incident involving Kemi Adegbuyi, but the referee upheld her decision after another review.

Nigeria pressed for an equaliser, but Poland held firm to secure all three points.

The Flamingos will seek to bounce back against Puerto Rico on Tuesday, 20 October, before facing Korea DPR on Friday, 23 October, in their remaining Group B fixtures.
