The administration will also coordinate media activities, organize public forums and undertake measures intended to promote reconciliation, rebuild public confidence and prepare residents for reconstruction and development.

The government said the caretaker administration must base its activities on Ethiopia's national interests and territorial integrity, as well as the fundamental interests of the people of Tigray.

Its authority will be limited to providing routine regional services and creating conditions for the next election. It will not undertake matters with longer-term strategic implications, the government said, and will operate under the direction and supervision of the federal government.

The administration's senior officials are Asefa Abraha Hagos, chief executive for administration and public services; Tewodros Aregay Woldeselassie (PhD), chief executive for the economy and reconstruction; Gebre Egziabher Beyene Hailu (Brig. Gen.), chief executive for security and peace; and Redae Hailuom Woldeselassie, chief executive for political affairs and public organization.

Shishay Amare (PhD) was appointed mayor of Mekele, the regional capital.

The federal government will provide direction, support and oversight for the officials' activities, according to the announcement.

World.title: Malawi: Gold Rush or Gold Bust? Malawi's Smuggling Crackdown Faces Credibility Test
World.content:
Malawi's latest bid to turn gold into a lifeline for its struggling economy is facing uncomfortable questions about the evidence on which it has been built.

A state-backed scheme designed to intercept gold before it is smuggled out of the country rests on a headline-grabbing claim that $100 million worth of the precious metal is lost annually through illegal trade. Yet, according to an analysis by Collins Mtika for the Mail & Guardian and the Centre for Investigative Journalism Malawi, the figure has never been publicly explained.

The programme, spearheaded by the Malawi Mining Investment Company (Mamico), aims to buy gold from artisanal miners operating at roughly 100 sites nationwide, funnel it through buying centres in Lilongwe, Kasungu and Nkhotakota, and ultimately sell it to the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But a closer examination of the numbers reveals a troubling inconsistency.

Earlier this year, Mamico reported findings from a month-long assessment which estimated that more than $700 million worth of gold was being lost each year through illicit activity and identified 81 illegal mining sites.

The latest estimate is seven times lower. At the same time, the number of mining locations linked to the programme has increased to around 100.

The analysis asks a simple question: which number is accurate?

Without a published methodology, there is no way to test either claim. For a project requiring hundreds of billions of kwacha in public and private financing, that gap matters.

Mamico says it will need K85 billion to fund its first three months of operations and around K300 billion annually thereafter. The company has enlisted FDH Bank and NBS Bank as partners, but key parts of the commercial framework are still unresolved.

Most notably, the arrangement depends on an offtake agreement with the RBM that has yet to be concluded.

The uncertainty extends beyond the figures.

The analysis points to potential duplication between Mamico's planned operations and an existing RBM gold-purchasing initiative run through the Export Development Fund.

By September, that programme had already acquired about 1.63 tonnes of gold, raising questions about whether the government is creating parallel structures within the same market.

There is also a more fundamental challenge. Artisanal miners will only sell through official channels if they can secure competitive prices and prompt payment.

If unofficial traders offer better deals, the incentive to bypass the formal system remains intact, regardless of how many buying centres are established.

Close 

Yet the pressure to make the project work is immense.

Malawi's foreign exchange position remains fragile. Official reserves stood at $600.6 million in September, enough to cover just 2.4 months of imports, below the internationally recognised three-month benchmark.

Gold has emerged as one of the few commodities capable of generating substantial foreign currency earnings. In April alone, the RBM exported 589.95 kilogrammes of locally purchased gold valued at $75.09 million.

For ministers and policymakers, the allure is obvious: bring more gold into formal channels and bolster dwindling reserves.

But as Mtika's analysis suggests, the success of the strategy may hinge less on ambition than on transparency.

Until Mamico discloses how it calculated its smuggling estimates, clarifies how it will coexist with existing state-run gold programmes, and produces verifiable data on production, purchases and exports, the initiative will continue to face a credibility problem.

For now, the government's gold rush is asking the public to trust numbers it has yet to prove.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia's Govt Welcomes Election Timetable and Urges Political Dialogue
World.content:
Mogadishu — Somalia's federal government on Thursday welcomed an election timetable announced by the Independent National Electoral and Boundaries Commission, covering elections for both houses of parliament and the president.

In a statement dated October 15, 2026, the government described the timetable as an important step towards implementing the electoral process and strengthening democracy in the country.

The government said it had spent the past 18 months offering opportunities for consultation and negotiations aimed at helping Somali political stakeholders reach agreement on key national issues, particularly the electoral process.

It said the consultations would continue, adding that it remained committed to securing a broad-based understanding among the country's political actors.

The government described its support for the election timetable and its continued commitment to dialogue as complementary efforts that would help preserve stability, strengthen national unity and safeguard citizens' constitutional rights.

It called on all political stakeholders to engage in consultations in good faith and with a sense of national responsibility, urging them to work together to ensure peaceful elections that strengthen public confidence and Somalia's state institutions.

The statement comes amid political differences over Somalia's electoral process, including disagreements over the proposed arrangements and calls for an inclusive political agreement.

World.title: College football faces another clock controversy after BYU upsets Notre Dame
World.content:
It was a wild Saturday in college football, and if top team after top team taking losses wasn’t crazy enough, another game ended with a one-second clock controversy.

BYU pulled off an upset over Notre Dame — but social media seems to think the game may not have actually been over.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Thanks to the No. 1 Georgia Bulldogs losing at home to Auburn, No. 2 Notre Dame had a chance to take over the top spot with a win.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Unfortunately, they would have to do that on the road against the Big 12's top team, the unbeaten No. 8 BYU Cougars.

And, to make matters worse, the Fighting Irish were without one of their best defensive players almost immediately.

On BYU's first series, defensive lineman Boubacar Traore was called for targeting on a hit on BYU quarterback Bear Bachmeier.

That was a costly penalty for a team that doesn't take a lot of them, and the Cougars made them pay.

They marched downfield — even forcing Notre Dame to burn a timeout — with Bachmeier finding the end zone to open the scoring.

Notre Dame hit a field goal in the first quarter and then found the end zone in the second with running back Nolan James Jr. hitting paydirt to give them a 10-7 lead.

However, BYU had more, particularly a trick play that saw Bachmeier trotting into the end zone with the help of a blocker.

Then, as if that wasn't enough, Bachmeier scored another touchdown using his legs just before the half, and with the extra point, that gave BYU a 21-10 lead.

However, there was still enough time for Notre Dame to get another possession, and with just nine seconds on the clock, the Fighting Irish found themselves on the BYU 5-yard line.

Notre Dame QB CJ Carr attempted to spike the ball, but he never had total control of it, and upon review, it was ruled a fumble, with the Irish leaving points on the table and forking over possession.

Notre Dame battled back in the second half, and eventually found themselves up by a field goal.

BYU responded when Bachmeier — who had already shown he can find the end zone as a rusher and receiver — threw his first passing touchdown of the game by finding tight end Walker Lyons with just under two minutes left in regulation.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

That gave BYU a four-point lead and meant Notre Dame couldn't settle for a field goal.

The Irish converted on a crucial fourth-and-2 to keep their drive alive, but after failing to get into the end zone, they found themselves facing fourth-and-five with ten seconds remaining. They managed to convert with four seconds on the clock, setting up the final play of the game.

There was some contact on that one, but no flags. That'll frustrate Notre Dame fans, but not as much as this will.

Uh... not that again.

The field had been stormed, and both teams had headed to the locker room before that started making the rounds on social media.

Nonetheless, what a game.

That ended Notre Dame's 16-game winning streak and is one of several outcomes that are going to shake up the rankings and CFP picture in a big, big way.

Notre Dame will take a week off and then get back at it against Navy, while the Cougars will keep chugging along with a visit to Orlando to take on the UCF Knights.

Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged Saturday night that his sister-in-law was involved in a federal terrorist watchlist lawsuit during the Obama administration, just days before former President Barack Obama is scheduled to campaign alongside him.

El-Sayed was confronted by Fox News senior correspondent Mike Tobin about court documents identifying his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, as a plaintiff in a 2016 lawsuit challenging her alleged placement on the federal Terrorism Screening Database, commonly known as the terrorist watchlist.

"There's reporting in a lawsuit that now backs it up. And documentation with the lawsuit that Mariam Jukaku, who's your sister-in-law, that she was on the terrorist watch list?" Tobin asked.

"Yeah," El-Sayed responded.

MICHIGAN SENATE DEBATE ERUPTS INTO PERSONAL ATTACKS AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED CLASH OVER ISRAEL, IRAN AND MORE

El-Sayed then defended his sister-in-law, insisting she had committed no wrongdoing and turning his criticism toward Republican Senate rival Mike Rogers.

"She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off," El-Sayed said. "You've got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they've got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up."

The exchange comes as Obama prepares to campaign alongside El-Sayed in Michigan on Oct. 24, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election.

EL-SAYED ASKED IF HE BELIEVES AMERICA IS 'READY FOR A MUSLIM PRESIDENT' AHEAD OF SENATE RACE

According to the 2016 complaint, Jukaku underwent additional airport screening in 2012, and alleged she was never told why she had been flagged. The filing said she was believed to have been removed from the watchlist by 2016.

El-Sayed said she sued and won, but a federal appeals court overturned a ruling favoring the plaintiffs in 2021. A separate lawsuit seeking damages was dismissed in 2017.

Despite El-Sayed's claim that she sued and won, a federal appeals court overturned a ruling favoring the plaintiffs in 2021, while a separate lawsuit seeking damages was dismissed in 2017.

World.title: Top takeaways from JD Vance town hall: Costly gas, DC corruption, immigration hot takes and the war
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Vice President JD Vance faced questions from Michigan voters during a town hall in Flat Rock as the state emerges as a key battleground in the fight for Senate control in November's midterms.

The town hall hosted by CBS News came just weeks before the midterm elections as Republicans are fighting to keep their majorities in the House and Senate. Vying for the open Senate seat in Michigan is Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former member of the House of Representatives.

Here are the top moments from the town hall:

Vance places blame on Biden administration for high gas prices

The first question Vance fielded Saturday came from a 43-year-old Detroit barber, who asked him why gas prices remain significantly higher than during Trump's first term.

Vance first pointed to Iran’s attacks on commercial shipping and the resulting disruption to global energy markets, but he also placed blame on the Biden administration.

"That's actually the biggest reason why gas prices are so high, because when Joe Biden was president, we had about 20% of American refining capacity that went offline," Vance said.

Vance said the Trump administration was using the Defense Production Act to help restore domestic refining capacity, but cautioned that rebuilding that infrastructure would take time.

CBS News anchor Tony Dokoupil pushed back on Vance's attempts to blame Biden, noting that Trump and Vance have been in office for nearly two years while Americans continued to face high gas prices.

MORNING GLORY: PRESIDENT TRUMP AND THE AMERICAN MILITARY HAVE BEATEN IRAN

Vance pressed on White House corruption allegations

Dokoupil shifted the conversation to government corruption, citing a Fox News poll showing that 60% of voters were extremely concerned about the issue. He asked Vance whether anything he had witnessed inside the Trump White House made him feel "squeamish."

"You certainly see evidence of corruption in Washington, D.C. Do I see evidence of corruption from the president of the United States, from the administration? No, Tony, I just don’t," Vance said.

The exchange came days after Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations that she sought $100,000 from a donor seeking access to Trump administration officials. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.

Dokoupil pressed Vance on the allegations involving Guilfoyle, along with concerns about restrictions on IRS scrutiny of Trump's tax returns and the president's cryptocurrency earnings.

Vance said selling access to the White House would be "disgusting and despicable" and that anyone responsible should face consequences.

Dokoupil then asked whether Vance would comply with subpoenas investigating alleged corruption if Democrats took control of Congress in January.

"Of course, of course I will," Vance said. "Look, we follow the law. I follow the law."

KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE FACES POTENTIAL SENATE PROBE OVER BOMBSHELL $100K ALLEGATION

Vance acknowledges 'imperfect' immigration rhetoric

Vance was confronted over his immigration rhetoric by a naturalized U.S. citizen who said she voted for the vice president but questioned why the administration was "scapegoating immigrants."

The voter, who immigrated to the United States 20 years ago, challenged Vance over his characterization of certain H-1B visa workers as "foreign indentured servants."

"To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said.

But Vance defended his remarks, arguing that his criticism was aimed at companies exploiting foreign workers rather than immigrants themselves. He said the H-1B visa system gives employers too much power over foreign workers whose ability to remain in the country depends on their employment, while also allowing companies to replace American workers with visa holders.

"That's not a criticism of the H-1B visa holder. That's a criticism of a company who brings a person in, who sometimes will literally lay off an American worker," Vance said.

Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether his rhetoric and that of the Trump administration dehumanized immigrants.

"My goal here is not to dehumanize any immigrant. And in fact, I love a number of immigrants," Vance said.

But Vance argued that allowing too many immigrants into the country too quickly could undermine social cohesion and fundamentally change American communities.

"I have neighbors, I have friends of mine who literally don't know a single person in their neighborhood who speaks the language they do," Vance said. "I don't think it's unreasonable for an American citizen to want to share their community with people they have something in common with."

Though the town hall was pre-recorded, Vance took to X shortly after it aired to share footage from showing a burning building in France amid mass riots. He said what's unfolding in France is a cautionary tale for the United States.

"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance posted on X.

"They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen. I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn," Vance continued.

Vance claims U.S. has destroyed Iran's nuclear program

Dokoupil pressed Vance on why the war with Iran had dragged on longer than the Trump administration anticipated, asking the vice president, "Why haven't we won decisively?"

Vance argued that the U.S. had "in some ways" already won the war, claiming that American military strikes had successfully destroyed Iran's nuclear program, which he described as the central reason Trump launched the operation.

"Have we destroyed the Iranian nuclear program? The answer is yes," Vance said.

But Vance said the administration was still working to secure a "long-term" and "verifiable" commitment from Iran that it would not rebuild its nuclear capabilities, while also preventing Tehran from disrupting global energy supplies.

Vance said the Iranians responded by terrorizing commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global oil supplies and driving up gas prices.

He claimed gas prices would be "three times as high" if it weren't for the U.S. Navy protecting commercial shipping through the waterway.

VANCE TAKES AIM AT SOFT-ON-CRIME DEMS AS GOP FACES UPHILL MIDTERM BATTLE: ‘LOST THEIR MINDS’

Vance blasts El-Sayed over synagogue attack response

Vance was also urged by a Michigan voter to condemn antisemitism within his own political base, including rhetoric from prominent conservative figures such as Tucker Carlson.

The question came from Eddie Rubin, a lifelong Democrat whose 5-year-old daughter and 3-year-old son survived the attack at Temple Israel, which occurred in March in Michigan.

The attacker, a Lebanese-born U.S. citizen, rammed his pickup truck through the synagogue's entrance before exchanging gunfire with security. The attacker was killed, but no children or synagogue staff members were injured.

"I condemn anti-Semitism. I condemn Jew hatred," Vance said.

But Vance also turned the conversation to Michigan's Senate race, criticizing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for his response to the synagogue attack. Vance pointed to El-Sayed's remark that "hurt people hurt people."

"He went around and said, 'hurt people, hurt people', showing empathy, not with you and your family, which is where I think that we got to show empathy. But showing empathy to a guy who nearly killed hundreds of innocent children," Vance said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

El-Sayed had condemned the attack and later apologized for his wording, saying he never intended to justify the violence.

World.title: Steve Sarkisian vows to 'evaluate everything,' won’t rule out benching Arch Manning amid Texas' two-game skid
World.content:
Florida's 2026 season got off to a strong start, with the Gators moving to 4-0 after upsetting then-No. 4 Ole Miss in Week 4. Florida then dropped their next two games.

Despite entering this Saturday's game at Texas on a two-game skid and as an underdog, a late game sack-fumble by Arch Manning sealed a 30-27 upset victory for Florida. The past eight days have been particularly painful for the Longhorns, who suffered a crushing loss to Oklahoma last week that cost them the No. 1 ranking. Following back-to-back losses to struggling SEC opponents, Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said everything was under consideration as he looked to get the team back on track.

UNRANKED OKLAHOMA KNOCKS OFF NO. 1 TEXAS IN WALK-OFF FASHION AFTER ARCH MANNING'S ROUGH 4TH QUARTER

"Everything’s going to be evaluated," Sarkisian said. He also did not rule out a potential change at quarterback.

"Everything means everything," Sarkisian said. "It would be easy for me to say, 'Hey, Arch was the problem today.' Was Arch perfect? No. But nobody was perfect on offense today."

Sarkisian added that the opening quarter was the Longhorns’ lone bright spot.

"Obviously, I'm extremely disappointed," he said. "We didn't play very good football today, outside about the first quarter. We kind of bled out."

Texas finished Saturday's game with only 50 offensive snaps, the lowest total in Sarkisian’s tenure. Florida sacked Manning five times. Manning's day ended with 173 passing yards and one touchdown pass.

Texas entered the day having defeated 22 consecutive unranked opponents at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium. UNRANKED AUBURN UPSETS TOP-RANKED GEORGIA WITH WALK-OFF FIELD GOAL, MARKING WILD FEAT NOT SEEN IN 36 YEARS

Sarkisian offered a blunt assessment of how Texas has performed recently. "We're not playing very good football right now," he said. "I have to evaluate everything. It's gonna be a long night."

Sarkisian also calls Texas’ offensive plays, meaning his own role will likely be part of the evaluation process. "I don't know how many times I need to say it," Sarkisian said. "We're going to evaluate everything from an offensive perspective. Part of that is playcalling."

Texas will host Ole Miss in Austin next Saturday.

World.title: ‘No Kings’ protesters spurn organizers' rules: ‘This is as partisan as you can get’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — On South Washington Street, 26-year-old environmental engineer Nayely Cruz Hernandez had a straightforward message for voters as she joined a phalanx of protesters lining the street for nationwide "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump: "Vote blue."

"We got to take the power away from Trump, from the Republicans," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. "So we got to win the House, we got to win the Senate, not only in Virginia, but across the country."

Standing beside her boyfriend, Noah Schwarzott, 25, their 13-year-old Maltese-poodle, Maybellene, in her arms, Hernandez acknowledged that national No Kings organizers had their own rules for the protests to be "nonpartisan," but she wasn't following orders.

'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS

"The No King ... organizers can say whatever," she said. "But I'm saying vote blue, because why are we here? Who's in the House? Who's in the Senate? Who is the President? It's red, it's Republicans, and it's Trump."

A Fox News Digital investigation documented about 300 organizations with $2.5 billion in combined annual revenues behind the "No Kings" protest network, including Democratic-aligned advocacy groups, major labor unions and nonprofits including MoveOn, the American Federation of Teachers and the ACLU.

Cruz Hernandez ended by introducing Maybellene and declaring that the dog was "telling you to vote for Don Beyer," a Democratic member of Congress who represents Alexandria, Arlington and other Northern Virginia communities.

The national organizers' position is that the Oct. 17 events must be "nonpartisan." That's to comply with the federal laws that regulate the nonprofits that fund the No Kings protests.

PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH

Her comments directly contradicted the written instructions of the national "No Kings" organization and its leaders at the Indivisible nonprofit, prohibiting calls to "vote Blue," elect Democrats or endorse candidates and target individuals.

Nearby, a man held a sign by a far-left group called "Refuse Fascism" with another message defying the organizers' guidance: "TRUMP MUST GO NOW!" Another man held an inflatable balloon mocking Trump as a baby in a diaper. Another sign said "86 47," the controversial message former FBI Director James Comey posted on social media and which federal prosecutors deemed an overt threat against Trump.

As the young couple cheered honking cars, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, national spokesperson for No Kings, called Fox News Digital to insist "No Kings" is a "nonpartisan, peaceful movement that has brought millions of Americans together to stand up for democracy, defend our freedoms, and reject authoritarianism."

DAVID MARCUS: AS DEMOCRATS PROTEST IN DALLAS, CONSERVATIVES ARE QUIET AND CAUTIOUS

Told that a Fox News DIgital investigation found "No Kings" events from Maine to Oregon were clearly partisan, Epstein-Ortiz said, "We are aware of partisan events circulating online that are not affiliated with or officially organized by No Kings. Many people utilize the No Kings name as a rallying cry."

But, in this case, the protest on South Washington Street was an official "No Kings" event, advertised on the organizers' official website.

Among the demonstrators, one woman beamed while waving a sign that was explicit about the protest's agenda: "THE USA Needs a Big Beautiful BLUE WAVE."

But hours after the Alexandria demonstration, Fox News Digital encountered another protester marching on H Street NW by the White House who openly rejected the nonpartisan description. She marched at an official "No Kings" event.

Nadine Seiler, a self-described "professional protester" recently mentioned by Trump, was asked whether she agreed with organizers' insistence that the demonstration was nonpartisan.

"No, no, the people who agree with Trump are not out here," Seiler responded from behind an inflatable costume. "So it's never gonna be non-partisan if it's a resistance to the fascist regime."

"They can pretend, but it's not," she added.

Asked directly whether the event was partisan, Seiler answered: "Yes, this is a partisan protest."

She explained that participants were resisting what she described as illegal policies of the Trump administration.

"Yeah, so this is as partisan as you can get," she concluded.

The exchanges offer a ground-level perspective on the political character of a movement whose organizers have gone to considerable lengths to insist its voter-mobilization activities are "nonpartisan."

FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS

"No Kings" has distributed detailed election-law guidance prohibiting partisan slogans, campaign materials, candidate endorsements and coordination with political parties.

Yet the movement's own leadership has openly discussed its broader Democratic electoral objectives.

During an Oct. 15 livestream, Indivisible co-founder Ezra Levin contrasted the parties' candidates.

"Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said.

In an Oct. 9 webinar, Levin explained how activists could criticize Trump while avoiding explicit Democratic endorsements.

"Uh, you've got to let people connect the dots on that one," he said.

Indivisible co-founder Leah Greenberg, meanwhile, described No Kings as a "nonpartisan coalition" intended to welcome participants across the political spectrum.

The distinction matters legally. Individual protesters expressing partisan opinions don't automatically establish that event organizers violated election law. Tax-exempt charities also face restrictions different from those governing political advocacy groups. In yet another sign, a protester again targeted Trump, writing, "EVERY DAY I HATE HIM MORE THAN I DID THE DAY BEFORE." Another sign read: "NO CROWN FOR THE CLOWN."

From northern Virginia to the White House, participants were making no effort to conceal their political preferences.

For Seiler, the description was simple: "This is as partisan as you can get."

Fox News Digital's Reagan Schroeder and Tessa Hoyos contributed to this report.

World.title: ‘The house was toast’: Surf swallows California homes
World.content:
LONG BEACH, Calif. — It was 3:30 a.m. on Oct. 9 and the unthinkable was happening all around Shawn Curtis: The boardwalk in front of his two-story beachfront apartment building was gone. The 25-foot-wide sand beach was gone. Salt water poured in from all sides. And now the building was slanting down into the ocean.

Curtis couldn’t make sense of what he saw. “The doorframe was crooked. The window was crooked, and then I saw a big wave crash,” he told NBC News on Thursday.

The surf crashed all the way up to the second floor. Neighbors across the street said they could see water cascading down onto the roof of Curtis’ home of nine years. Booming waves were loud enough to wake him and shake his apartment as though an earthquake rippled through, he said.

World.title: Boy and man killed, 10 injured after woman drives through youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas
World.content:
A 6-year-old boy and 35-year-old man were killed, and 10 others were injured, when a woman drove a truck through a youth soccer game at a city sports complex in Wichita, Kansas, Saturday afternoon, police said.

The 34-year-old driver, from Garden City, Kansas, was in custody, though it wasn’t immediately clear if the incident at the Stryker Sports Complex was intentional, police said.

“She has been cooperative up to this point in the investigation,” Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said at an evening news conference.

Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses speaking outside the Stryker Sports Complex during a press conference in Wichita, Kan. on Oct. 17, 2026. NBC News

Both of the dead were from the city of McPherson, Moses said, but were not related to one another.

The injured include five children, ranging in age from 5 to 9 years old, as well as five men and women between 28 and 68 years old, he said.

“Those injuries span from minor injuries, like bruises, to extremely severe injuries,” the captain said. “But at this point, we believe those to be non-life-threatening.”

An additional patient, a 61-year-old woman, was hospitalized with “non-traumatic medical issues,” he said.

People began calling 911 shortly before 3:30 p.m., Moses said, “reporting that a vehicle had driven through a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex.”

First responders, including Kansas Highway Patrol officers, Sedgwick County sheriff’s deputies and police from nearby Bel Aire, found the boy and the man dead at the scene, he said.

They also saw bystanders tending to the injured.

“They saw community members and citizens rendering medical aid to those who were injured,” he said.

The driver was still in the truck, as were two children, Moses said. One of the women’s children had a game at the complex, though at a different field to where the crash occurred, he said.

Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said on her personal Facebook page that the incident left her filled with sorrow.

“I’m heartbroken by reports of a tragic incident at Stryker Sports Complex,” she said. “My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved.”

Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement that she’s monitoring the situation and has offered state resources to Wu.

“My condolences go out to the families of the victims, the survivors, and all those impacted by this event,” she said, adding that she was “very grateful” to first responders.

The Stryker Sports Complex is a city facility with 11 turf fields used for “all sports,” it states on its website. The city of Wichita said all events at the facility have been canceled for now.

The Kansas State High School Activities Association said its scheduled flag football state championship has been suspended, along with any other of its matches through the weekend.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, police said.

In a statement posted to Facebook, the Wichita Police Department asked anyone with video of the incident to upload it so investigators could take a look.

World.title: Man fatally shot during dispute at Midtown Manhattan subway station, police say
World.content:
A man died Saturday after being shot during a dispute at a subway station in Manhattan’s Theater District, according to police.

Officers responded to reports of gunfire at the 53rd Street and Seventh Avenue subway station around 12:21 p.m., police said. The victim was taken to a nearby hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1:06 p.m.

The station serves Midtown Manhattan, an area crowded with tourists and theatergoers.

Authorities did not name the victim, pending notification of his family, and said he was “possibly” in his 30s.

Police are searching for a man in connection with the shooting. In a statement, NYPD said the man approached the victim on the northbound E train platform, shot him once in the chest and fled on foot.

At a news conference, police said a dispute between two men moved from the platform onto a train and back onto the platform. Investigators were still determining where the shots were fired, police said at the briefing.

Police said the shooting was not a random act.

The perpetrator “should face maximum consequences from the justice system,” MTA Chief Security Officer Michael Kemper said.

“It is fortunate nobody outside the fight was hurt,” he added.

Yellow police tape blocked the entrance to the Seventh Avenue subway station Saturday afternoon.

World.title: 71-year-old man dies after alligator attack while fishing in Florida, police say
World.content:
A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said on Friday.

Steven Hamilton was fishing at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park in Winter Garden, Florida — a city about 15 miles west of Orlando — when he was bitten by an alligator, according to a statement from the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission.

Responding emergency personnel relayed reports that witnesses had seen someone possibly grabbed by an alligator and pulled into the water, according to a recording radio traffic. He was pronounced dead at the scene, the FWC said.

The Winter Garden Police Department confirmed the incident in a statement, adding that FWC authorities trapped and killed the roughly 12-foot-long alligator.

The FWC said that “serious injuries caused by alligators are rare in Florida.”

In June, a 31-year-old woman died after an alligator bit off one of her arms and mauled the other at nearby Little Big Econ State Forest.

“Always be aware of your surroundings. Always be safe,” Winter Garden police Capt. Michael Mason told reporters, according to NBC affiliate WESH 2 News. “Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance. It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.”

Mason encouraged witnesses of the incident to reach out to authorities.

World.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV was discharged from the hospital on Saturday after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with his surgeon saying he could be fully recovered in about 10 days.

Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News there were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pontiff from making his planned trip to Latin America next month.

The pontiff, who had been recovering at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday, walked out unaided before spending a couple of minutes speaking with well-wishers. He appeared to accept a gift of a homemade smiling Pope figure before getting in a car and being driven back to the Vatican.

“Following the conclusions reached by the medical team this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Polyclinic Hospital, where he was admitted for surgery on his right lung,” the Holy See Press said Saturday in a statement, before the Leo left the building mid-afternoon.

He is expected to recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica on Sunday, according to the statement.

The pontiff’s personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and Margaritora, said that in light of blood tests and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, and after an assessment of his clinical condition, “the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge from the hospital.”

So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.

Leo, who is a Chicago native, resumed working from the hospital on Thursday, his doctors and the Vatican reported.

Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung. Tiziana Fabi / AFP via Getty

The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass inside the hospital, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.

The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him. Spokesman Matteo Bruni said he presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.

His discharge from the hospital comes less than a month before Leo is scheduled to jet off for a two-week trip to South America, which is set to start Nov. 11.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru.

“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said Wednesday.

A drawing of Pope Leo XIV outside the Gemelli Hospital in Rome. Alberto Pizzoli / AFP via Getty

Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.

Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.

This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer last week.

Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.

As Margaritora led the procedure, Gemelli’s medical staff recited the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel.

World.title: Iowa son fights to overturn his father's conviction in mother's murder
World.content:
Erin Moriarty: Trysten, where are we?

Trysten Mullis: We're at the farm that I grew up on. This is where … me and my brother and sister grew up … these big white buildings here are the hog barns.

Trysten Mullis, along with his younger siblings Taylor and Wyatt, and his parents Todd and Amy, lived on a 400-acre Iowa farm where they grew soybeans and corn and raised pigs.

Trysten Mullis (at the farm): It's a whole family effort to … run a farm this size.

Erin Moriarty: And what are you feeling when you like look out here and --

Trysten Mullis: Just nostalgia. … it's just kind of peaceful, you know?

What happened at the farm the day Amy Mullis died?

That November morning in 2018, started off routinely. While his sister and brother stayed in the house, Trysten, then 13 years old, was with his parents preparing for a shipment of baby pigs.

Erin Moriarty: This is the office? The shop?

Trysten Mullis: This is the office. Yes.

Trysten showed me inside the hog barn where they were working.

Trysten Mullis (inside the hog barn): Now we're going into the main area of the hog barn. This is where your pigs would actually be in.

Trysten's job that morning was to carry heaters from the front of the barn to each pen. Todd was working on the water supply pipes. Amy was cleaning the lights.

Trysten Mullis demonstrates for "48 Hours" correspondent Erin Moriarty how his mother Amy Mullis was cleaning glass light fixtures in the hog barn. CBS News

Trysten Mullis (inside the hog barn): What she was doing is she would get on the bucket here and stand up, and she would unscrew it like that (demonstrates). … Drop it down, get off the bucket, clean it in a separate bucket, and then get back up here and screw them back in.

At one point, Trysten remembers noticing that his mom looked dizzy and unsteady.

Trysten Mullis: She was getting down kind of slow and really grabbing on to the gate … You could kind of see her loopy and swaying a little bit.

Just four days earlier Amy had had a minor medical procedure, and Trysten says he and his dad were concerned. This was her first day back on her feet.

Trysten Mullis: We knew something was not right.

Trysten says his mom agreed to go into the house and rest. But before she left, they asked if she could do one thing on her way: get a pet carrier out of the red shed. Trysten says they needed it later that day to protect some kittens from heavy machinery.

Trysten Mullis: We asked her if she could get it outside of the door.

Trysten says he saw his mom leave.

Trysten Mullis: She walked down the side there.

Erin Moriarty: OK.

Trysten Mullis: And walked out that door … The last time I saw her was through that window, right in the wall there (points to the front end of the barn).

Trysten says he and his dad continued working for about an hour-and-a-half before taking a break.

Trysten Mullis: We noticed that … the pet carrier wasn't outside. So he said, hey, can you go, uh, get the pet carrier out? … We just figured she couldn't get it.

Trysten went to the red shed to get the pet carrier, and that's when he found his mom on the ground with a corn rake in her back.

Trysten Mullis: I was just praying that she was still alive.

Trysten yelled for his dad, and they got Amy into the truck — calling 911 as they rushed to the hospital.

911 OPERATOR: Delaware County 911. What's the address of your emergency? TODD MULLIS (to Trysten): Is she breathing? TODD MULLIS: I just grabbed her and threw her in the truck. My son's holding her. 911 OPERATOR: OK, you're headed to the hospital and she's in your vehicle?

Erin Moriarty: How did you hear that your mom didn't make it?

Trysten Mullis: Dad walked in the room and he had tears in his eyes … and told us that mom had passed away.

Amy's mother Peggy, her brother Jeff and her stepfather Randy are still coming to terms with what happened that day.

Peggy Munson: Your heart stops.

Jeff Fuller: She was my best friend … growing up … Amy was a very vibrant person. She had a big personality.

Randy Munson: She was always concerned about other people, about her family, about her children.

Trysten says that he and his father assumed his mother's death had been a horrible accident; that she had just fallen on the rake. But less than a year later, Todd was on trial for her murder.

Even though Todd and Trysten maintained that Amy's death was an accident, the state medical examiner, Dr. Kelly Kruse, said it was a homicide. She found a large bruise on the side of Amy's jaw and scrapes and bruises on Amy's knuckles — possible signs of a — noted that while Amy had six puncture wounds on her back, the corn rake only had four tines.

DR. KELLY KRUSE (testifying at trial): There were two different directions of the six puncture wounds. …

PROSECUTOR MAUREEN HUGHES: And what do those different directions indicate to you?

DR. KELLY KRUSE: To me they indicate that she would have to be impaled with the rake at least twice. … possibly three times.

Dr. Kruse determined that Amy's injuries had to have been caused by someone striking her with the rake. Iowa Division of Criminal Investigation special agent Jon Turbett, now retired, was called in to help local law enforcement.

Jon Turbett: I'm thinking at some point Todd and Amy end up in that red barn, and Todd attacks Amy … and … she's hit two or three times with a corn rake.

And he says Todd had a motive.

Jon Turbett: We learn that the marriage … is not … maybe what it would look like on the outside … There were things boiling underneath.

Todd and Amy Mullis Facebook

Amy was having an affair, and according to her brother Jeff, she wasn't happy and planned to leave Todd.

Jeff Fuller: Her words to me were, "Todd's gonna flip out."

Erin Moriarty: And what did that mean to you? What did flip out mean to you?

Jeff Fuller: To me, that meant that he would … not go quietly, he would not give up half of … his land … in a divorce.

Jon Turbett: And that becomes … a big part of his motive of killing Amy.

And according to her friend Patricia Christopherson, Amy was afraid of Todd.

PATRICIA CHRISTOPHERSON (testifying at trial): I asked her why she stayed and she said she was scared of Todd and if he found out about, um, wanting a divorce or an affair, that he would kill her.

Investigators say Google searches found on Todd's iPad show that not only did he think about killing his wife, he planned it in advance.

Jon Turbett: You see searches on … unfaithful wives … and killing cheating wives at different points in history.

According to prosecutors, Todd's plan was to send Amy to the red shed that morning and then ambush and kill her, But that wasn't all.

PROSECUTOR MAUREEN HUGHES (at trial): He sent his 13-year-old son to go and find his mother, who he had just slaughtered.

At his trial, Todd Mullis maintained he was innocent and said he had not known Amy was having an affair. Dave Kettering /Telegraph Herald

When Todd testified, he told the jury he never did those damning Google searches, that he did not know his wife was having an affair, and that he did not kill her.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY GERALD FEUERHELM (at trial): Todd … did you ambush your wife, Amy, in that shed that day and brutally beat her and chop — chop her up with that corn fork?

TODD MULLIS: No, I did not.

Since Trysten was the only other person working on the farm that day, his testimony was crucial. He initially told police that he had been with his dad all morning — essentially providing an alibi for his father. Trysten later added that he did leave his dad's side twice to get a drink of water and that he briefly lost sight of him. Because he was a minor, Trysten wasn't shown on camera.

PROSECUTOR (at trial): Do you know exactly how long your dad wasn't in your sight?

TRYSTEN MULLIS: No.

PROSECUTOR: … Trysten, would it be accurate to say that you don't know how much time you were away from your dad ... when you were working in the hog barn?

TRYSTEN MULLIS: Yes.

And according to prosecutors, that gave Todd the time to kill Amy. But Trysten says he was pressured to testify the way he did — pressured by Amy's stepfather.

What Trysten Mullis wants a jury to know about what happened the day his mother died

Erin Moriarty: How would you describe the last eight years?

Trysten Mullis: Hell. I would say hell.

Trysten Mullis says his testimony at his father's murder trial didn't tell the whole story and if he could do it all over again, here's what he would want the jury to know about how long it took to get a drink of water that day.

Trysten Mullis: … I said I don't know how much time. I wasn't saying it could have been 20 minutes or whatever … It was a matter of seconds.

All he had to do, he says, was walk around a corner at the front of the barn.

Trysten Mullis: Right here is the hose that I drank out of that day.

Erin Moriarty: And so where do you drink out of it, like right here?

Trysten Mullis (drinks from the hose): Right out of the nozzle right here.

Erin Moriarty: You didn't do anything else in here?

Trysten Mullis: Nope. And then you walk right back in.

And that, he says, is just not enough time for his father to leave, kill his mother and come back. There were two ways Todd could have gone. Either through a door at the front of the barn —

Erin Moriarty: If he went that way.

Trysten Mullis: He would walk right past me.

Erin Moriarty: You would have seen him.

Trysten Mullis: I would have seen him and I would have heard him.

Erin Moriarty: So what's the only other way he could have gone out?

Trysten Mullis shows "48 Hours" corresondent Erin Moriarty the exit at the back of the hog barn. CBS News

Trysten Mullis: The only other way he could have gone out is to the end of the barn, all the way down at the end there.

Erin Moriarty: Oh, I see the door —

Trysten Mullis: See the door?

Erin Moriarty: — right down there.

Trysten Mullis: Yep.

Erin Moriarty: Then to get to the shed, how would he have to do that?

Trysten Mullis: would have to run all the way across the barn and then run all the way down.

Then —

Trysten Mullis: He'd have to jump the gate, run through the trees, go into the barn, do whatever, and run all the way back.

Graphic depiction of the route Todd Mullis would have had to take from the barn to the shed and back. CBS News

The round trip would have been about the length of four football fields.

Trysten Mullis: Come through the door, get back to the spot. Not be out of breath, not be panicked, not be, you know, frightened in any way, shape or form.

Erin Moriarty: … did your dad seem to be disheveled when — any time when you saw him there or out of breath or —

Trysten Mullis: Absolutely not.

For a young boy, it was a lot to handle.

Trysten Mullis was 13 when his mother died. "I know for a fact he didn't do it," the now-21-year-old tells "48 Hours" correspondent Erin Moriarty in his first interview. "And how do you know that?" asks Moriarty. "Because I was there, nobody else was there but me. … they got it wrong." Amy Mullis/Facebook

Trysten Mullis: I've had to grow up really fast … going from a 13-year-old kid now taking care of two … younger siblings … trying to lead them.

When his father was arrested for the murder of his mother, Trysten, his sister Taylor, then 11, and brother Wyatt, 9, went to live with Amy's family three hours away.

Peggy Munson (emotional): I'd always promised her that I would look after her children. … But little did I know they would be living with us.

Amy's mom Peggy.

Peggy Munson: It was hard for us too, because we were still grieving.

It was painful all around. The kids had to adjust to a new town and a new school. But for Trysten, there was no adjusting to the fact that he was living with family that he says believed his father was a killer.

Trysten Mullis: And I — to this day I've tried to get them to change their mind … and they still don't believe that he's innocent. … it's caused a lot of tension in that side of the family because of what they believe and what I believe.

So at 17, with the help of a lawyer, Trysten took action. He signed an affidavit accusing Amy's stepfather Randy and an attorney hired by Amy's family of pressuring him on how to testify at trial if asked about how long his father was out of his sight:

They said that if I did not answer the question with "I don't know" to the question then I would get in trouble for my mom's death and be sent to a jail for kids called juvenile detention and that I would be taken out of school and away from my friends.

Erin Moriarty: As you know, Randy … He said in his affidavit that that you had pressured him …

Randy Munson: Yeah. No, just tell the truth. …

Erin Moriarty: Was that hard to read?

Peggy Munson: Yes.

Randy Munson: Yes, it is.

Peggy Munson: Very much so. Because that's the last thing that we did with those kids is tell them to say anything — they speak their own mind … The truth is what we want them to say. Yeah, that was hard, very hard.

Today, Trysten does not want to talk about his affidavit.

Trysten Mullis: it's kind of a sensitive area.

But when he rewinds back through the murder trial, all he can see are mistakes and missed opportunities to prove that his mother's death was accidental — starting with his father's defense counsel. In a letter to his lawyer written from jail before the trial, Todd asked, "is there any 'expert' that could verify possibility of it being accident." In another, Todd made a rudimentary sketch of how he thought it happened.

In his effort to prove Amy's death was accidental, Todd Mullis made this sketch of how he thought the incident could have happened.

But when the trial began Todd's defense attorney Gerald Feuerhelm didn't even argue it was an accident. He told the jury that Amy was murdered.

DFENSE ATORNEY GERALD FEURHELM (at trial): Amy Mullis was viciously and deliberately murdered …

... Just not by Todd. Todd's sister Lynne and brother Mike watched on helplessly.

Mike Mullis: Well, when the – when the defense comes out and says, well, we know this was a murder, and but Todd didn't do it. Well, that was an opening statement, my God –

Lynne White: Where did this come from? It made no sense.

When "48 Hours" reached out to Feuerhelm, he declined our request to be interviewed but he has said that he never considered an accidental death for Todd's defense.

Dina Nesheiwat: Nobody got to hear anything — any evidence of accidents.

Now Todd's family is leaning on new lawyers who hope to overturn his murder conviction. Brother and sister Daniel and Dina Nesheiwat have taken over the case. Years earlier, the Nesheiwats were consultants for "48 Hours" when we covered Todd's murder trial. And when they dug into the case, they too concluded that Todd didn't have enough time to kill Amy. Daniel did the leg work himself.

Daniel Nesheiwat: I literally ran the distance that the prosecution was accusing Todd of — of doing so he could have committed this alleged murder. And being there and seeing it, it's impossible. It's a — quite a distance … there's no way it could have been done just on that fact. … And — and at that point, I was 100 percent convinced.

How did the corn rake end up in Amy Mullis' back?

Convinced that Todd Mullis had not murdered his wife, his new attorneys Dina and Daniel Nesheiwat did what Todd said he had wanted all along.

Erin Moriarty: What is this here?

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: So this is the shed. This is where Amy was actually found.

They hired experts, including Forensic Pathologist Dr. Jennifer Hammers – a former New York City and Boston medical examiner — and Dr. Valentina Ngai, a biomechanical engineer. And after going to the scene, examining the evidence and doing tests of their own, they both say Amy was not murdered that day.

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: This does not appear to be a homicide to me. …

At trial the state medical examiner testified that Amy had that bruise on her jaw and scrapes and bruises on her knuckles. But if Amy had been hit in the face by Todd, Hammers says, there also would've been swelling.

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: The area isn't swollen. … if this area is impacted in, let's say, a physical altercation, we very often see pretty quick bruising … swelling of that area

As for the scrapes and bruises on Amy's knuckles, Hammers suggests that those injuries could have come from cleaning those glass light fixtures that Amy was doing earlier that day. As Trysten showed me, they were very narrow.

Erin Moriarty (in the hog barn holding glass fixture): Your mom was cleaning this out by —

Trysten Mullis: Hand.

Erin Moriarty (putting her hand inside the fixture): This is hard.

Trysten Mullis: Mm-hmm.

Erin Moriarty: I don't have big hands.

Trysten Mullis: Mm-hmm.

But the most crucial question for these experts is how the corn rake ended up in Amy's back.

Erin Moriarty: At trial, basically everyone said four tines, six injuries. Simple math. Murder. …

Dr. Valentina Ngai: That is not right.

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: That's incorrect.

Using the state medical examiner's notes, Hammers drew an approximate diagram of the wounds, labeling them A through F. And then she and Ngai examined the direction of each wound. They, like the state medical examiner, say the wounds go in two different directions.

Dr. Hammer's approximation of Amy Mullis' wounds. Dr. Hammers and Dr. Ngai agree with the State Medical Examiner that the wounds go in two different directions but say they don't believe Amy was struck with the corn rake.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: If you look at A, B, C, D … these wounds travel through the body almost perpendicular …. and E and F are sharply upward.

But unlike the state medical examiner, they don't think the wounds came from Todd striking her with the rake multiple times.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: That scenario of … swinging and re-swinging does not fit … it does not match the physical evidence.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: … if you swing it, the entry points are much more steep. … swinging with these tines causes a much steeper entry point and would not generate these wound trajectories.

So, if someone didn't strike Amy with the corn rake, how did she end up with six puncture wounds in her back?

Erin Moriarty: Are you trying to reconstruct what must have happened to Amy?

Dr. Valentina Ngai: Yes.

They concluded that Amy accidentally fell on the rake and helped to create an animation. After initially falling on the rake, Amy, they say, struggled to free herself from it.

A still frame from an animation created by Todd Mullis' attorneys showing what they believe happened to Amy Mullis. After initially falling on the rake, they say, Amy struggled to free herself from it – and wounded herself further. Legal Arsenal

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: None of those injuries are gonna immediately incapacitate her. So she would be able to move, to … try to remove it from her body.

And in trying to remove it from her body, they say, she wounded herself further.

Erin Moriarty: So, what you're saying is that when Amy tried to get the corn rake out of her back … she inadvertently caused greater injury?

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: Yes.

Here's their opinion of what happened. When Amy fell, three of the four tines pierced her coat and her back, creating three puncture wounds. Hammers and Ngai say Amy then tried to get up.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: She can't roll to her left, otherwise she rolls over top of the rake. … She can't sit upright because the rake handle is too long and it hits the ground … The only way for her to be able to get up is to roll to her right.

As she struggled, they say, she managed to free one tine from her back, but it still stayed under her coat. They say she fell again, causing the fourth puncture wound. Then Amy once again tried to free herself from the rake.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: She gets up to her knees and grabs the rake handle.

Still trying to break free, Hammers and Ngai say that Amy inadvertently turned the rake, changing the direction of the tines. They say she fell again, causing the fifth and sixth puncture wounds while the tines were pointing upward.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: … falling back onto those last two tines explains … that upward internal trajectory.

The coat Amy Mullis was wearing has less holes – indicated by arrows -- than the number of puncture wounds in her body. The experts hired by Todd Mullis' attorneys say it's proof that Amy's death could not have been caused by swinging the rake multiple times.

Doctors Hammers and Ngai say the clearest proof that Amy's death could not have been caused by someone swinging the rake is the coat that Amy was wearing that day. A photo of the inside of the coat, shown above, taken at autopsy— but never shown at trial — the four arrows indicate where the medical examiner saw holes in the coat.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: Is a extremely important piece of evidence. … because it indicates that the clothing has less holes than the number of holes in her body. …

Erin Moriarty: And why is that so significant?

Dr. Valentina Ngai: He was convicted on swinging this rake multiple times into her body. How do you swing a four-tine implement multiple times and have less holes in the outer clothes and more holes in the body? That is illogical.

And they think they know why Amy fell in the first place. Dr. Hammers discovered a potential clue in Amy's medical records – something the medical examiner later said she didn't look at. Not only did Amy have that medical procedure a few days earlier —

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: … she had three medications, all of which can cause some sort of dizziness … or sleepiness.

Remember, Trysten had said his mother appeared dizzy and unsteady. As part of their work, Hammers and Ngai walked through the farm. They say that the layout of the red shed likely contributed to the accident.

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: It's very dark. It's very narrow … there's a lot of things in there.

To get the pet carrier, Amy had to walk down one narrow pathway, turn right, and then walk down another. Police photos from that day show the pet carrier sticking out. And Ngai and Hammers noticed something else in those photos – on the ground there were two pieces of farm equipment, called augers, that look like giant drill bits.

Dr. Jennifer Hammers: With the pet carrier being partially pulled out … it seems most likely that she was starting to pull that out.

Dr. Valentina Ngai: The barn being dark …. the augers at your feet, a tripping hazard, falling backwards. … this is the most likely plausible scenario.

For Trysten and the Mullis family, the experts' conclusion is what they'd been waiting for.

Lynne White: Finally, Todd's explanation's right here. … they proved it … science doesn't lie. … it was a farm accident. Simple as that.

Trysten Mullis: I felt like we had our answer.

But when Todd's new attorneys get the chance to present this information to a judge, would it be enough?

Todd Mullis seeks new trial

Determined to prove that Amy Mullis' death was an accident —

Dina Nesheiwat: … you can't argue with the science. You can't argue with the biomechanical engineers.

— they need to convince an Iowa judge in this courtroom that Todd's defense counsel who never investigated the possibility of an accidental death was ineffective, and that if the evidence they have collected now had been presented at his original trial, there might have been a different result. If they can do that, they hope to win Todd a new trial. On that day in court, Todd saw his children for the first time in six years.

At the hearing, Todd Mullis saw his three children for the first time in six years. Trysten, pictured far right, was overcome with emotion.

Trysten Mullis: I broke down. I — I broke down. Just to see his face like tore me apart. … I just wanted to jump over the rail and hug him, tell him I loved him.

The Nesheiwats— along with a team of lawyers from both the Iowa Wrongful Conviction Unit and the Exoneration Project —are working pro bono to challenge Todd's murder conviction.

Tara Thompson: Nobody listened to Todd at trial … the outcome of his trial would've been different if the jury had heard everything that the court is gonna hear over the course of this trial.

At his murder trial, the prosecution argued that Amy's affair was the reason Todd killed her. But the Nesheiwats say there's no clear evidence that Todd had any idea that his marriage was at risk.

Dina Nesheiwat: … she was having an affair at that time, um, unbeknownst to Todd. … but never took any action to actually take the steps to leaving.

Amy Mullis Lynne White

And in the month before she died, says Dina Nesheiwat, there were affectionate texts between them.

Dina Nesheiwat: There's messages where they're saying I love you back and forth. …

But what about that conversation that Amy's friend said they had about being afraid Todd would kill her?

Dina Nesheiwat: I think they were … for lack of better words, kind of throwaway … statements … Just like if I said it, you know, "my husband's gonna kill me if I'm home late," you know or things of that nature. … if she believed he was going to kill her … she would have done something different, and she didn't. She stayed.

As for those Google searches discovered on Todd Mullis' iPad — searches about cheating and killing unfaithful women — which Todd denied making but the prosecution said proved premeditation —

Erin Moriarty: How do you explain the Google searches? … "what happens to cheaters in history?" "Killing unfaithful women." That looks bad.

Dina Nesheiwat: Yes. On their face, they do look bad. … In isolation, they do look bad.

Dina Nesheiwat says that all those searches were made before Amy even began her affair — and she says that many of the searches were about history.

Dina Nesheiwat: But if you follow the search sequence it goes into different cultures.

Including one that asked: "what happened to cheating spouses in historic Aztec tribe"

Dina Nesheiwat: … The state told the jury that all of the searches from Todd Mullis' Gmail account were done on the iPad, but that's not the case.

Todd's Google account was used on more than just his iPad, including Amy's phone and a family laptop, so Nesheiwat says anyone in the Mullis home could have done those searches.

Dina Nesheiwat: We don't know who did the search. ...

But for Todd's attorneys, it's not enough to raise questions about the circumstantial evidence against Todd Mullis. Success at this hearing hinges on the new defense witnesses. They testified without using the animation. It was not yet ready.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON (in court): Did you reach an opinion in this case, Dr. Hammers, about how you would classify the manner of Ms. Mullis' death?

DR. JENNIFER HAMMERS: I did.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: And what is your conclusion after consideration of all of the background evidence and the evaluation of the hypotheses that you considered in this case?

DR. JENNIFER HAMMERS: My opinion is that the manner of death is best classified as an accident.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: Good afternoon, Dr. Ngai.

DR. VALENTINA NGAI: Good afternoon.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: During your investigation, did you come across any physical evidence that did not fit with this hypothesis of Ms. Mullis falling onto the rake in the way that you've described?

DR. VALENTINA NGAI: No. Every single piece of physical evidence supported this hypothesis.

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: And are these opinions that you could have — you or someone else in the biomechanical field could have offered back in 2019 based on the state of the science then?

DR. VALENTINA NGAI: Yes.

Given the evidence, Hammers and Ngai said that Amy's injuries could only be the result of an accidental fall. That contradicts Dr. Kelly Kruse, the state medical examiner, who declined to speak with "48 Hours."

ATTORNEY TARA THOMPSON: Is it true that at the time of Ms. Mullis' autopsy, that because you could not envision a circumstance in which Ms. Mullis sustained these injuries, other than … someone impaling her with the corn rake, that that is the reason you determined that this was a homicide?

DR. KELLY KRUSE: There is no other way. Yes.

ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: Any of those, um, opinions or characterizations have those changed for you at all over this course of time?

DR. KELLY KRUSE: No.

ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: OK. You've reviewed a report that has essentially criticized your findings in this case, correct?

DR. KELLY KRUSE: Yes.

ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL SCOTT BROWN: And has that review caused you to change any of the opinions that you've given in this case?

DR. KELLY KRUSE: No.

Lawyers for the state questioned Kruse and did not bring any new witnesses to dispute the evidence presented by Hammers and Ngai. But they argued at the end of the hearing that Todd Mullis' murder conviction should not be overturned.

ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL THOMAS BAKKE (in court): The state submits that Mr. Mullis has not met his burden of proof on any of his claims. We ask the court to deny his application in its entirety.

Trysten did not testify at the hearing but a deposition, in which he described being pressured, was submitted. He was a fixture in court throughout – sitting right behind his father.

Erin Moriarty: …You were there every day.

Trysten Mullis: Every single day. I mean, why wouldn't I be there every single day … I know he's innocent. And for the judge to see that … Well, his son is the one sitting behind him the whole time, you know.

TARA THOMPSON (in court): … Mr. Mullis has established there is at least a reasonable likelihood that the outcome of this trial would've been different with the overwhelming evidence that the Court has seen, this is evidence of an innocent man. This is evidence of a man that deserves a new trial, and a trial where he can have his day in court.

And with closing arguments said and done, Trysten felt confident.

Trysten Mullis: I thought he was gonna walk out of the courtroom that day after the experts testified. I thought they were gonna let him walk right out of there, to be honest with you.

Now they wait.

Trysten Mullis' Fight Continues

Trysten Mullis: I thought it was going to be a quick, yeah, this is obvious. He needs a new trial. This is completely unfair.

It wasn't quick.

Daniel Nesheiwat: … every day seems like a month. And then when those days turn into months, turn into over a year … It's very tolling on everyone involved.

The hearing lasted six days but it would take nearly 15 months before Judge Laura Parrish made her decision.

Dina Nesheiwat: She denied Todd relief and getting a new trial.

Everything Todd's new lawyers argued was rejected. The judge ruled that "Todd Mullis received a fair trial represented by competent counsel." What's more, she placed blame on Todd himself. Dina Nesheiwat described the judge's ruling.

Dina Nesheiwat: … the … gist of it was Todd wanted to go to trial, so the attorney didn't have enough time to investigate … he knew he was going without … an expert. … which we disagree with.

The judge also said the jury found Dr. Kruse, the state medical examiner, "credible" and that her "testimony was consistent with the other evidence they relied on." But as for the arguments at the heart of the Nesheiwat's case, the work they did that shows that Amy Mullis died as a result of an accident, Judge Parrish said little.

Dina Nesheiwat: … she summarized the science, but she didn't analyze the science …

Erin Moriarty: If the jury had heard the science, do you think that would have made a difference at trial?

Daniel Nesheiwat: Absolutely.

Dina Nesheiwat: Todd would not be in prison right now if a jury heard the evidence that we have here or saw that animation.

The decision was devastating to Trysten and the rest of the Mullis family who had been so hopeful.

Mike Mullis: We went through all the work … to prove all this.

Lynne White: To prove this.

Mike Mullis: And then –

Lynne White: Yeah, basically have it dismissed.

Mike Mullis: Disregarded basically.

Erin Moriarty: How frustrated is your family?

Mike Mullis: Very frustrated.

Lynne White: Very frustrated.

Trysten Mullis: ... I was dumbfounded that a — a judge could look at that and decide that.

Dina Nesheiwat had to break the news to Todd.

Dina Nesheiwat: …he was just crushed. …sucked the air right out of him. Just couldn't believe it. … what else do they want? What else do they need?

Dina Nesheiwat: … science doesn't pick sides.

Still, there are plenty of people who already have, and believe that Judge Parrish and the jury at Todd's trial got it right.

Erin Moriarty: Is there any chance in your mind that this could have been an accident? …

Jon Turbett: No. I think Todd Mullis killed Amy Mullis … the evidence was put before and tested by juries and appellate, you know, judges. And, um, I absolutely believe we got the right outcome on that.

Jeff Fuller: … if you look at the evidence, there was no way that it was an accident.

Amy's brother Jeff said he found the defense experts conclusion far-fetched.

Jeff Fuller: … it seemed to me that they were trying to retry the case … with some alternate facts and alternate theories. … it seemed almost nonsensical, some of the things that were being said.

Amy's brother, mother and stepfather are hoping the judge's decision will finally shift the focus from Todd and put it back on Amy.

Peggy Munson: There's a hole in our lives, but we know she's up there in Heaven looking down on us.

Erin Moriarty: What's the most important thing that you want people to know about Amy?

Jeff Fuller: Um, the number one thing is how much she loved her kids. And how great of a mom she was.

Randy Munson: … we know how we feel about losing her, but I can't imagine how they feel.

Erin Moriarty: So what do you do now?

Dina Nesheiwat: We keep fighting. We have an appeal to go to next and we're just going to keep fighting. … the science is still on the record just because she didn't analyze it or agree with it or — it's still there, still on the record. So we're going to ask an appellate court to hear it now.

Erin Moriarty: You're not giving up.

Lynne White: No.

Mike Mullis: Absolutely not.

Erin Moriarty: Why not?

Mike Mullis: 'Cause we know he's innocent.

Trysten Mullis: I lost both of my parents at 13. …

Trysten Mullis, now 21, is speaking out for the first time as he fights to challenge his father's murder conviction. "There is an innocent man rotting in prison right now for something he did not do." CBS News

Trysten told us he's not giving up either. He often thinks of his mom and is determined to get justice for his father.

Erin Moriarty: What keeps you going?

Trysten Mullis: Prayer, prayer and faith that one day this will all be set straight …

Erin Moriarty: If he were sitting here right now, what would you say to your dad?

Trysten Mullis: I love you and I'm — I'm fighting every day for you. I'm fighting to get you home.
