The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.

“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

World.title: EU leaders clash over migration, Ukraine and budget in Brussels — but delay big decisions
World.content:
Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU.

Luc Frieden and Emmanuel Macron speak ahead of a round table during the EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels.

But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.”

“In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded.

World.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
World.content:
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.

Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.

Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.

"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.

He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
World.content:
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

World.title: Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
World.content:
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.

That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”

The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.

While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.

SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.

The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.

World.title: ‘Every sunny surface’ is being put to work. Europeans transforming their homes with solar driveways
World.content:
Europeans are transforming their driveways and patios into mini solar farms, bringing the continent closer to a “cheaper, more secure” energy system.

 

The war on Iran and subsequent stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route that usually carries around one-fifth of global oil supplies, has sent oil and gas prices soaring.

Solar has stepped in to help cushion the fossil fuel price shock, saving the EU €40 billion in avoided gas imports since the conflict began – according to the latest analysis from Solar Power Europe. But electricity and gas bills across the continent remain high – which experts say has spurred households to “take control” of their own energy.

In Germany, renewable energy firm Enpal BV saw inquiries for solar panels rise by 30 per cent following the first weeks of the US-Israel war against Iran. Over in the UK, energy firm EON witnessed interest in solar spike by 23 per cent between 23 February and 1 March, before surging a further 63 per cent between 2 and 8 March.

And it isn’t just rooftops that are harnessing the power of sunlight, as more and more companies get creative with the ways in which solar panels can be integrated into the home.

Europe’s driveways get a solar makeover

PLATIO is one of a number of start-ups selling solar panels specifically designed for decking and patios after unveiling their first prototypes in 2016.

Now covering 13 countries across Europe, the firm aims to replace paving stones and asphalt in urban spaces, parks and homes with solar technology.

In 2018, PLATIO placed a nine-metre-square installation on the driveway of a family house in Kecsmét, Hungary. The 1.7 kWp system can theoretically generate enough electricity to power base loads such as a fridge and fridge-freezer, as well as LED lighting and small kitchen appliances like a blender or slow cooker.

In 2021, the company installed solar paving in the courtyard of a six-flat apartment building near Frankfurt, Germany. Due to the larger size, this 6.64 kWp system is more than enough to cover the annual electricity needs of a typical three bedroom home if it performs at maximum generation.

SolarPave, based in the UK, also specialises in transforming outdoor spaces with sustainable energy solutions. On its website, the company has three already finished projects in the Yorkshire region, including a residential solar driveway and a residential balcony floor.

How do solar driveways and patios work?

Companies like PLATIO use a toughened, anti-slip glass to protect the solar panels – meaning you can walk across it or even park your car on it.

Cleaning the panels to remove any dirt will help maximise the amount of energy the panels can create, but PLATIO says the performance loss from dusty panels is as little as three per cent depending on the specific installation.

A public pathway in the Netherlands made out of solar panels. PLATIO

Of course, solar panels fixed horizontally on the floor opposed to angled on a rooftop will generate less electricity. This is because they miss the sun’s direct rays for most of the day, while accumulated dirt reduces their efficiency.

However, depending on their location, they may still be able to generate enough electricity to help lower your energy bills.

It is therefore difficult to say exactly how many years such a system would take to pay back.

‘Every sunny surface’ is being put to work

“People are choosing solar because it puts them back in control,” Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council, tells Euronews Earth.

“After years of volatile energy bills, households in Europe and across the world want to take energy into their own hands and solar is one of the most affordable ways to do that.”

While traditional rooftop solar panels may remain the back-bone of home-grown solar, not everybody has a suitable roof.

For example, heavily shaded roofs may generate little energy – increasing the payback time and making installation unfeasible. Roofs made from materials like thatch are also unsuitable for traditional solar panels.

“As prices have fallen and designs have become more versatile – driveways, patios, fences and car parks are becoming part of the picture,” Dunlop says.

“Every sunny surface we put to work brings Europe closer to an energy system that is cheaper, more secure and owned by the people it serves.”

World.title: Tee off in Europe’s most underrated golf holiday destinations
World.content:
Golf has long been one of the biggest drivers of the sports travel sector and in Europe there are stunning options for golfing getaways right across the continent.

 

Aside from picking which club to use, golfers face another tough choice: where to go in Europe for a golf holiday, especially when seeking somewhere under the radar and away from the traditional hotspots.

According to Golfbreaks, UK Google search interest in “golf package holiday” increased 750% year on year, while interest in “quiet golf courses” rose almost 140% over three months. The Google Trends figures were current to September 2026.

In response to the demand, the golf travel operator’s experts have selected seven destinations they consider "underrated", supported by internal booking data comparing 2026 with the equivalent period in 2025.

Varna in Bulgaria leads the list, while Portugal features twice, alongside destinations in Spain, Norway, France and Greece.

"Golf is steeped in tradition, and course quality is often judged by history and reputation," said Cameron Ritchie, Head of Product - Europe at Golfbreaks. "But some of Europe's most rewarding experiences can be found away from the established resorts.

“Choosing a less conventional destination often means quieter courses, better value for money and a more authentic experience, while still enjoying championship-quality golf in spectacular surroundings."

Underrated golf destinations in Europe

Varna, Bulgaria

Comporta and Tróia Peninsula, Portugal

North-east Majorca, Spain

Gimsøya, Norway

Biarritz, France

Tavira, Portugal

Costa Navarino, Greece

Golf in Greece has ‘long flown under the radar’ Costa Navarino

The top golf courses to play

Varna, Bulgaria

Bulgaria is often overlooked, but golfers are "starting to discover its excellent-value courses and hotels", with Golfbreaks reporting a 173% rise in demand in 2025, and a further 47% in 2026 to date. The area around Varna, on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, is picked out as an underrated golf destination and Thracian Cliffs Golf & Beach Resort is the headline attraction, with sea views from every hole. Other options where golfers can stay and play include BlackSeaRama Golf & Villas and Lighthouse Golf & Spa Resort.

Comporta and Tróia Peninsula, Portugal

The Tróia Peninsula and Comporta are better known for surfing than golfing, but demand is up 85% year-on-year, according to Golfbreaks data. Golfers can tackle the Dunas and Torre championship courses at Terras da Comporta, alongside the Robert Trent Jones-designed Tróia Golf Club. Beaches and the Sado Estuary add appeal between rounds.

North-east Majorca, Spain

Away from Palma and the island’s south-western resorts, Club de Golf Son Servera offers tree-lined fairways and water hazards. It is also Majorca's only private members' club but still welcomes visitors. Capdepera Golf Club brings mountain scenery and Mediterranean views, while Club de Golf Alcanada is another option. When not playing 18 holes, golfers can explore beaches and traditional towns in Majorca’s north-east.

Gimsøya, Norway

Above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten Links Golf Club offers the chance to play beneath the midnight sun during summer. Its coastal layout winds through dunes and rugged terrain, framed by sea and mountain views. Lofoten Links Lodges provides a nearby base for visiting golfers.

Biarritz, France

One of the oldest golf courses in France, Golf de Biarritz le Phare combines a long history with fast greens and challenging bunkers. At the nearby Golf d’Arcangues, rolling terrain and Pyrenees views welcome players, while Golf de Seignosse expands the regional choice.

Tavira, Portugal

The charming town of Tavira in the eastern Algarve is often overshadowed by Vilamoura and Albufeira. Nearby playing options include Quinta da Ria Golf Club, overlooking the Ria Formosa Natural Park, and neighbouring Quinta de Cima, with undulating fairways and water hazards. Monte Rei Golf Resort adds a Jack Nicklaus Signature course to the options around Tavira.

Costa Navarino, Greece

Golf in Greece has “long flown under the radar”, said Golfbreaks, but that’s “starting to change” with a 140% rise in demand for Costa Navarino. Its four golf courses include The Dunes and The Bay, plus the International Olympic Academy Course and The Hills Course. The latter two were designed by José María Olazábal and opened in 2022, adding further variety to this golf destination in Greece’s Peloponnese.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 18th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Historic Limoges town hall engulfed in flames amid protests in France
World.content:
A fire engulfed the historic town hall in Limoges, central France, after a group set the 143-year-old building alight amid unrest following nationwide cost-of-living protests.

 

Local prefect Maurice Barate said the roof had collapsed onto the lower floors, except for the west wing, and that around two-thirds of the building’s exterior had already disappeared.

The blaze followed demonstrations that escalated into violence in several French cities on Saturday. The extent of the damage to the town hall was still being assessed.

World.title: 'No room for violence,' says Macron after rioters and looters hijack peaceful demonstrations across France
World.content:
Police and protesters clashed violently in Paris and other French cities on Saturday as half a million people marched against soaring inflation, with one demonstrator's hand blown off, multiple blazes set and dozens of shops stripped bare by looters.

 

The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty in France as it readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.

“No room for violence in our Republic. Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished,” wrote Macron late on Saturday in a post on X.

“To the law enforcement forces, guarantors of the right to demonstrate, I express the support of the Nation.”

“We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who seek only to bring down our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he added.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu slammed the "violence of extreme intensity" during the day.

“Peaceful demonstrations have their rightful place in our Republic. Arson, looting, and attacks have no place whatsoever. Today, ultraleft groups have orchestrated violence in several French cities; delinquents have joined in to pillage and destroy,” he wrote on X.

Around 550,000 people turned out for the demonstrations, with some 400 arrests made, the interior ministry said, while the CGT union said 800,000 people turned out.

A protester holds a board with a photo of French president Emmanuel Macron in front of a burning tourism office during a protest in Lyon, France, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 Laurent Cipriani/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Police used tear gas and water cannon against masked protesters in Paris and other cities who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. Several parked cars were torched in the capital, with smoke rising over the centre.

In the southern city of Saint-Etienne, a male protester had his hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, a police source revealed to the AFP news agency.

His maiming came after a 15-year-old lost his hand on 5 October to a police stun grenade during another protest in the northern city of Lens.

Protesters attack a tourism office during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Lyon, France, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 Laurent Cipriani/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

In Lyon, protesters set ablaze a tourist office in the city centre, and smashed their way into town halls in the cities of Marseille and Lille, and a police compound in Bordeaux, vandalising the premises before leaving.

In the city of Limoges, flames reached the roof of the town hall after a group attacked the building after protests.

Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux and Lille, where an Apple store was stripped, according to eyewitnesses.

Protesters scuffle with police during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 Emma Da Silva/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

A crowd of more than 300 protesters tried to move up Paris's Champs-Elysees, home to flagship luxury stores. As police fired tear gas to block their way, they yelled "All cops are bastards” (ACAB) – which was one of the main slogans of the protest.

Paris mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said "entire streets have been devastated" in the capital region.

World.title: Romanian F-16s shoot down two drones over Black Sea, authorities say
World.content:
Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the Black Sea in the latest drone incident impacting the southeastern European nation, authorities said on Saturday.

 

Defence Minister Radu Miruta said the first drone had entered Romanian airspace at around 17:59 and was shot down "within two minutes," 25 km south-east of the town of Sulina.

"The second drone, in the same area, was engaged and shot down at 18:05, five minutes after entering national airspace, 20 km east of Sulina," Miruta said.

According to a Defence Ministry press release, two F-16s carrying out air policing missions were involved in the operation to intercept the drones after being scrambled from the 86th air base at Borcea, near the city of Fetești.

The aircraft were called into action after radar surveillance systems detected a number of aerial targets, per the ministry. It later announced that the targets were "jet-powered attack drones from the Geran family."

"The Black Sea serves as a critical maritime artery for the global export of grain, energy resources, and industrial commodities, making its stability vital to international food and energy security," Oana Toiu, Romania's foreign minister, wrote on X, adding that NATO would discuss Black Sea "defence and deterrence" at an upcoming meeting.

"The Black Sea will be safe again," she added.

Sitting on NATO's eastern flank, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security threats stemming from Russia's war in Ukraine, and the country has been dealing with a surge in drone-related incursions and incidents believed to be linked to the conflict in recent months.

World.title: Albanian police fire rubber bullets and arrest hundreds as anti-government protests enter fifth day
World.content:
Students and other protesters gathered outside the Ministry of Education in Tirana on Saturday as anti-government demonstrations entered their fifth consecutive day.

 

The protests, which have spread to cities across Albania, intensified after high school and university students joined a broader movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation over allegations of corruption.

The students are also demanding better education, greater financial support and improved job opportunities.

The wider movement has been fuelled in part by opposition to a controversial luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Violent clashes were reported in the capital, Tirana, where protesters threw stones at police, who responded with tear gas, according to Euronews Albania.

Police also deployed two water cannon vehicles and fired rubber bullets in an attempt to disperse demonstrators and bring the situation under control. Protesters briefly scattered before returning to throw stones at officers.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said he supported the right of students and other Albanians to protest but warned that masked individuals vandalising businesses were committing crimes.

He said those responsible for damaging property would be held accountable.

The country's police said 167 people had been arrested and 132 officers injured during the five days of unrest.

Seven police officers have also been suspended pending investigations into allegations of excessive force, according to Skender Hita, the country's police chief.

Rama, who has been in power since 2013 and is serving his fourth term, has ruled out resigning and accused his conservative opponents of inciting the clashes.

“I will not allow anyone to jeopardize the future of this country … not for the political gain of those who use their wicked hand to create disorder and destruction,” Rama said in a video message.

“My responsibility is clear in these difficult hours: to protect our citizens, guarantee justice and move Albania forward,” he said.

World.title: Protesters clash with police in Belgium as demonstrations turn violent across Europe
World.content:
Protesters in Brussels and Liege clashed with police on Saturday as a series of rallies turned violent across parts of Europe.

 

Video footage circulating on social media shows police firing water cannons and tear gas in an effort to break up people taking part in cost-of-living protests in the capital.

In Brussels, officers fired tear gas against youths throwing bottles and other projectiles in the Bourse district, a journalist for the AFP news agency said, whilst water cannons were also reportedly used against smaller groups of demonstrators in the eastern city of Liege.

Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said on Saturday that the situation was "no longer simply a protest."

"It is pure and simple violence, organised and repeated with the aim of destabilising our society," he wrote in a post on social media, adding that "all necessary measures will be taken to restore order in the face of the rioters."

High school students in Belgium have demonstrated in recent weeks against rising education costs, joining students in France who have been rallying against teacher shortages, poor facilities, and overcrowded classrooms.

It comes as mass protests in France spiralled into scenes of chaos over the weekend.

Firefighters extinguish a fire after a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

A Euronews crew were assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris on Saturday, near the Place de la Republique, as they covered the ongoing demonstrations.

The crew were making their way to another location when they were confronted by masked individuals looting a nearby Intermarché Express supermarket.

"We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us," Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris, said.

"They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They also hit me. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing goggles and a mask, he was not harmed," she added.

A march in Paris along the Boulevard de Clichy in the 18th arrondissement. Nathan Rennolds/Euronews

A march moving along the Boulevard de Clichy towards the Place de Clichy across the other side of Paris remained peaceful, another Euronews journalist on the ground reported, but tensions were ramping up as more and more people arrived in the area.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: India news: Kolkata stampede dampens Durga Puja festivities
World.content:
10/18/2026 October 18, 2026 Kolkata stampede: Police detain 12, chief minister vows strict action

Relatives of the stampede's victims described confusion and darkness inside the venue before the incident Image: AFP

Police in India's eastern metropolitan city of Kolkata detained 12 people on Saturday night, including the organizers of Chor Bagan Durga Puja, as they probe a stampede that killed nearly 20 people.

The latest update from the state's Chief Minister's X account puts the death toll at 17, with another 25 injured. However, Indian media, including news agency Press Trust of India (PTI), reported that at least 19 people had died.

The detentions came after West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari promised strict action against those who failed to carry out their duties to maintain crowd safety.

"We have detained 12 people in connection with our probe into the Chor Bagan incident. Our officers are talking to them to find out the cause that led to today's mishap. If any lapses are found, we will act as per the law," the officer told PTI.

Meanwhile, the West Bengal government has announced an independent investigation into the matter, led by a sitting judge of the city's high court.

"We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.

The politics of Durga Puja

Stampedes at religious and cultural festivals are not uncommon in India, but Adhikari's government is under pressure to make the city's biggest annual festival a hit this year.

Several major venues housing idols of the Goddess Durga were temporarily closed on Saturday night Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Adhikari belongs to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party which won the state elections in West Bengal for the first time in India's history, ending former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee's 15-year rule there.

The festive season was facing pressure even before it began. Food and fuel inflation, worsened by the conflict in the Middle East and lower than normal rainfall at home, is eating into people's disposable incomes.

Amit Shah, India's Union Home Minister — and Modi's right-hand man — is set to visit the victims and their family members on Sunday morning. The minister had arrived in Kolkata on Saturday evening for a series of festive programs which have now been postponed.

World.title: Canada: Major fire reported at military base in Alberta
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta. He did not provide details on the cause of the fire.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta.

"A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta," Carney said in a post on X.

He added that the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities.



Defense Minister David McGuinty later confirmed that there have been "fatalities and injuries" as a result of the incident on the base.



Located about 180 kilometers (112 miles) southeast of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds.

"The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said.



Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected.

"We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

World.title: 'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections
World.content:
Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control of Congress.

Protesters gathered across the United States for the latest "No Kings" demonstrations as Americans begin casting ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," Saturday's event aimed to fire up Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, rather than protest against President Donald Trump and his administration.

"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.

Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

There were more than 3,000 'No Kings' events planned across the US Image: Daniel Heuer/REUTERS

Trump opposes mail-in voting

Trump repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought to restrict the practice ahead of the midterms. He regularly votes by mail-in ballot, arguing that his job makes him an exception to his criticism of the practice.

The US president blamed election fraud, without providing evidence, for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election against Democrat Joe Biden.

Various surveys have concluded that restricting mail-in ballots could benefit Republicans, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.

Opponents fear that the Trump administration may try to interfere with the midterm results, particularly if Republicans lose the majority.

Opinion polls suggest Democrats are poised to regain control of the House ​of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.

World.title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump
World.content:
Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why her?

"Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

Minneapolis, the capital of Minnesota, is home to the largest Somali community in the United States Image: Jessie Wardarski/AP Photo/picture alliance

Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.

Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

Officers from the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026 Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.

'Timing wildly suspicious' — Unpacking the search of Ilhan Omar's home To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic Party's candidate to represent the state of Michigan in the US Senate Image: Emily Elconin/Getty Images/AFP

There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Romanian fighter jets shoot down 2 drones over Black Sea
World.content:
Romanian Air Force F-16s shot down drones over Romanian territorial waters. Earlier this week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast.

Romanian F-16 fighter jets have shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to the Romanian Defense Ministry.

"Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country," Defense Minister Radu Miruta wrote on Facebook.

So far, no information has been released regarding the country of origin of the drones.

What do we know about the incident?

F-16 fighter jets shot down the drones some 20 kilometers (13 miles) southeast of Sulina.

"The first drone entered national airspace at 17:59 (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes," Miruta said.

He added that the second one was shot down at 6:05 p.m., five minutes after entering Romanian airspace.

"The Black Sea will be safe again," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote on X. She added that NATO will discuss the issue at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.

Drone attacks endanger navigation in the Black Sea

This drone incursion is the latest in a series of incidents believed to be a result of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In October, several drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea were reported off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.

The most recent attack occurred on Thursday, when two chemical tankers were attacked off Romania's coast, leaving seven crew members missing.

Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal serves as an export route for Ukraine.

Romania, an EU and NATO member, shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, part of which is along the Danube.

The country has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania began shooting down these drones earlier this year.

World.title: Egypt's Ssisi says he'll defend Saudi Arabia, if asked
World.content:
The Egyptian president said his country was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested." The comments come amid escalating Houthi attacks.

Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sissi on Saturday said that his country stood ready to defend Saudi Arabia, if asked to so.

Sissi said that while Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, it was "inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, ⁠its security ⁠or stability to be harmed."

The comments came as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi targets, including strikes on energy facilities and Riyadh's main airport.

'We are speaking only about defense,' says Sisi

"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," Sissi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy.

"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sissi said. "We are speaking only about defense."

"I know this ​requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that ⁠authorization ​if we are asked," the Egyptian leader said.

An emergency session in Egypt's parliament is expected to be held on Sunday to consider whether to authorise potentially assisting in Saudi Arabia's defence.

Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthi-Saudi conflict

The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.

The Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia, also attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

A week ago, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.

Egypt and Saudi Arabia share strong strategic and economic ties. Egypt was part of the Saudi-led coalition that stepped in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.

Disruption in the Red Sea as a result of Houthi attacks has impacted the revenue coming from shipping traffic in the Suez Canal.

World.title: West Bank: Israeli settlers attack EU diplomats, French mayor
World.content:
A group of Israeli settlers attacked vehicles carrying European diplomats in the West Bank, a day after an American photographer was beaten. Belgium and France have condemned the attack.

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Saturday that masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives, and Western diplomats and officials.

Prevot said the Belgian consul general and French and Polish diplomats, as well as a French mayor, were among those attacked.

In a post on X, he condemned "in the strongest terms" the attack in which a Belgian vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli police said they have opened an investigation into the alleged assault of diplomats in the occupied West Bank.

In a separate statement, the Israeli military said the visit was not coordinated with it and there were no soldiers present.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office reacted to the incident by criticizing an alleged "smear" campaign against settlers.

"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said in a statement, using the biblical name for the West Bank.

What do we know about the incident

According to witnesses, cars from the French, Belgian, and Polish embassies had brought diplomats to visit Taybeh, a predominantly Christian village in the occupied West Bank.

Settlers then descended on the area to prevent Palestinians from gathering olives.

Masked men reportedly surrounded a diplomatic vehicle with their off-road vehicles, then demanded identification and smashed a window.

A witness and two diplomats also told the AFP news agency that the settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old leftist mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, a town in northern France.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on Israeli authorities to arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux.

"They must urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence and ensure the safety of civilian populations, as they are obligated to do under international law," he added.



West Bank olive harvest under attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French mayor says attackers were 'completely enraged'

Badoux told AFP that he was fine, having suffered minor injuries. He also expressed concern about the residents in the area.

"The whole world needs to know what's happening there," Badoux said.

Badoux said he was visiting Taybeh with the French consul general in Jerusalem, along with a priest from his home parish, to sign a goodwill cooperation agreement with his city, which has an olive emblem.

The mayor, who was wearing a sash in the French tricolor, said that the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.

"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."

"It's absolutely incredible that settlers can behave like this," he said. "I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government."

Israel FM condemns 'rioters'

In a rare statement critical of settlers, which was released before Netanyahu's statement, Israel's foreign minister condemned the attack by Israeli "rioters" on the European diplomatic delegation in the West Bank.

"I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters in the area of Taybeh," said Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, who also faulted the diplomats for not coordinating with the Israeli military.

The West Bank has experienced an especially violent olive harvest season this year. Israeli settlers have tried to stop Palestinians from harvesting their crops by using physical force.

Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday when she was attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while reporting in the occupied West Bank.

This violence is occurring during the final days of the election campaign. In hopes of gaining their support in the upcoming election, Netanyahu has championed the cause of the settlers.
