World.title: What makes a story film festival-worthy?
World.content:
While local films at Puregold's CinePanalo do what they do best by making audiences laugh, grieve, remember, and feel, the festival actively seeks out stories rarely told on screen

The lights come up slowly inside Gateway Cineplex 18, and nobody moves right away.

Outside, the Cubao mall hums with its usual Wednesday noise, the escalators, the food court, the smell of butter popcorn drifting in from the concession stand. This festival season, the noise is shut out, and the dark cinema becomes the loudest room.

Inside it, Puregold CinePanalo films are doing the thing local movies do best: to make audiences laugh, grieve, remember, and feel.

The selected full-length films each received a P5-million production grant, while student short films secured P200,000. The festival’s support extended well past the cash awards: sponsors supplied free equipment worth P1.2 million, alongside post-production discounts and grocery packages to help cover production costs.

As the festival ends, a consultant helps bring the films to international festivals, with the Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) partnership widening their reach.

From 203 full-length submissions and 267 shorts, seven full-length films and 19 shorts made the cut.

As the festival rolled into its screening dates, early moviegoers were already weighing in on the full-length film slate.

For longtime festival-goer Raymond Reynosa, the festival improved in several areas this year: more venues, more ticket booths, an arranged queue, and a published screening schedule.

Raymond Reynosa updates his followers on the turnout of events during the Cinepanalo screenings. Jade Tan/Rappler

Between the living and the dead

One of CinePanalo’s picks this year features Carl Joseph Papa and Ian Pangilinan’s Patay Gutom. The film follows a grumpy delivery driver, Tristan, whose third eye is opened after eating an offering meant for a charming but lonely ghost, Arthuro “Art” Aquino.

The directors of Patay Gutom together with the cast. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press

Bound together, they uncover family secrets, boys’ love (BL) heartaches, and a love that blurs the line between life and the afterlife.

Papa, who has made a name for himself with his distinct use of rotoscoping in his work, created two different worlds rendered in two different textures, making Patay Gutom visually unique.

Play Video

Reynosa admitted some of the drifting between worlds confused him at first, until the film revealed that the past and the present were interrelated all along.

Another viewer, Janice, connected most with the character of Tristan and one scene involving pag-aatang, a traditional Filipino food offering that connects the living with the dead to honor departed loved ones.

“‘Yung binibigyan pa rin ng food yung mga namatay na, kasi ‘di ba tayong mga Pilipino meron tayong mga paniwala na kinakain nila ‘yun,” she said, adding that the film brought her back to the days she failed to bring food to her departed loved ones.

(The way we still offer food to those who have died, because us Filipinos believe that they actually eat it.)

If Patay Gutom grieves what was left unsaid to the dead, Multwoh centers on a confession that never happened at all.

Written and directed by queer artist Rodina Singh, the film follows a college queer student who dies suddenly and returns as a ghost, not to seek revenge, but to say the one thing they never found the courage to say in life: “I love you.”

Director Rodina Singh (left) with leading lady, Sassa Gurl. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press

The film bills itself as haunting, hilarious, and tender, a story about fear, desire, and the kind of love that refuses to die.

In the cinema, that mix is physical. The prosthetics on the film’s ghosts, the pantheon of departed souls played by the likes of Inah Evans and Joao Constancia’s allies-in-death, are startling enough that one first-time festivalgoer leaned over mid-film just to whisper how scary the makeup was.

Director Rod Singh of Multwoh (Patay na Patay Sa’yo) together with the cast. Photo courtesy of Cinepanalo Press



“Death may end a life, but love remembers how it will,” Singh said, adding that a huge part of the discussion goes missing when queer deaths reach the news only as “victims of murders, crimes, and accidents.”

“We want to normalize queer love, because this is like a Disney film for queer kids,” Sassa Gurl said in a mix of English and Filipino.

For Luis Mercado, 21, who watched Multwoh for the first time at the festival, the film felt personal.

Luis Mercado shows up to watch both Patay Gutom and Multwoh. Jade Tan/Rappler

It was Sassa Gurl’s character, Marcel, whom he saw himself in — a role that captured the anxiety of harboring a secret crush on a classmate and the fear that speaking the truth aloud would change everything between them.

”Huwag kang matakot mag-confess, kasi although hindi ‘yun yung gusto mong outcome, at least naexpress mo lang before mag-end ‘yung life mo,” Mercado said.

(Don’t be afraid to confess, because even if you don’t get your desired outcome, at least you expressed yourself before your life ended.)

Four confessions, one festival

These are just two of the four films that feature four kinds of unsaid: a ghost’s love for the living, a family’s words to its dead loved one, a boy’s first attempt to understand love for a teacher, and a father’s indebtedness dressed up as a gratitude.

But the festival stories do not stop with its full-length films.

Cahilig also shared that 19 submissions for the short films lean heavily toward social commentary, with themes on abortion, mental health, socio-political issues, and complicated family setups.

He said Puregold had specifically searched for stories that weren’t commonly told on screen.

Play Video

Among the shorts presented as part of this year’s lineup is Alumahan, a story about a grieving 13-year-old seeking to join a violent gang.

There’s also Ang Huling Banlaw ni Susan, which follows a Filipina labandera (laundry woman) whose fantasies begin to overtake her reality.

No Mad Is An Island, meanwhile, is about a young dancer in a fishing town whose dreams keep meeting the limits placed around him.

Play Video

For Keith Ian Serfino of the short film Limlim, the festival’s effect was almost physical. After staying away from cinemas since watching Oppenheimer, returning to the theater felt like something inside him had been switched back on.

As a self-confessed lola’s boy, Serfino felt that the nostalgia-packed Alumhan struck a chord with him most out of all the short films — the kind of story that unexpectedly stays with viewers long after they’ve left the cinema.

Outside Gateway Cineplex 18, the mall is still bustling. But for two hours at every Cinepanalo film, the carefully handpicked stories all come to life on the big screen. – Rappler.com

Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

World.title: PMA’s first female summa cum laude takes command of cadets
World.content:
HISTORIC. Incoming Commandant of Cadets Colonel Leah L. Santiago delivers her remarks and introduces the presiding officer at Yap Hall.

Nearly three decades after becoming the Philippine Military Academy's first female summa cum laude, Colonel Leah Lorenzo Santiago returns to help shape the next generation of military leaders

BAGUIO CITY – Leah Lorenzo entered the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) in 1993 as one of its first 17 female cadets, stepping into an institution that had never admitted women in its decades of military training.

Only seven would graduate four years later. Lorenzo was among them, finishing third in her class and becoming the Academy’s first female summa cum laude.

On Saturday, October 17, nearly three decades after her graduation, she returned to PMA to make history again.

Now a colonel in the Philippine Army, Leah Lorenzo Santiago became PMA’s first female commandant of cadets, overseeing the military training, discipline, and leadership development of future Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) officers.

As a former member of Charlie Company, Santiago belonged to a generation of women who had to prove they deserved a place at PMA. She will now help shape the next generation of military leaders.

Santiago, a member of the Kalasaglahi Class of 1997, formally assumed her post during a change of command ceremony at Yap Hall, Fort General Gregorio H. del Pilar, in Baguio City.

She succeeded Colonel Eugene Henry Cabusao, who served as acting commandant following the retirement of Brigadier General Nelson Aluad on September 26.

YOUNG. Colonel Leah L. Santiago during her days as a cadet at the Philippine Military Academy. Photo courtesy of PMA

One of the Magnificent Seven

Santiago’s journey at PMA began on April 1, 1993, when the Academy admitted its first female cadets following the passage of Republic Act No. 7192, or the Women in Development and Nation Building Act.

The law opened the Academy’s doors to women, ending its long-standing male-only admission policy.

Of the 17 female cadets who entered, only seven completed the demanding four-year program. They became known as the Magnificent Seven, the first women to graduate from PMA.

Three ranked among the top 10 in the 136-member graduating class. Santiago placed third overall.

Her achievement drew international attention. In an Associated Press report published on March 17, 1997, Santiago described the resistance some female cadets initially faced from their male counterparts.

“It’s been a learning process for both us and our male counterparts,” she said at the time.

The report also recounted how she persevered through physically demanding training, including an incident in which she fainted during an exercise.

Rather than abandon the course, she stayed and completed it, eventually graduating with one of the Academy’s highest academic distinctions.

A career beyond academic honors

After graduating in 1997, Santiago was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Philippine Army.

She began her military career with the 30th Infantry Battalion of the 4th Infantry Division, serving as a platoon leader and executive officer of Bravo Company before becoming its commander.

Her subsequent assignments spanned military administration, field artillery, personnel management, and cadet training.

From 2016 to 2019, she returned to PMA as its first female Senior Tactical Officer, overseeing aspects of the Cadet Corps’ military training and development.

She later commanded the 9th Field Artillery Battery (Provisional) of the Army Artillery Regiment in Sulu before taking on senior personnel management responsibilities at Army headquarters.

Her assignments included serving as executive officer and deputy of the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel (G1), as well as director of the Philippine Army’s Personnel Management Center.

Before her appointment as Commandant of Cadets, she served as the Army’s Assistant Chief of Staff for Personnel, G1.

Santiago also pursued advanced military and civilian education, earning master’s degrees from the Development Academy of the Philippines, the Australian National University, and the Ateneo Graduate School of Business.

She completed additional military courses in the Philippines and Australia, along with training in gender and development planning and budgeting at Miriam College.

ARRIVAL. The Philippine Military Academy renders foyer honors to incoming Commandant of Cadets Colonel Leah Santiago in front of Lim Hall. Photo courtesy of PMA

Shaping the next generation

Santiago’s appointment places her in charge of a central part of PMA’s mission, preparing cadets to become officers capable of leading soldiers, exercising sound judgment, and fulfilling their responsibilities to the country.

PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico, who presided over the ceremony, expressed confidence in her ability to take on the role, citing the demands that future military leaders will face.

“As Commandant of Cadets, she will have the responsibility of helping shape the character, competence, and leadership of the next generation of officers,” he said.

“She will help prepare them not only to meet the demands of today’s operational environment, but also face the challenges of a future we cannot fully predict. That is tremendous responsibility. And I have every confidence that she is prepared to meet it.”

For Santiago, the assignment brings her back to an institution where she once endured the rigorous training and pressures now facing the cadets under her command.

In her remarks, Santiago committed to developing officers guided by integrity, professional competence, and dedication to duty.

“Remember, you are not here merely to earn a degree or a commission. You are here to prepare yourselves for the responsibility of leading soldiers and defending our Republic,” she told the cadets.

She also stressed that military leaders are not expected to be perfect.

“I do not expect you to be perfect. I expect you to be honest about your weaknesses, receptive to correction, and determined to improve.”

She reminded the cadets that, despite her rank, accomplishments, and years of military service, she had once stood where they stand today. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Two Pronged] Fighting an erection problem by sleeping with a woman?
World.content:
Our letter sender writes, 'I sometimes lose my erection when I do that with a man. I really want to try having sex with a woman, but I’m afraid that I might also lose my erection with her.'

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

I’m usually more of a bottom/receiver, but sometimes when I’m vers, there are occasions when I receive oral sex or masturbate, and I’ve also tried being the insertive partner during anal sex.

However, I sometimes lose my erection when I do that with a man. I really want to try having sex with a woman, but I’m afraid that I might also lose my erection with her.

Please respect my confession — I genuinely need advice.

– Peter

Dear Peter,

Thank you for your message. You seem to have two issues at work here — the loss of erection and the wish to try sleeping with a woman.

Erectile problems are very common. The causes are varied — substance abuse, typically alcohol or drugs, medication (prescribed or not), depression, anxiety, stress. Often, a new situation or a new partner can cause anxiety that then kills an erection. This can create performance anxiety which subsequently leads to more erection loss. The key is to break the loop.

Firstly, it helps to remember that penetrative sex is not the only type of sex. Touch, oral, kissing, cuddling are also part of the sexual repertoire. Embracing this variety will help avoid performance pressure.

Take careful note of what enhances your erection and what kills it. Indulge the former and avoid the latter, especially alcohol.

Choose your partner with care. You want them to be kind and considerate of your erection issue. Take them into your confidence if you can so that there is patience, not judgment, if there are problems.

Take note of excessive expectations. If you are embarking on something that is outside your normal experience, it is sensible to aim not for Olympic but instead novice standards. If not, you set yourself up for likely failure. It is very helpful too if you can share your inexperience with your partner so that their expectations are also tempered.

As for sleeping with a woman, what has changed your thinking now? There are several possibilities: for example, variety for variety’s sake or trying to express some more confident “you”. Analyzing your past behavior will provide you with a window to the future. Once you understand where you are coming from, it will be much easier to chart a new course.

Wishing you every success on your journey of new discoveries.

– JAF Baer

Dear Peter:

Thank you very much for your letter. I agree very much with almost everything Mr Baer says. However, I believe he is being overly optimistic when he writes: “There are several possibilities (to explain what has changed your mind about sleeping with women) — for example, variety for variety’s sake or trying to express some more confident ‘you.’”

In truth, maybe I am too harsh with Mr Baer. Maybe he was just trying to be kind to you when he said one reason for your possibly sleeping with women is variety for variety’s sake.

I think the reason you want to sleep with a woman now is that you want to find out if it is easier to maintain your erection with a woman than it is with a man… In which case it is very unfair of you to want to use a woman like that.

No, no, no, I am not suggesting you have to be in love with someone before you sleep with them. Indeed, there can even be a different need/lust fulfilled when you have a quickie with someone you hardly know.

But you see, even in this case, you are responding to the actual person you are having sex with. In this case, you are not having sex with the person simply because they fit the correct category (woman as opposed to man). That would be a very cold, and hence unfair, reason to have sex with someone.

At least… if you have not been honest with her to begin with. If you had not told her, in clear and certain terms, that you want to sleep with her mainly because you want to know if you can “get it up” with a woman.

This is the major reason it is best to have sex with someone you have a certain affinity for. No, it does not mean you have to have known them for ages (though that can help). Sometimes you might have met them just that night.

DISCLAIMER: This can only happen if you have impeccable instincts for people and even if you cannot guarantee your penis will remain hard when you try and penetrate, you can be damn sure they will not make you feel bad that you tried.

And trying is what matters most. AND seeking help from the right professional if need be – and that can be anything from a urologist, a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist, and/or a counselor who can help give you a better perspective on what being a top truly means to you and how best to achieve it if you decide it is truly important.

Good luck and wishing you all the very best.

— MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

World.title: Dubai visa scam leaves hundreds of OFWs in financial, legal woes
World.content:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Two alleged scammers have reportedly fled the country after pocketing AED 3.6 million (P61.7 million) from around 400 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), in what could be the United Arab Emirates’ largest visa fraud case in recent years.

The alleged suspects — Junie Sorsano, a prominent Dubai-based content creator for over a decade, and Ryan Ronel Baco — left the UAE during the first week of September and are now reportedly hiding in the Philippines.

An undetermined number of victims still in the Philippines have also organized to seek help from authorities.

Sorsano serves as the CEO and founder of Trip Expert Business and Marketing Solutions, which opened on May 15, 2025, while Baco operates as the managing director.

The firm offered “legitimate and legal” freelance visa packages priced at AED 9,000 (P154,500) per applicant. The packages bypassed standard Philippine government safeguards, including contract verifications by the Migrant Workers Office (MWO) and the Overseas Employment Certificate (OEC), as well as the UAE-prescribed electronic salary transfer system.

Suspects’ apology, office closure

Prior to fleeing, Sorsano and Baco issued a joint public apology in September.

“We ask for your patience and kind consideration while we work through this challenging period,” the statement read.

However, victims reported that the two have been completely unreachable since the statement was released. Furthermore, Trip Expert’s primary corporate office in Deira, Dubai, has been closed due to an alleged failure to pay rent.

Victims noted that a major factor that drew them to the company was the involvement of two popular vloggers, who regularly appeared in s promoting the merits of the freelance visa package.

The digital creators, Abdul Hamid Bandon and Enrico Cardoniga, have strongly denied any involvement in the fraudulent scheme. On the contrary, both said the controversy has severely damaged their vlogging careers.

Cardoniga, acting on legal advice, declined to go on record but disclosed that two major brands have already suspended their partnerships with him.

Meanwhile, Bandon said he is waiting for the situation to “cool down” before speaking extensively. “May mga nagtatanong sa akin (People are asking me),” he said.

Diplomatic, legal response

Ambrosio Brian Enciso III, Consul General at the Philippine Consulate General (PCG) in Dubai and the Northern Emirates, confirmed that authorities are actively investigating the scheme.

“The Migrant Workers Office (MWO) Dubai, through its retained legal counsel, is providing appropriate support to individuals who have sought assistance,” Enciso said.

He noted that victims are receiving legal consultations and guidance on the documentary requirements needed by UAE authorities.

“Given the ongoing consultations and the need to respect the desire of the individuals concerned to maintain confidentiality, we are unable to provide further details at this time,” he said.

PCG lawyer Eisa Khalife noted he is compiling evidence to formalize a case and may escalate the matter internationally.

“I may ask the Interpol (international police),” Khalife said, noting that he met with a delegation of 25 victims on October 7.

Interpol involvement would be required to extradite and bring the two suspects back to the UAE for prosecution.

Scam telltale signs

Many victims paid for the steep visa fees by using up their personal savings or taking out high-interest loans from lending agencies. They became suspicious only after Trip Expert abruptly scrubbed its digital presence.

Cherry Laroga, an applicant, noticed the red flags when the company’s heavy stream of Facebook s suddenly stopped.

“September 24 yung time na nag-scroll ako sa Facebook, ‘di na lumalabas ads nila. Duon ako nagtaka kaya naghanap ako sa TikTok, dun may nabasa akong comment na ‘wag bumili ng visa diyan kasi marami ang di na-process…kaya nag-message ako sa agent ko nung same day,” said Laroga.

(It was September 24 when I scrolled on Facebook and noticed that their ads were not showing anymore. I grew suspicious and searched TikTok, where I saw comments warning people not to buy visas from them because applications weren’t being processed. I messaged my agent that same day.)

She said her agent responded honestly.

“’I will be transparent with you, ma’am,’” Laroga said, recalling the agent’s response. “Wala daw pong funds ang company… kaya pati kaming empleyado walang sahod at hindi rin matapos ang application ninyo sa visa.’”

(The company reportedly has no funds…that’s why even us, employees, do not have salaries anymore, and it’s the reason why your visa application hasn’t been processed.)

Run by Filipinos

The fallout quickly escalated across social media, prompting victims to storm Trip Expert’s abandoned corporate offices demanding refunds and report the incident to the PCG.

The victims are mostly domestic helpers, caregivers, and retail sales staff — who sought freelance visas to legally pursue independent, self-sponsored employment.

Gwendolyn Cajutol said she has accumulated more than AED11,000 in fines for overstaying because she still does not have her Emirates ID due to the scam.

“Fully paid na ko sa visa. Sakit ng naranasan ko ngayon. Masakit. Mahirap tanggapin po,” she said.

(I’ve already paid in full for the visa. What I’m going through right now is so painful. It hurts. It’s hard to accept.)

Fatima, who requested anonymity, said she had trusted the visa company because they were run by Filipinos. She had also felt assured by their regular social media s.

“Noong una po, sila mismo ang sobrang kulit. Panay ang tawag at chat nila sa akin para kumbinsihin akong mag-avail ng kanilang self-sponsored visa processing,” she recalled.

(At first, they were the ones who were really persistent. They kept calling and messaging me to convince me to avail of their self-sponsored visa processing service.)

“Dahil mga kababayan ko rin po sila at mukhang maayos at legitimate ang kanilang operation, nagtiwala po ako,” Fatima said, adding that she paid AED9,000 in May this year.

“Binayaran ko po agad ng cash kasi sabi nila hindi daw ipa-process kapag hindi fully paid. Ang usapan po namin ay matatapos ang proseso within approximately 60 working days o dalawang buwan.”

(Since they are also my Filipinos and their operation seems to be sound and legitimate, I trusted them. I paid in cash immediately because they said the process wouldn’t move forward unless it was fully paid. We agreed that the process would be completed within approximately 60 working days, or two months.)

Expired visa, frozen bank account

Fatima said things changed after she made the payment.

“Kung anu-anong dahilan na po ang sinasabi nila. Paulit-ulit nilang sinasabi na delayed daw sa authorities, kaya patuloy lang kaming naghihintay at umaasa. Ngayon po, magli-limang buwan na, pero wala pa rin akong residency visa,” she said.

(They kept giving all sorts of reasons. They repeatedly claimed that things were being delayed by the authorities, so we just kept waiting and hoping. It has now been nearly five months, yet I still do not have a residency visa.)

Her grace period has since expired, forcing her to exit the UAE to Oman twice on costly tourist visa extensions.

Fatima’s UAE bank account has also been frozen. She has been jobless for two months, and she cannot send money home to her family.

“Hindi na po ako halos makatulog. Hindi na ako makakain nang maayos dahil sa kakaisip kung ano ang mangyayari sa visa ko, sa pera ko at sa kinabukasan ko dito sa Dubai,” Fatima said, noting that she even borrowed the AED 9,000 needed to pay the visa fee.

(I can barely sleep or eat properly from worrying about my visa, my money, and my future in Dubai.)

“Kami po ang mga OFW na araw-araw nagtatrabaho at nagsasakripisyo para makaipon. Nagtiwala kami dahil mga kapwa Pilipino namin ang kausap namin,” added Fatima.

(We are OFWs who work and make sacrifices every single day in order to save money. We placed our trust in them) because we were dealing with fellow Filipinos.)

“Mas masakit po dahil sa ibang bansa na nga po kami, kapwa Pilipino pa sana ang aasahan namin. Kung sino pa ang kapwa Pilipino mo sa abroad, sila pa pala ang makakapagbigay sa ‘yo ng ganitong problema.”

“Gusto lang po namin ng hustisya.”

(It hurts even more because we’re already in a foreign country, so we’re expecting to be able to rely on fellow Filipinos. It turns out that the very people you’d expect to support you, your fellow Filipinos abroad, are the ones who end up causing you this kind of trouble. We just want justice.) – Rappler.com

World.title: How world No. 1 Anna Leigh Waters balances life and pickleball
World.content:
Anna Leigh Waters, the world’s top-ranked pickleball player, visits the Philippines and encourages fans of the country’s fast-growing sport to commit to improving, ‘whether it works out professionally or not’

For Anna Leigh Waters, being the best in the world is a full-time job. But off the pickleball court, Anna, regarded as the sport’s most dominant player, has a family and a close-knit circle that keep her grounded.

At 19, Anna has already established herself as the world’s top female pickleball player, building a career defined by relentless work and success to rise to No. 1 in women’s singles, women’s doubles, and mixed doubles.

Behind that dominance is a support system that allows her to enjoy life beyond the sport.

“It’s important to me, and it’s something I’ve obviously been doing since the beginning,” said Anna on having life outside pickleball.

Anna recently won her 200th career Professional Pickleball Association (PPA) Tour title in the mixed doubles final at the 2026 PPA Veolia Chicago Cup alongside partner Ben Johns.

She credited her family, specifically her mother, Leigh, for helping her maintain a balance in the sport and life. A former world No. 1 professional pickleball player herself, Leigh is her daughter’s longtime doubles partner turned full-time coach and manager.

“My parents have really helped keep me grounded and taught me life values along the way, as well as values in pickleball,” Anna said. “My mom is a great pickleball coach, but she’s also my life coach. She’s my mom, and I really couldn’t do what I do without her. I wouldn’t have a head on my shoulders if it weren’t for them.”

Anna visited the Philippines this October for the Franklin Asia Pickleball Showcase, with upcoming stops in Malaysia and Hong Kong.

But she’ll be back in Manila on December 9 to grace the IAM Worldwide Pickleball Showdown, which will also feature several celebrities, at the Smart Araneta Coliseum.

Anna turned professional at just 12 years old, becoming the youngest professional pickleball player in history.

This year, the American teen was also named to the TIME100 Most Influential People in Sports, earned multi-year sponsorships from some of the world’s biggest brands, and has become one of the most recognizable faces of pickleball’s rise into the mainstream.

Anna began homeschooling in third grade and continued her education through programs such as the International Virtual Learning Academy before graduating from high school in June 2024.

She has since chosen to focus on her professional pickleball career rather than pursue college, despite drawing recruitment interest from US NCAA programs.

Her mother, Leigh, also played collegiate tennis at the University of South Carolina before transitioning to professional pickleball. Together, the mother-daughter tandem formed one of the sport’s most successful doubles partnerships before Leigh moved into coaching following an ACL injury.

Before committing to pickleball, Anna was likewise a high-level youth soccer and tennis player.

She competed in soccer in Florida, received invitations to train internationally, and attracted interest from college coaches. The COVID-19 pandemic, however, disrupted those opportunities and travel plans, prompting her to turn to pickleball.

Today, her success hinges not only on her talent and work ethic but also on the people who have supported her along the way.

“We’ve also been able to build a really strong team around us. I’ve also got people back home in the US who couldn’t join us [here in Manila], but have helped me throughout my journey,” she said. “I feel like it’s a combination of things that has kept me on top, but family is probably the most important, along with hard work.”

For all the demands of competing at the highest level, Anna believes the joy of playing should never get lost in the pursuit of success.

That’s why she’s glad to see pickleball grow into a popular recreational sport, bringing together communities of players who may never aspire to compete to be professional..

Anna believes that enjoyment is just as important for those chasing a career as it is for those who simply want to play.

“If you want to pursue a professional pickleball career, you should definitely start playing and enjoying the process,” she said. “Whether or not you make it professionally, pickleball will always have a place in your life. Committing to getting better at the sport, whether it works out professionally or not, is a good idea.”

“Pickleball has helped me meet so many of my best friends in life, both on and off the court. It’s also taught me so many lessons,” she said. “I think it’s important to train and have fun, but also remember why you’re doing what you’re doing.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler’s Gelo Gonzales named 2026 East-West Center Jefferson Fellow
World.content:
FELLOW. Rappler's Gelo Gonzales, senior multimedia reporter for tech, is one of the 12 fellows for the 2026 Jeffersons.

The three-week fellowship will bring journalists to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul to examine artificial intelligence’s impact on societies and economic security in the Asia-Pacific region

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler senior multimedia reporter Gelo Gonzales, who covers technology and its impact on society, is among 12 journalists selected for the East-West Center’s 2026 Jefferson Fellowships.

This year’s fellowship, themed “New Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence: Navigating AI’s Impacts on Societies and Economic Security in the Asia-Pacific Region,” will explore the opportunities and challenges posed by artificial intelligence (AI) across the region.

The program, organized by the Honolulu-based East-West Center, will run from October 25 to November 12, 2026, taking fellows to Honolulu, Tokyo, and Seoul for a three-week reporting and study tour.

The Jefferson Fellowships is the East-West Center’s flagship journalism program, aimed at enhancing public understanding of cultures, issues, and trends in the Indo-Pacific region through news media.

This year’s program will examine how AI is transforming economies and societies, from its potential to improve public administration, healthcare, manufacturing, and agriculture to its implications for employment, economic inequality, data privacy, and the environment. It will also explore concerns that developing economies could be left behind in the AI revolution due to limited connectivity, unreliable power grids, and shortages of technological skills.



During the fellowship, journalists will meet with government officials, researchers, business leaders, and civil society representatives. They will also visit healthcare facilities, laboratories, schools, AI-driven manufacturing facilities, chip makers, and farms to see firsthand how the technology is being deployed.



Gonzales served as Rappler’s technology editor from 2016 to 2025, then specialized on covering technology as a senior multimedia reporter in 2026. He also worked as a lifestyle writer and editor for FHM Philippines from 2009 to 2016.



His reporting focuses on technology and its intersections with society, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and technology policy.



Gonzales is one of two Filipino journalists among this year’s 12 fellows, along with Purple Romero, digital verification editor, at Agence France-Presse’s Hong Kong bureau.



Here is the full list of fellows for 2026:

World.title: Filipino composer Rom Dongeto and the song we thought we knew
World.content:
Decades after a TV commercial propelled it into the mainstream, the activist-born anthem ‘Kanlungan’ — popularized by the voice of Noel Cabangon — continues to transcend generations as a bittersweet classic, though few realize it was composed by Rom Dongeto

“Kanlungan” remains an enduring staple of Philippine popular music, recognized across generations for its emotional weight and social relevance. And while Noel Cabangon has become synonymous with the song, few know the story of the man who wrote it.

Rom Dongeto, the composer of “Kanlungan,” traces his artistic origins to the 1980s protest movement, recounting the song’s journey from an obscure track in the early 1990s to a timeless anthem.

Play Video

Tondo roots

Dongeto’s activism began in Tondo, where he joined student organizing efforts at Torres High School.

During those formative years, he attended a concert at the University of the Philippines Diliman featuring prominent protest musicians Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, and Susan Fernandez. Watching them perform made him realize that music was far more than just art.

“Na-inspire ako…sabi ko, ‘Ito ang gusto kong gawin. Ito ang gusto kong maging vocation bilang isang aktibista,’” said Dongeto.

(I was inspired…I said, ‘This is what I want to do. This is what I want my vocation to be as an activist.’)

Later in college at Far Eastern University, Dongeto founded the cultural group Sinaglahi, performing across the University Belt and Sta. Mesa.

During this period, he crossed paths with Rene Boncocan, a Fine Arts student at UP Diliman and founder of the artist collective Lingkod Sining.

From Bukluran to Buklod

In the early ’80s, the artist network gave birth to Bukluran ng Musikero para sa Bayan, an alliance of progressive bands, such as Nuklus Band and UP Sintunado, as part of the growing movement against the dictatorship.

As Dongeto described it, “Nagsama-sama ‘yan para lumikha ng mga progresibong kanta, mag-perform sa rallies, makatulong sa consolidation ng protest movement, at makapag-inspire ng marami pang mamamayan.”

(They came together to create progressive songs, perform at rallies, help consolidate the protest movement, and inspire many more people.)

Play Video

The political landscape shifted dramatically following the assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983. The tragedy rapidly accelerated mass mobilizations and galvanized artists, students, and workers nationwide.

Around this time, Dongeto was introduced to folk singer Noel Cabangon through the latter’s activist brother.

“Dahil trabaho kong mag-organize, ‘yon ang ginawa ko. Pinuntahan ko siya sa isang tugtugan sa Kamuning. Kinausap ko siya,” said Dongeto, recalling how he recruited Cabangon to join their growing circle of cultural workers, paving the way for their long-term musical partnership.

(Since my job is to organize, that’s what I did. I went to see him at a gig in Kamuning. I spoke with him.)

EDSA years and beyond

The 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution brought a wave of political uncertainty to the movement, particularly among student activists. At the time, Cabangon was in Malaysia.

Reflecting on the pivotal night Ferdinand Marcos Sr. fled the country, Dongeto found himself in Morayta alongside student leader Lean Alejandro.

“Magkasama kami ni Lean sa Morayta noon…I can still remember Lean was crying noong gabing ‘yon at sinabi niya, ‘Huwag tayong manlulumo, magpapatuloy ang pagkilos,’” he said.

(Lean and I were together in Morayta back then…I can still remember that Lean was crying that night, and he said, ‘Let us not lose heart, the movement will continue.’)

Returning home that night, Dongeto channeled the lingering tension and uncertainty into the lyrics of “Ang Ating Awit,” a track that would later appear on Buklod’s second album, Tatsulok (1991).

In the aftermath of EDSA, Buklod dissolved as an umbrella organization. Dongeto noted that fatigue had likely set in after years of relentless struggle, and many believed that the fight had ended following the fall of the dictatorship.

Dongeto, Cabangon, and Boncocan, however, made a conscious decision to carry on as a musical trio, retaining the name.

“So ang ginawa namin, minaintain namin ‘yong pangalan ng Buklod bilang isang musical organization,” said Dongeto.

(So what we did was, we maintained the name Buklod as a musical organization.)

The illusion of a democratic transition was shattered in January 1987 when state troops under the Aquino administration opened fire on protesting farmers in Manila — a tragedy now known as the Mendiola Massacre.

This incident, according to Dongeto, partly inspired the creation of Buklod’s debut album, Bukid at Buhay (1988), a purely acoustic album which he fondly refers to as “classic Buklod.”

Writing ‘Kanlungan’

“Kanlungan” would ultimately become part of Buklod’s third album, Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan (1992), a project intended to reach a wider mainstream audience while expanding their advocacy toward environmental awareness.

Writing the song was a fluid experience for Dongeto, taking him just two days to compose it. Unlike earlier protest tracks like “Tatsulok” — where he felt the heavy burden of political analysis through an activist lens — the words and melody for “Kanlungan” simply flowed freely and naturally.

Dongeto noted that he did not feel emotionally or intellectually exhausted after completing it because it came straight from what he was feeling.

Though the song’s vivid imagery leads many listeners to assume Dongeto grew up in a rural coastal town, he clarifies that he wrote it in Tondo using pure creative imagination.

For Dongeto, “Kanlungan” is more than a nostalgic love song; it is an ecological lamentation on fragile ecosystems and human responsibility.

“Meron din siyang lamentation na, ‘Tsong, pag pinakawalan mo ‘to, pag nagkamali ka dito, baka hindi ka na makabalik,’” he shared.

(It features a lamentation, ‘Buddy, if you let this go, if you make a mistake here, you might not be able to come back.)

Dongeto emphasized the direct link between human affection and stewardship of nature: “Kasi gaano man ka-romantiko buhay mo, ‘pag tinamaan ka ng bagyo, bumagsak ang lupa, bumagsak ang bundok, patay ka, ‘di ba? Romantiko ka nga, pero patay ka naman…Kasi kaya tayong lipulin ng pagkakamali natin ‘pag pinabayaan natin ‘yan.”

(No matter how romantic your life may be, if a storm hits, if the ground gives way or a mountain collapses, you’re dead, right? You might be romantic, but you’d be dead… Because our own mistakes can wipe us out if we leave them unaddressed.)

Through its poetic metaphor, the song serves as an urgent reminder to safeguard our shared environment. In the end, no one wants to destroy their own sanctuary, only to be left grieving in the ruins and asking, as the song does: “Maibabalik ba ang kahapon? (Can the past be brought back?)”

Commercial shift and controversy

In 2003, while studying in the United States, Dongeto was surprised to receive a call from the Philippines. It was Cabangon, who wanted to discuss licensing “Kanlungan” for a McDonald’s commercial. After clearing up concerns regarding copyright, Dongeto agreed.

The release of the ad, which reframed the song around familial homecoming, triggered a backlash from national democratic activists.

Critics called the licensing a sellout, given McDonald’s status as a symbol of US imperialism. The friction was further heightened by the ad’s visual narrative, which featured a family member in military uniform — a stark point of contention given the Armed Forces’ long history of human rights violations in the country. Neither Dongeto nor Cabangon knew the commercial’s specific storyline in advance.

Dongeto shared that he understood and respected the sentiments of his fellow activists, but they stood by their decision. They wanted to push the song’s environmental and social themes beyond progressive circles and into the general public, believing that a far wider audience deserved to hear their work.

Beyond the commercial

While the McDonald’s commercial that elevated it to fame has long faded into memory, “Kanlungan” transcended generations to become one of the most beloved Filipino songs. Its mainstream success cemented its status in Philippine culture and sealed Noel Cabangon as its definitive voice.

“Si Noel talaga ang boses ng ‘Kanlungan.’ Kaya nga ang tao ‘pag sinabing ‘Kanlungan,’ si Noel kaagad ang naiisip,” Dongeto acknowledged.

(Noel is truly the voice of ‘Kanlungan.’ That is why, whenever ‘Kanlungan’ is mentioned, people immediately think of Noel.)

“Kanlungan” broke into the mainstream through the commercial world that its creators once stood apart from. Whether that journey represented compromise or cultural victory remains a matter of perspective.

But the song survived the backlash, outgrew the  that made it famous, and acquired a life of its own — continuing to resonate as both a song of longing and a warning against the destruction of our natural sanctuary. – Rappler.com

World.title: As Asia grays, can an aging Philippines avoid its neighbors’ fate?
World.content:
Japan, South Korea trends

Japan's working-age population (people 15 to 64) peaked at about 87 million in 1995 and has since fallen to about 73.5 million. Roughly three in 10 Japanese are now 65 or older, the highest share of any country with a population over 100,000.

The overall population has shrunk for 17 consecutive years. Tokyo has spent more than three decades trying to reverse the trend, including a pledge of about Â¥3.5 trillion a year (roughly P1.6 trillion) since 2024. Its fertility rate still fell to a record 1.14 in 2025. Adult diapers now outsell ones for babies, and the country has over 9 million vacant homes.

South Korea is on a similar path. In 2024, its working-age population fell below 70% of the total population for the first time.

After spending an estimated P17.5 trillion over 18 years to boost births, South Korea still has gaps in emergency care and too few neonatal doctors for its already small number of newborns. Its fertility rate is 0.80, among the lowest in the world.

The money in both nations has gone into a wide range of measures. Many are aimed at births, such as cash for new parents, better-paid parental leave, and housing help for young families.

Pronatal incentives, or efforts to encourage an increase in the births of children, "are not shooting up the fertility rate at all," said Ng.

That does not make them worthless. They matter for children's well-being and women's workforce participation, she said, even if they cannot necessarily reverse a decline in population growth.

Even with deep pockets, Japan and South Korea have seen limited results. What does that mean for countries with less money?

âThe current systems in Asia, in general, are not quite ready in terms of the influx of aging populations,â said Ng.

The pattern isnât limited to rich countries. Thailand became an aging society in 2004 with a gross national income per capita of P281,184, according to UN and World Bank data. In 2025, just 416,514 babies were born there, the fewest since 1950, and deaths outnumbered births by more than 143,000.

Vietnam is not far behind. It entered its aging transition in 2015 and is projected to become an aged society by the mid-2030s, according to the World Bank, when 14% of its population will be 65 or older.

Across Asia, a 2024 Asian Development Bank report found, 40% of people over 60 have no pension, and about 60% donât get regular health checks. Among workers 65 and older, 94% are in the informal sector.

Many Filipinos are no different: workers who are contractuals or in informal jobs have no pension and little savings. As they age, many will have to lean on a stretched public health system and on their children. But there will be fewer children to lean on.

World.title: US Holds Second Round of Talks With Myanmar Regime as Concerns Grow Over Policy Shift
World.content:
U.S. officials held a meeting with Myanmar miliary regime officials in Tokyo last week, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the meeting.

It was the second round of talks between the two countries within a month. A U.S. delegation led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance visited the regime’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September.

Vance also led the delegation in Tokyo, which included over a dozen U.S. officials, while the identities of regime representatives and the issues discussed remained undisclosed, according to Reuters.

At the September talks, the U.S. delegation met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and secured the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who had been detained upon returning to Yangon in June 2026 over a lawsuit filed against him.

The U.S. outreach led by Vance has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters reported, citing current and former officials as well as others familiar with the U.S. policy shift.

The Irrawaddy has learned that during the Naypyitaw meeting, the U.S. side urged the regime to reduce attacks on civilians, crack down on money-laundering gangs, engage with ethnic armed groups, release political prisoners and allow unfettered distribution of humanitarian assistance.

Observers noted that the Trump administration has shifted its policy from isolating the Myanmar military-installed government to engaging with it.

The National Unity Government (NUG), a leading anti-regime revolutionary organization, said it was not overly concerned by the increasing engagement between the U.S. and the military junta.

Speaking to The Irrawaddy, NUG Foreign Affairs Minister Zin Mar Aung said the U.S. is engaging with both sides—the military regime and the revolutionary groups—purely based on promoting its own interests, without granting legitimacy to anyone.

“Its [U.S.] policy is already clear. They are taking a transactional, practical approach to tackle issue like TOC [transnational organized crime]. They will discuss matters that are crucial to U.S. interests,” she said.

“So, this is nothing unusual. Nor is it a shift in policy. Since the Trump administration took office, this is how the U.S. has been dealing with [all] countries, not just Myanmar.”

Banya Khung Aung, Secretary 2 of the Interim Executive Council of Karenni (Kayah) State, which largely controls the eastern Myanmar state, told The Irrawaddy he is concerned that increased U.S. engagement with the regime will harm the country’s federal democracy and human rights movements, whether financially, technically or operationally. As evidence, he pointed to the Trump administration’s recent cuts to USAID funding for Myanmar.

“If you look carefully at Donald Trump’s policies, everyone knows that he engages with all [sides] and highly considers his national interests. So, I am not surprised with [the administration’s ongoing] engagement with the regime,” he said.

He noted that foreign governments are no longer prioritizing democracy and human rights, and are instead focusing on their national and common interests.

“Because of that, whether it is a government or a dictatorship, if there are benefits for America, it is almost certain they will engage.”

Bertil Lintner, a Swedish journalist, author and strategic consultant who has been writing about Asia for more than four decades, echoed Banya’s comments.

“I am not surprised. Democracy has never been a top priority for the Trump administration. And more countries are starting to acquiesce to a fait accompli. The military-dominated government is there to stay for the foreseeable future.”

Following the 2021 coup, the U.S. under Joe Biden imposed sweeping sanctions against top regime generals—including Min Aung Hlaing and his family—as well as military-owned conglomerates.

But Trump has shifted U.S. policy from isolating the regime to engaging with it, including delisting junta cronies accused of aiding and abetting regime war crimes and crime against humanity committed against their own people.

Meanwhile, the country, whose economy has collapsed under the regime, has become a hotspot of transnational organized crime. Chinese-run scam syndicates under the protection of several armed organizations, including regime-controlled or aligned militia groups, defraud huge sums from victims globally, including Americans, who have lost billions of dollars annually in recent years.

Regarding U.S. engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, said, “It looks like President Trump has been scammed by sham President Min Aung Hlaing. Trump is rewarding a criminal for committing more crimes.”

She warned that U.S. engagement with the regime not only poses risks to the country’s pro-democracy movement, but also endangers civilians in Myanmar and across the region. She noted that Min Aung Hlaing has escalated the country’s conflicts, causing mass displacement, while also driving a boom in transnational crime that targets victims regionally and globally.

“Embracing Min Aung Hlaing is embracing a nest of vipers. He has been intensifying threats to regional human security and economic stability,” Stothard said.

The U.S. State Department said it engages will all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting U.S. interests and has raised the need to cease violence and release political prisoners, according to the Reuters report.

World.title: Chinese Jet-Fuel Refinery to Bypass Sanctions, Myanmar’s Blood Timber Flows to China, and More
World.content:
China‑backed refinery lets regime bypass jet fuel sanctions

Myanmar’s military regime has restarted the Thanlyin No.1 Oil Refinery near Yangon, allowing it to bypass jet fuel sanctions and sustain its deadly air raids on the civilian population. According to Nikkei Asia, Phase 1 is designed to produce 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually, roughly equal to Myanmar’s import volume last year.

The refinery, operated by Myanma Petrochemical Enterprise (MPE), was taken offline in 2017 but rebuilt after the 2021 coup. The engineering, procurement and construction contract was awarded to Peiyang Chemical Engineering Service Corporation (PCCS), a Singapore-registered subsidiary of Peiyang Chemical Equipment in Tianjin.

Anhui Tiankang Group supplied nearly 400 measuring devices for the various chemical processes, coordinated by Tianjin Sainuo Oil & Gas Technology. Some modules were fabricated in China and shipped via Singapore to Thilawa Port.

The regime says the project will reduce foreign currency outflow and stabilize supply. It has heavily relied on air power since 2022, killing thousands of civilians, and this dependency has only increased as the territory it controls continues to shrink. In the most recent atrocity, 50 civilians died and nearly 60 were injured when the regime bombed a busy market in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw.

China becomes biggest buyer of Myanmar’s blood timber

China has become the dominant buyer of Myanmar’s timber since the 2021 coup, according to UN Comtrade data cited by Australia’s Wood Central.

Last year, China’s purchases climbed to US$147.3 million, nearly double the pre-coup total of $78 million, while Western imports collapsed from roughly the same amount to just $1.2 million worth, according to Forest Trends, a Washington‑based non‑profit that monitors global forest trade and conservation finance.

The group’s analysis shows China’s share of Myanmar’s reported wood exports rose from 25.5 percent in 2019 to a peak of $228.7 million in 2024, nearly 80 percent of the total, before settling at 74.1% in 2025. Nearly three‑quarters of China’s imports since the coup were bound for companies registered in Yunnan Province.

Myanmar’s total reported wood exports rose from $304.3 million in 2019 to $370.6 million in 2022 but then fell to $198.9 million last year after the regime lost control over most of the border with Yunnan in Shan and Kachin states. But China continues to import timber through border crossings now controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Western buyers’ share now accounts for just 0.6 of Myanmar’s blood timber, but Forest Trends warns that the decline does not necessarily mean sanctions are working. Instead, the group believes much is “re-exported” to the West after “transiting through China,” though the flow is harder to trace.

Kokang scam warlord sentenced to death

A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three leaders of Myanmar’s notorious Wei clan to death as Beijing continues its public reckoning with the Kokang scam syndicates. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court convicted Wei Huairen and two others of running violent fraud compounds that trafficked Chinese nationals, forced them into online scams, and murdered at least two victims.

According to Chinese state media, the Wei family’s network generated 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) through online scams, drug trafficking, illegal casinos, and prostitution. Courts also handed life sentences to three associates and prison terms to 55 others, describing the gang as the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar.”

The Wei clan was one of four family crime syndicates in Kokang, which is now controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). Wei Huairen was the chief of the regime-aligned Kokang Border Guard Force (BGF), in which capacity he created a much-emulated model of quasi-official armed protection of online fraud parks. The ruling follows earlier executions of Ming and Bai clan members.

Beijing renews outreach to Myanmar’s party leaders

The director‑general of the Chines Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, Peng Xiubin, met leaders of nine Myanmar political parties in Yangon on Tuesday, though none associated with the bona-fide opposition.

Present at the meeting were the usual suspects from the ruling Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) as well as a few co-opted ethnic political parties like the Arakan Front Party (AFP) and Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party (SNDP). Discussions focused on “bilateral ties” and Myanmar’s “peace and reconciliation,” according to participants.

SNDP chair Sai Aik Pao told the Popular News propaganda outlet that he urged Peng to help the central regime regain control over the Muse–Mandalay trade corridor, pushing out the MNDAA and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

“China has influence” over those armed groups, he was quoted as saying.

While the USDP remains at the center of party-to-party ties, China also often flies other party leaders to Kunming and Beijing for “study tours” and “cooperation forums.” Shortly after the regime announced its planned elections last year, the department hosted a delegation of several Myanmar political parties in Beijing.

Shan groups warn against MNDAA’s ‘Sinicization’

Eight Shan civil society and youth groups published an open letter to the MNDAA on Oct. 9, warning that its boorish cultural and administrative practices in northern Shan State threaten ethnic coexistence and China–Myanmar border stability.

The letter warns that the MNDAA’s military control is only temporary and urges it to respect local ethnic traditions, languages, and rights. The groups accuse the Chinese-speaking group of erasing Shan, Ta’ang and Burmese scripts from public signboards and replacing them with Chinese characters. They argue that imposing Chinese-style governance and financial systems without consultation undermines trust and risks fueling resistance.

Such actions could even jeopardize the future of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), the letter warns, referring to the pet project of the MNDAA’s paymasters in Beijing.

Ta’ang civil society groups have similarly condemned the MNDAA’s actions. In April, six Ta’ang organizations said replacing Ta’ang signs with Chinese amounted to erasing an ethnic identity—a violation of international human rights law.

The MNDAA is busy consolidating its control of all major trade corridors linking to Yunnan Province.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Turns to Belarus for High Interest Loans as Fiscal Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime, squeezed by a worsening fiscal crisis, has turned to its ally Belarus for high‑interest loans, with its rubber-stamp parliament granting approval to borrow at rates nearing 10 percent.

On Wednesday, lawmakers endorsed coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s proposal to secure loans from Belarus just eight days after he submitted the request to the Union Parliament. The loans will be used to purchase goods from Belarus.

The loans will come from the state-controlled Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, with maturities ranging from one to five years. The regime has not disclosed the total amount, but the high interest rates have already drawn criticism.

Deputy Finance Minister Than Than Lin told parliament on October 6 that rates would range from 2.25 to 9.33 percent. Her colleague Kyaw Htin argued on October 14 that the short‑term nature of the loans — capped at five years — would limit exposure to market volatility.

The loans can be denominated in Russian rubles, Belarusian rubles, yuan, US dollars, or euros, with interest rates varying by currency type and commodity group. The regime says it will pre‑screen payment channels to avoid currencies subject to sanctions.

Authorities plan to use the loans to import capital goods (machinery), intermediate goods (raw/semi-finished products), consumer products, and other commodities. Purchases of Belarusian‑made goods, machinery, technology, and services will be financed through Belarusian banks, with Myanmar ministries, agencies, or private firms acting as buyers. In effect, Belarusian exporters will supply the goods while Myanmar entities serve as importers.

Three state‑owned banks, Myanmar Economic Bank, Myanmar Foreign Trade Bank, and Myanmar Investment and Commercial Bank, have already signed banking arrangements with Belarus, and talks are underway to open accounts.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s August trip to Minsk, the regime signed nine agreements, including a loan framework deal between Myanmar’s Ministry of Finance and JSC Development Bank of Belarus.

While the junta chief has repeatedly insisted Myanmar must rely on domestic resources rather than foreign loans, his regime’s rush to secure Belarussian credit underscores the depth of its fiscal crisis. The loan approval came the same day that lawmakers nodded through the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its 2026-27 budget deficit.

“Myanmar’s public will suffer from the high-interest loans, which will be repaid at the expense of education and health budgets,” said a Myanmar analyst.

Myanmar’s ties with Belarus were once limited to arms sales, but since the 2021 coup cooperation has expanded into politics, economics, and now finance. Belarus has emerged as a key ally alongside Russia, with Min Aung Hlaing visiting Minsk frequently while also hosting Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko in Naypyitaw.

Lukashenko was the first foreign leader to visit Myanmar after Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as head of state in April.

Reports suggest the regime may next lean on Russia for credit, with President Vladimir Putin pledging financial sector cooperation in August while hosting Min Aung Hlaing in Moscow.

Meanwhile, the junta has cut imports of basic goods including fuel, cooking oil, and steel to save foreign currency, while squeezing revenue through tax hikes, natural resource sales, and tighter remittance rules for migrant workers.

After the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and Western governments suspended aid and imposed sanctions following the coup, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime has been increasingly dependent on loans and support from his authoritarian allies, analysts say.

World.title: China’s Shrinking Politburo Has a Diversity Problem
World.content:
China’s Communist Party chose 24 men for its Politburo in October 2022, all of them Han Chinese. It was the first Politburo without a woman in 25 years, and it included nobody from any of China’s 55 officially recognized ethnic minority groups. After four years, the group is even more exclusive.

In October 2025, the party expelled Central Military Commission Vice Chairman He Weidong. Former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui followed in July 2026, and top general Zhang Youxia last month. Official notices accused all three of serious violations; the notice on Zhang also alleged disloyalty, “faction-building” and a remarkably large number of bribes. Their removal leaves an active Politburo of 21—a concentration that tells us something important about power under Xi Jinping. Diversity exists farther down the political system, often through quotas and administrative rules. It disappears where the most consequential decisions are made.

A narrowing funnel

The contrast starts with the membership. At the end of 2025, women accounted for 31.5 percent of the Communist Party of China’s 101.3 million members, while ethnic minority members made up 7.8 percent. Among people admitted in 2025, women made up 46.5 percent and ethnic minorities 10.2 percent, according to the Central Organization Department.

Representation was also visible at the 20th Party Congress. Its 2,296 delegates included 619 women or 27 percent, and 264 ethnic minority members or 11.5 percent, drawn from 40 minority groups. Then the funnel thins. Only 11 of the 205 full members elected to the 20th Central Committee were women, while nine came from ethnic minority groups. At the Politburo level, both figures fell to zero.

This isn’t a simple story of too few qualified candidates. Shen Yiqin, an ethnic Bai woman, had served as Guizhou governor and provincial party secretary before the 2022 congress. She became a state councilor in 2023 and later president of the All-China Women’s Federation, yet never entered the Politburo. Her current brief covers civil affairs, human resources, social security, veterans, sports and liaison with the ethnic affairs bureaucracy. Those duties matter, but a state councilor ranks below the Politburo members.

Rules stop below the top

China has spent decades building representation requirements. A 2001 party directive called for at least one woman in provincial and prefectural party, government, legislature and political advisory leadership teams, as well as in county party and government teams. It gave early priority to women in education, culture, health, family planning, civil affairs and similar departments. The 2021-2030 national program for women calls for more women in local government leadership, more female principal officials and better access to training, rotation and key posts.

Yet many targets use the phrase “gradually increase” without a numerical floor for the Central Committee, Politburo or its Standing Committee. The result is presence without a reliable route to the top.

A peer-reviewed study of every prefectural mayor and party secretary serving between 2003 and 2020 found that women followed faster but more restricted careers. Female officials were younger and better educated, but more often came through the Women’s Federation, Communist Youth League and other less powerful portfolios. Men had greater access to finance, development and core party offices. Women held only 135 of 1,987 mayoral posts and 88 of 1,694 party secretary posts.

The study also found a revealing pattern: about 20 percent of women mayors were ethnic minority members, compared with 13 percent of male mayors. One appointment could therefore satisfy expectations for both gender and ethnic representation, while leaving more positions open for Han Chinese men. The evidence supports this “tandem quota” effect at the prefectural mayor level, but it doesn’t establish that top leaders consciously use the same calculation when selecting the Politburo.

Ethnic glass ceiling

Ethnic minority cadres face a parallel divide. China’s ethnic autonomy law reserves the head-of-government in autonomous areas for a member of the relevant minority, but the more powerful party secretary post has generally gone to a Han Chinese official. For decades, minorities held roughly 10 percent to 11 percent of full and alternate Central Committee seats, yet most sat in the alternate tier.

No ethnic minority official has ever joined the Politburo Standing Committee. A handful reached the wider Politburo: Zhuang general Wei Guoqing and Mongolian leader Ulanhu served there during the Mao and early reform years; Hui Liangyu later served in the body and became a vice premier. Those cases show the barrier isn’t formal, but they also highlight how rarely it has been crossed.

Under Xi, official ethnic policy increasingly centers on “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” At the 2021 Central Ethnic Work Conference, Xi linked good cadre standards to firm support for centralized party leadership and commitment to his national community project. The policy stresses political unity, shared identity and security more than representation by distinct groups.

Perhaps this policy did not directly cause the all-Han Politburo. Public records don’t reveal the bargaining, vetting or rejected candidates behind elite appointments. Still, the roster fits a system where minority identity can warrant representation in congresses and autonomous governments but offers little access to the center.

Diversity and decision quality

An all-male, all-Han Chinese Politburo doesn’t mean every member thinks alike. Nor does adding women or minority officials guarantee different policies. Officials who rise through the same selection system may share its priorities. But there is evidence that representation can affect what institutions do. Women held about one-fifth of the seats in China’s 12th National People’s Congress but sponsored 44 percent of legislative bill proposals and more than half of proposals concerning women’s rights and interests. That finding comes from the first systematic study of female legislators’ behaviour in the national legislature.

The useful question isn’t whether one woman or minority official would transform policy but whether the leadership is drawing on the country’s full pool of political experience. The body, after all, makes decisions on birthrates, employment, Xinjiang, Tibet and social welfare.

The practical tests are clear. Party authorities could publish measurable targets for women and ethnic minority officials at each rung of the promotion ladder, report compliance and place more candidates in finance, security, organization and provincial party secretary jobs that feed Politburo selection. They could also stop treating one minority woman as sufficient evidence that two representation goals have been met.

Watch the 21st Party Congress, expected in 2027. Count who enters the full Central Committee, who receives powerful provincial and central portfolios, and who reaches the Politburo. Speeches about equality are easy to issue. Twenty-one occupied seats provide the harder evidence.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: New ID Rules Tighten Regime’s Grip on Migrant Remittances From Thailand
World.content:
Desperate for revenue, the Min Aung Hlaing regime is again using the Certificate of Identity (CI) process to extract money from undocumented Myanmar migrants in Thailand, forcing them to shoulder even greater financial hardship.

The regime recently added new rules to the CI process, requiring migrants to use the regime’s official channels for 25 percent of their remittances before applying for the certificate.

The CI is a temporary document intermittently issued by Myanmar that serves as an alternative to a passport for migrant workers in Thailand, allowing them to secure a legal work permit.

Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint told Parliament on Thursday that five centers issuing CIs started operating on Wednesday in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Chiang Mai, Chon Buri and Surat Thani.

The new order requires workers to provide proof of remitting 6,000 baht (about US$180) through official channels, equivalent to 25 percent of three months’ wages calculated on a fixed monthly salary of 8,000 baht, as well as proof of payment of 2 percent income tax. Newly appointed regime Labor Minister Maung Myint said remittances are a matter of “national interest,” and workers should consider them “a donation” to the country.

The move is part of the regime’s longstanding effort to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, including through the income tax and mandatory 25-percent remittance rule introduced in 2023.

Groups assisting migrant workers said the new requirements would complicate the employment process, potentially leading to higher costs for workers.

“Many workers do not have stable jobs,” a member of a migrant assistance group told The Irrawaddy. “How can they transfer the money, when they are already struggling with the cost?”

Complicating the process by requiring more documents would create space for service providers to charge more money, he said.

The CI application costs around 3,600 baht, but workers must rely on service providers or agents, who normally charge between 7,000 and 15,000 baht, including service fees, though precise costs under the latest rules remain unclear.

A migrant worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy that the agent who managed his CI application process charged around 15,000 baht.

The amount is paid in installments to his employer through deductions from his monthly wages, reducing the amount he could send home.

“I send less money to my family. Everyone around me has to do the same thing,” he said.

Meanwhile, service providers said families of some workers in Myanmar do not have access to the banking system, making it more difficult to obtain proof of remittance transfers.

“Some workers’ families live in remote areas. It is not easy for them to withdraw the money,” a service provider told The Irrawaddy. He added that the regime was also likely to introduce stricter checks on applicants and their supporting documents.

U Set Aung, an economist and former deputy minister of planning and finance under the ousted civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, wrote on his Facebook page on Thursday that low-wage Myanmar workers in Thailand were struggling to cover their living expenses and could not afford to remit 25 percent of their wages.

“The amount workers send home should be their own decision,” he said.

He added that the policy was designed solely to benefit the regime, rather than to support families and formal banking use.

“When remittances are converted at exchange rates below prevailing market rates, workers and their families suffer additional financial losses,” he said. “It raises serious concerns about freedom of movement, the right to pursue a livelihood, and fundamental labor rights.”

As the Myanmar regime steps up efforts to squeeze remittances from overseas workers, workers in Thailand are a prime target. Thailand hosted nearly 3 million Myanmar workers as of November 2025, according to official Thai figures. But the real number is likely to be much higher as many workers are undocumented.

Labor Minister Maung Myint said on Thursday that remittances from Myanmar migrant workers abroad totaled $5.6 billion in 2025. Experts say the regime’s remittance controls have cut a vital financial lifeline for the Myanmar population, which has been badly affected by conflict and economic collapse triggered by the 2021 coup that brought the regime to power.

World.title: Kyat Slides Again as Regime Wins Approval for 2.1 Trillion-Kyat Borrowing Plan
World.content:
The kyat lost value again this week after the regime-backed parliament on Wednesday approved borrowing of up to 2.1 trillion kyats (approximately US$1 billion at the fixed official rate) for a junta struggling with ballooning defense costs.

The kyat has weakened drastically since the 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into a dollar crisis, with economic sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment, declining exports and fighting in border trade zones taking a toll on the regime’s coffers.

On Wednesday, the rubber-stamp parliament approved the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026-27. The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.

Analysts warn that borrowing from the Central Bank will accelerate inflation and the kyat’s depreciation. Currency traders report the dollar rose to 4,670 kyats in the unofficial market on Thursday, up from 4,450 kyats earlier this month, while the baht has risen from 129 to 139 kyats. Before the coup, the kyat was trading at less than 1,300 to the dollar.

“This surge is linked to the new loans. The market jumped from 4,400 to nearly 4,700 within days. Whether it will continue to increase, or decline—or if the regime will make arrests—remains to be seen,” one trader told The Irrawaddy. The regime has repeatedly arrested foreign exchange traders during currency spikes, accusing them of speculation and market manipulation.

The loan proposal has triggered fears that the revenue-deprived regime will simply print more banknotes to address the shortfall.

Deputy Finance and Revenue Minister Kyaw Htin explained that the regime has other plans to address the shortfall, apart from borrowing money. “We are working to reduce reliance on Central Bank financing to boost state revenue. We are developing taxation policies,” he told the parliament.

Recently, the regime has escalated its efforts to enforce remittance rules requiring Myanmar migrant workers to send at least 25 percent of their salaries back home at the official exchange rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar.

Officially, the Central Bank pegs the dollar at 2,100 kyats, while the trading rate between banks is 3,660 kyats and the market rate currently hovers at around 4,670 kyats. Meanwhile, the regime has restricted imports to reduce dollar spending, which has proved counterproductive for a war-ravaged economy heavily reliant on imports ranging from cooking oil and pharmaceuticals to fuel and fertilizer.

Rising dollar rates are expected to push up the cost of imported fuel, medicines, food, consumer goods and machinery, with knock-on effects for transport and production costs. Domestic industries face mounting pressure as expenses rise.

Meanwhile, the Belarus loan package, arranged through the Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, carries interest rates of between 2.25 and 9.33 percent. The loans will be used to import goods including capital goods from Minsk, but the total amount was not revealed.

Myanmar can receive loans in five currencies—the dollar, euro, Russian ruble, Belarusian ruble and Chinese yuan—said Kyaw Htin, who admitted exchange rate fluctuations would affect the amount of money Myanmar will actually receive.

Unlike concessional loans from Japan’s aid agency JICA—which carry a 40‑year repayment term at just 0.01 percent interest—analysts note that the Belarusian loan is a “tied” arrangement, warning the regime is locking itself into costly debt that will further deepen Myanmar’s economic crisis.

International organizations and Japan suspended development aid to Myanmar following the coup.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Launches ‘ASEAN Affairs’ Panel to Clinch Full Reintegration
World.content:
