World.title: Inside the Chinese city helping sustain hermit kingdom North Korea
World.content:
Before I even walk into the restaurant in the Chinese city of Dandong, there are obvious signs of its ties to North Korea.

Upbeat North Korean songs blare from a loudspeaker placed outside the entrance counter, where two small North Korean flags are standing in a vase.

Inside I'm given a menu written in North Korean, while images of Pyongyang army and navy soldiers pass across a giant TV screen adorning one wall.

There is no overt propaganda, but there is a veil of secrecy.

Multiple A4 white pages are taped to walls and pylons with warnings saying "no camera", "no filming the wait staff" and "no photo".

I keep my phone in my bag, but discreetly ask some of the wait staff who are rushing from table to table, are you from North Korea?

"Yes," they reply, "… and so is the chef."

A Dandong restaurant featured clear North Korean influences. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

The presence of North Korean workers inside China is technically illegal, but in this city it's an open secret.

A United Nations Security Council resolution in 2017 made it unlawful for member states — including China — to allow the employment of North Korean workers in their jurisdictions.

But it's clearly happening here in Dandong, on the China-North Korea border.

New fast food restaurants have opened in Dandong in anticipation of North Korean visitors. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

This city has become an economic lifeline for Pyongyang, which has been hit with decades of international sanctions over its illegal nuclear weapons program.

China has always denied hosting workers from North Korea, but a report last year found there were 20,000–70,000 North Korean labourers in China.

The Chinese foreign ministry was contacted for comment.

China accounts for about 95 per cent of North Korea's official trade — most of which flows through Dandong over an old border bridge across the Yalu River.

Tourists pose for photos by the water. (ABC News: Kat Tse)

Every day, people gather on the shoreline of Dandong to watch the trucks drive over a single-lane, old and rickety bridge, travelling a short few hundred metres into the North Korean city of Sinuiju.

They also stare with binoculars and phones at the North Korean buildings and apartment blocks on the other side of the Yalu River.

A warming relationship

This week, the two countries deepened their relationship by opening the biggest and most significant border crossing between the two cities — a four-lane bridge that some experts say has the potential to dramatically increase cargo loads.

It was a big moment for the people of Dandong, who turned out in mass crowds to cheer and take photos as the trucks passed over for the first time.

Ms Zhang was supportive of China growing closer to North Korea. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

Onlooker Ms Zhang said she had never been to North Korea, despite living in Dandong her whole life.

But she supported the new trade route and China's attempts to strengthen ties with its neighbour.

"[Our relationship with North Korea] should be friendly," she said.

"North Korea is a neighbouring country; protecting them is helping ourselves, and their safety is our own security."

At the foot of the new bridge, streams of tourists line up to take selfies and group photos with the mega-structure.

"Long live the China-North Korea friendship," one onlooker, Mr Yang, said with a laugh.

"We and North Korea have always had very good relations. Why? Because the foundation was laid during the Korean War, and the next generation continued to carry it forward.

"So, the relationship between the two countries is very good."

Mr Yang was optimistic about China's relationship with North Korea. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

Sino-North Korea watchers say the opening of the bridge is a clear sign of the growing closeness of the two countries, after a period of tension.

The border route was originally financed and completed by China in 2014, but its opening was postponed indefinitely by North Korea when relations soured over China's support for UN sanctions.

To visit Kim, Xi made an exception Xi Jinping and Kim Jong Un's bilateral talks in North Korea were a big departure from the Chinese president's usual diplomacy playbook because, for this first time this year, he was the one travelling abroad to make the meeting happen.

But following a summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korea's Kim Jong Un earlier this year, the frostiness seems to be thawing.

China will see this as an opportunity to gain more economic leverage over North Korea, but will most likely go slowly, according to Dr Sow Keat Tok from the Asia Institute at the University of Melbourne.

"We are looking at China winning in the sense that it got its foot back into Pyongyang," he said.

"After a decade of very cool relationship, and the fact that China is now more willing to mellow down its tone [and] speech over nuclearisation in North Korea, that actually gets itself back into the game."

Chinese officials have also alluded to a new era of partnership between the two countries.

"(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address that was played at the bridge's opening in Dandong, according to state media.

Dr Tok said China was also trying to reassert its influence over Pyongyang, which has drifted even closer to Russia in recent years.

North Korea's new bridges to Russia and China Trade pathways or potential military corridors? Inside North Korea's latest push for bridges linking it to its closest allies.

North Korea has sent troops and weaponry to Moscow to aid in its war in Ukraine, in exchange for financial aid. Last month, the kingdom also opened its first road bridge with Russia.

"North Korea is now leveraging its relations with Beijing and Moscow against each other," Dr Tok said.

Dandong locals watching the opening ceremony were hopeful the bridge's opening would lead to an economic boost for their city, which once thrived as the primary trade gateway to North Korea.

Ms Wu, from Dandong, has never been to North Korea but wants to visit.

"I think this [new bridge] should bring great development to Dandong," she said.

"Although we don't understand technical terms like economics and trade, I think more and more people will come to Dandong, which should be very helpful for the region."

Ms Wu believes the new bridge will be a boost to Dandong. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

China's exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3 billion last year, an increase of 25 per cent on the year before.

Cruises take tourists closer

But it was still well below levels seen before UN sanctions tightened in 2017.

Dandong is well known for being a tourism hotspot for those curious about the hermit kingdom of North Korea.

The city is dotted with tourist shops selling North Korean goods including soap and alcohol, and offering experiences to dress up in North Korean clothing.

Market stalls sell North Korean products. (ABC News: Kat Tse)

Each day, boats take curious tourists on a cruise on the Yalu River that travels within about 100 metres of the North Korean shoreline, offering a glimpse of the secretive society.

From the boat's upper floor, tourists can see brown and white apartment buildings, open parcels of farmland and abandoned watch towers on the North Korean side of the river.

But on a cruise this week, one thing appeared to be missing.

"Where are the people? Why aren't there any people?" the tourists kept asking each other.

River cruises take tourists closer to the North Korean border. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

Suddenly there's a flurry of activity on board as a lone swimmer is spotted gliding in the North Korean waters.

His white swimming cap bobbed up and down out of the water as people rushed to point and take photos, though it's unclear if he's Chinese or North Korean.

Those onboard the boat say they're curious to learn more about the country that has such deep partnership with their own, but that they know so little about.

"Finally getting off the boat upstream on the Yalu River, I gained a deeper understanding of this China-North Korea friendship," says one woman.

"[After being here], it feels like I truly appreciate the importance of peace and feel my living environment in China is quite good [compared to North Korea]."

Tourists remarked on how quiet neighbouring Sinuiju appeared to be. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

At night, the streets in Dandong are still bustling with crowded restaurants and colourfully lit shops, in a kaleidoscope of blues, purples, greens and reds.

Just across the river, there's a stark difference.

Few of the apartments have lights on and the lack of lighting makes it hard to pick out any of the buildings.

The contrast between the two cities that are separated by a narrow stretch of water could not be more stark, and the secrets of life inside North Korea remain in literal and metaphorical darkness.

World.title: Woman dies while rock fishing on NSW far south coast
World.content:
A 25-year-old woman has died after being knocked into the ocean by a wave while rock fishing on the New South Wales far south coast.

Emergency services were called to North Durras Beach, north of Batemans Bay, about 6pm on Saturday after reports of two people in the water.

Police believe the woman was fishing with a 39-year-old man at Point Upright, a rocky headland at the eastern end of the beach, when a wave knocked her into the surf.

The man and woman were fishing off rocks near the headland when the incident occurred. (ABC News: Clarissa Thorpe)

The man entered the water in an attempt to reach her, but was unable to and was washed onto nearby rocks.

He was treated by paramedics for minor lacerations to his arms and legs.

A recreational fishing vessel that was passing at the time found the woman in the water and brought her to shore.

CPR was performed, but she could not be revived and died at the scene.

Police said neither the woman nor the man were wearing safety equipment.

The man was washed onto nearby rocks and suffered minor lacerations to his arms and legs. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Life jackets 'an absolute essential'

Surf Life Saving NSW chief operating officer Phil Ayres said the death was a reminder of the dangers of rock fishing and the importance of wearing a life jacket.

"Rock fishing is a really dangerous activity, and whilst the ocean might seem calm, there are times when the swell picks up and it is very easy to lose your footing and end up in the ocean," he said.

" Life jackets are an absolute essential part of the kit, as much as your fishing rod and your bait is. "

Man 'fortunate' to survive

Mr Ayres said the man who tried to rescue the woman was fortunate to survive.

"If you are going to go in and render assistance, you absolutely must have a flotation device with you so you don't become the second victim," he said.

" In this case, the man is fortunate he didn't lose his life. "

A sign at the beach advising rock fishers to wear life jackets. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Under NSW law, rock fishers in declared high-risk areas must wear a life jacket or risk a $100 on-the-spot fine.

The Eurobodalla Shire is currently not listed as a declared area.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: The intimate photograph that captures Trump’s hunger, just as his bubble bursts
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Opinion The intimate photograph that captures Trump’s hunger, just as his bubble bursts Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist October 18, 2026 — 4:23pm

October 18, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era. It happened when LBJ yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style. Former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia and Special Assistant Natalie Harp join President Donald Trump in Marine One on Tuesday. NYT It happened when a photographer captured George W. Bush being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle. It happened when Barack Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a Black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.



It happened again when Doug Mills, The New York Times′ dazzling White House photographer, took a picture on Tuesday of President Donald Trump on Marine One with his blonde aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his then press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing. Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy. The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knockoffs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss. It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in America. He desperately craves being the centre of attention and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.



Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetising slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House Why Trump’s new press secretary had to go after just five days In Mills’ photo, Marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble — at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview. Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called Human Printer, who trails — and sometimes sprints — behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies. Zacharia reposted Mills’ photo with the caption, “Best President in U.S. History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”



Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia. But actually, the two women – scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash-talk them – were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet, who told them to hang in there. But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot. They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only. “Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several longtime advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’ daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.



The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared, “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’” Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Natalie Harp has a magnificent obsession with Trump Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’ picture but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap. We can’t see the expression on Wiles’ face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture. Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted – in vain – to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.



Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when the Times’ Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar. “When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump – who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment – snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Why all the president’s women are looksmaxxed, blonde, and more likely to be fired Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard. Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fuelled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.



The past week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Centre, accused by Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the centre; and our ally Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution. Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent – and dangerous – court. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: So, you’ve been swallowed by a whale. What now?
World.content:
CultureMoviesFilm So, you’ve been swallowed by a whale. What now? Nell Geraets October 18, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For many, Whalefall will unlock a new nightmare. The film follows scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) as he attempts to retrieve his estranged father’s remains, which have fallen to the depths of the Pacific Ocean. But unluckily for him, he gets caught in a struggle between a giant squid and a sperm whale. Despite his best efforts to escape, Jay is sucked into the whale’s mouth, swallowed, and sent on a journey through its innards. Based on Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel of the same name, the film is ultimately a story of survival. Director Brian Duffield insists they made it as scientifically accurate as possible, even consulting whale experts throughout production. It isn’t untouched territory either – a Venezuelan kayaker survived being swept into the mouth of a humpback whale last year. Austin Abrams’ character is sucked into the belly of the beast – literally. What are his actual chances of survival? Alamy Stock Photo But what are the actual odds of escaping the belly of the Earth’s largest toothed predator? And could you even get gulped by one in the first place? Macquarie University whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta and professor of veterinary anatomy and marine science at The University of Queensland Michael Noad offer some answers.



Are sperm whales capable of swallowing a fully grown human? Michael Noad: [Sperm whales’] oesophagi aren’t very big – maybe 20cm in diameter in a big male. But the oesophagus can stretch when you swallow something, and if they swallow giant squid whole, they might just be able to swallow a person. A big squid is quite a streamlined sort of thing to swallow, though. A person, especially with a scuba tank on their back, is not. It seems highly unlikely. Loading Dr Vanessa Pirotta: Sperm whales don’t munch down on food like we do. There’s no chewing involved. But if this guy’s got a scuba tank on, the sperm whale isn’t dumb. They’re used to eating things that are squishy … the tank would be enough for the whale to be like: “Something’s not quite right here”.



If swallowed, where exactly would you go once past the mouth? VP: You’d go through the oesophagus. There’s no option, like for us, where you can go to the oesophagus or lungs … because the lungs aren’t connected [to its digestive tract]. It’s one way down and usually, one way out. You’d go down to the forestomach – they’ve got a multi-chambered stomach system. That has no gastric acid secretion, it just grinds and crushes the food. Don’t get in the water, Jay. Alamy Stock Photo Could you breathe inside the whale without a diving tank? MN: It’s very unlikely there would be any gas of any kind in there … It [also] looks like the whale might do a deep dive. This would simply kill the diver. The pressure inside the stomach would be the same as the water pressure outside … the scuba gear would keep supplying you with air at ever-increasing pressure so you could still breathe, at least up to a point, but the air would be used up faster and faster. You might only have minutes. The effects of the pressure itself wouldn’t be good for you, and then shooting up again in the other direction would probably cause massive barotrauma and the bends, all of which would almost certainly be fatal, even if you weren’t inside a whale.



What would it be like inside the stomach? MN: The stomach would likely contract tightly around the diver, making it impossible to move. If you were then pushed into the next stomach, there would be acid, but perhaps not enough to burn your skin immediately. It would certainly badly sting and damage your eyes. Related Article Marine life ‘Slimy, wet and rough’: What it’s like inside a whale’s mouth The smell probably wouldn’t be too bad. Things don’t rot in the stomach, especially the forestomach, which is about powerful muscular contraction and grinding things up, not chemical digestion. Even if in the middle stomach, things are digested over hours by the acidic environment. Semi-digested food then passes into the intestines where more digestion takes place. If you get bad-smelling gas, it’s probably further down the intestines rather than in the stomach. Put crudely, farts smell worse than burps.



Could you escape through the blowhole? VP: There’s no option to go from the throat to the nose. It’s anatomically impossible. What’s the most realistic avenue through which to escape a whale? VP: There’s no way you could get out. You’d be dead by the time you go out through the poo chute. There’s no way unless the animal regurgitates you.



Overall, how accurate does Whalefall look regarding whale behaviour and anatomy? VP: There’s definitely been scientific consultation, which is cool. There needs to be high praise for bringing to life what a sperm whale is. But how you watch this movie and how I watch this movie will be very different. What strikes me as cinematic gold is the fact that you have an incredibly deep-diving whale and a deep-diving squid, and somehow the sperm whale has failed to catch that squid at depths and is remaining on the chase up to the surface. Sperm whales use echolocation, biological sonar, and all of that happens in the dark ocean depths. But feeding activity is happening at the surface in this movie. How fabulously convenient. Related Article Whales Do animals grieve? Rare footage of a mother and her calf may hold the answer MN: I don’t think it looks very accurate. But the idea of someone being swallowed by a whale is ancient … it’s part of the history of myths and legends that, in a way, underlie our society [think Book of Jonah, Pinocchio]. So, I’m not going to completely pan this as a movie. Some sort of modern version of this fable isn’t completely off the mark, and the director has “altered” facts to make the impossible possible. Is it scientifically accurate? No. Is it a good story? Sure, and one that’s part of the rich tapestry of our society and relationship with nature.



Finally, how likely is it that someone could survive being swallowed by a sperm whale (on a scale of 1-10, with 1 being absolutely impossible)? MN: One. VP: I would say two because I’m going to give it some cinematic leeway. We need this – anything to get people to connect [with whales]. Thank God we’re getting Hollywood to engage with marine biology. I’m “whale-coming” of this movie. Whalefall is in cinemas now. World.title: Drones as first responders: welcome to the future of policing
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Drones as first responders: welcome to the future of policing Chris Zappone October 18, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ever-advancing information technology has digitised everything from paperwork, to how many of us go shopping or even how we socialise. It now steps deeper into the physical world - through drones. But as the skies fill with code-driven machines flying over our cities and streets, the question emerges: can the public’s right to privacy survive in an era of airborne, automated scrutiny? That’s an issue Seattle-based drone maker BRINC is confronting, as it designs and produces specialised drones for use by first responders such as police and fire departments. The company makes drones that can conduct indoor tactical missions (including breaking windows to enter premises), outdoor response vehicles for monitoring a fire from above, and a drone-as-a-first-responder model to attend police call-outs.



BRINC VP for strategy David Benowitz said whereas computers changed how the service-economy functions, “drones really change how we do work out there,” gesturing outside. Inside the BRINC drone factory in Seattle. The company makes drones for first responders. The Age/ Chris Zappone Whether its mining, utilities, public safety or disaster-recovery, “all these things that are inherently hard to digitise are now much easier” to convert to code. “Because drones can be used to fly ahead, take photos, videos, collect that information and get people to act on them,” Benowitz said. “So drones digitise the physical space.” David Benowitz, VP Strategy for Seattle-based dronemaker BRINC.



The company makes a number of first-responder drones, which can be used to monitor and investigate live crime scenes and fires. BRINC also makes self-contained docks, from which drones can be launched and guided remotely by law enforcement. While aerial drones are the majority of BRINC’s production, the company also makes a nearly indestructible two-way communication ball used by police for de-escalation and rescue situations. It allows first responders to throw the ball into the window or behind the door of a high-risk location, and communicate with inhabitants without putting officers at risk. But the prospect of police departments integrating drones into their workflow raises questions about privacy and police accountability. Add in the capability of the drone tech to use facial-recognition software and the concerns escalate. Indeed, in the US there is a growing backlash against the use of automatic licence-plate readers (ALPR) by police forces, a tool which has long been used in Australia. The prospect of drones flying overhead, hoovering up the personal information of bystanders, which can be fed into databases and mined, is a parallel concern for many.



BRINC drone docks on its factory in Seattle. Chris Zappone/The Age Benowitz acknowledges the risk of digital surveillance, from a company whose main customers are law enforcement. However, BRINC software is engineered to at least encourage accountability. One of the major differences between first responder drones and ALPR is that ALPR is a “persistent surveillance system, in where they’re always on, always listening, always checking for things.” The drone as first responder, meanwhile, is “responding to a call for service and so it’s inherently a response tool,” Benowitz said. “So you’re only going to see a drone out there if there’s a reason for it to be launched.”



BRINC also has an automated transparency dashboard in which flights get published to a public dashboard that’s specific to the agency, Benowitz said. So anyone can look up that flight, see what the case number is. The log shows who flew what drone and when, and who had access to the footage, he said. BRINC’s drone factory in Seattle. Amid concerns about privacy, the company says it has an automated transparency dashboard. Chris Zappone/The Age “So if you’re a member of the public who sees a drone flying in an area that a BRINC DFR product is being deployed in, you could Google that, find the agency, find the flight,” he said. Then you can put in a freedom of information request for that flight as well. “So there’s a lot of accountability built in,” Benowitz said. Related Article Analysis

Aviation How cheap drones are upending the big business of defence



BRINC drones’ cameras are horizon-facing when flying to the scene, so they don’t scan people’s back gardens and uncovered patios en route, he said. Australia’s law enforcement agencies have fully embraced the use of drones. WA police use a variety of drones made by China’s DJI in their operations. Surf Life Saving NSW use drones for shark patrol and other operations, and use “drone in a box” (self-contained drone systems that can be deployed remotely) for their operations, while CFA Victoria use drones for bushfire monitoring and operations. Loading Police in NSW have used drones in the regional town of Moree – controlled 500 km away in Bankstown, Sydney – to track suspects including a man wanted for an alleged machete attack, and another man arrested on outstanding warrants for alleged burglary.



The so-called PolAir-Remote trial has raised fears of surveillance in the regional community. The Department of Transport oversees drone privacy issues for commercial and recreational users. The Office of The Australian Information Commission enforces the Privacy Act, which covers Australian Government agencies’ rules in using drones. However, state police drone operations are typically governed by state and territory privacy and surveillance laws And there are other questions relating to the digital security of drones: where they come from. The drone industry is dominated by one major company, China-based DJI. Related Article Defence spending Virtual disruption: The unicorn reimagining military tech China controls 80 to 90 per cent of the global drone market, according to the Centre for European Policy Analysis, through control of critical minerals and raw materials supplies and the production of drone components.



Swinburne University senior lecturer in aviation Adetokunbo Arogbonlo said the major drone brand used by law enforcement was DJI, “by a long mile”. Australia has some sovereign-built drones, used more often by defence than law enforcement. But the barriers to the use of Australian-built drones are cost, and, the complexity compared to the “ease-of-use DJI provides”. Arogbonlo said: “There are some privacy implications, but they can be managed with careful planning and judicious operators. DJI drones are known to upload a lot of data back home.” While concerns about data security “may not be ideal” Arogbonlo said, “the economics and value forces the issue”. DJI has long rejected US concerns about data security and national security risks, saying: “Concerns about DJI’s data security have not been grounded in evidence and instead reflect protectionism.”



Benowitz says that from a supply-chain perspective, DJI has built up an outstanding ecosystem of components provided by different vendors, which has driven down the price of the parts to levels Western companies can’t directly compete with. The BRINC ball drone in the factory in Seattle. Chris Zappone/The Age The US has blocked the import and sale of new DJI drones, reportedly for national security reasons. The restriction will also encourage the growth of a domestic US drone industry to take hold. BRINC, among others, are racing to fill demand. The VC-backed company, formed in 2017 by Las Vegas-native Blake Resnick, now has 230 employees across four locations in the Seattle area. As Benowtiz explains, given the ever-changing nature of drone technology, simply building competitive drones is insufficient. “We have to also build the supply chain because it doesn’t exist here,” he said in his Seattle office. The world is currently seeing a splitting of the supply chain between China and the West, he said.



“So we’re seeing a bunch of new capabilities being built up, here in America, but also everywhere else in the Western world to really support unique novel applications for drones.” Loading In Melbourne, where Freespace Operations builds specialised drones for industrial use, chief executive Ken King notes that having a sovereign supply chain “is an important step naturally to security of supply”. But it must be balanced with consistent orders from government customers, he said, including enough upfront deposit payments to justify the drone manufacturers and their local suppliers investing in the business. “The customer need to have skin in the game and make a fair long-term commitment to their local drone manufacturing industry,” King said.



Chris Zappone travelled to Seattle as a guest of Alaska Airlines. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government LNP reveals preferred Bribie bridge plan – with finish still years off Matt Dennien October 18, 2026 — 3:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Crisafulli government has revealed its preferred design for a long-promised new bridge to Bribie Island, with Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg saying he expected the work to be complete before the 2032 Games. A new four-lane bridge is slated to double capacity of the existing bottleneck, which is pitched to be retained as a dedicated active transport crossing for pedestrians and cyclists to and from the island north of Brisbane. Announcing the proposal on Sunday, Premier David Crisafulli and Mickelberg said community consultation on the plans will be open until the end of November, with geotechnical investigations to start this week. The Bribie Island Bridge, with the Glasshouse Mountains in the background, is set to be duplicated by the state government. Glenn Campbell “The Bribie Island Bridge is a gateway to a beautiful part of the world, and we want people, whether they live here or they want to come and visit here, to be able to do so safely and do so accessibly,” Crisafulli told reporters on the island.



“And this is a game changer for the region. But, more importantly, it fulfils a promise we made that people here heard about for a long, long time. I believe when you say something, you do it, and we’re living that.” The LNP’s Ariana Doolan won the Pumicestone seat encompassing the island at the 2024 election from one-term Labor MP Ali King, after Labor shifted from dismissing long-standing LNP calls for a new bridge. In the months before the 2024 poll, then-premier Steven Miles said Labor would duplicate the bridge at an estimated cost of $700 million, before a business case had been finalised – which the LNP dubbed a “bribe”. An April 2025 summary of the business case, since published by the transport department, named the now-announced design as one of two shortlisted options: the second would have kept the existing bridge for westbound lanes.



The estimated cost for the business case-recommended option was $756.56 million. Related Article Public transport Bribie residents rely on cars because ‘public transport is inadequate’ On Sunday, Mickelberg said the existing 800-metre bridge would have required “a considerable amount of remediation to get it up to the standard”. “It’s obviously safe as it sits right now, but it was not built to deal with the volume of traffic, and hence why the community’s been dealing with congestion, and … the challenges in relation to that emergency response when there is an incident on or around the bridge,” he said. Mickelberg added that the original plans for a new two-lane bridge with an active-travel portion “would have seen a comparable cost”, but that all of the new design “can be delivered within the existing funding envelope, which is funded in the budget”.



Geotechnical investigations and community consultation will now feed into detailed design work, with federal environmental approvals also required for the construction work across the ecologically significant Pumicestone Passage. Mickelberg said the timeframe for such approvals was expected to be two-to-three years. “But we expect that construction time frame to be between three and four years once we get all those environmental approvals in place and the detailed design is finished. We’re doing everything we can to expedite that delivery as much as possible,” he said. “It’s my expectation this should be finished before the Olympics.” Labor’s transport spokesperson Bart Mellish said it was his former government which released concept designs for the new bridge and committed funding, and criticised the LNP for not laying out a clear budget or timeline. “The Premier and his Transport Minister as more focused on self-promotion than getting shovels in the ground,” Mellish said.

World.title: Downsizer pays $12.12m for stylish Bronte house in hot auction
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Downsizer pays $12.12m for stylish Bronte house in hot auction Elizabeth Redman October 18, 2026 — 3:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. A local downsizer paid $12.12 million for a luxe Bronte home at auction on Saturday – $870,000 above the reserve price – defying the weak Sydney market. The five-bedroom house at 160D Macpherson Street came with updated interiors in a coastal palette, a sought-after north-facing aspect, knockout beach views including from an al fresco terrace, a Caesarstone kitchen with walk-in pantry, a main garden and a separate courtyard. The property was one of 845 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 52 per cent from 501 reported results throughout the week, while 154 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The result is higher than the preliminary read of 46 per cent last week, which was the lowest this year. But the auction market remains well below the 60 per cent threshold that would indicate a market balanced between buyers and sellers. The preliminary figures are also likely to be revised lower as more results are reported.



Related Article Auctions Inner west heritage home sells for $200k over reserve as market ‘opens up’ Three parties registered for the Bronte auction – all locals – and two participated. Bidding began at $10 million and rose at first in $250,000 bids, then $100,000 rises. The price surpassed the guide of $10.5 million and reserve of $11.25 million, and once it reached about the $12 million level, the increments narrowed until the hammer fell at $12.12 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.



A downsizer from the same suburb bought the residence, beating a family from the neighbourhood. The vendors also hope to stay in the area and are downsizing from their home of more than three decades. The home last traded for $1.12 million in 1994, records show. “We are definitely running a lot more auctions,” Ray White (Phillips & Co) selling agent David Tyrrell said. “The majority are selling at the guided price, maybe just above. For it to smash the reserve like this was an exceptional result. “We are selling most things, although we have seen it [the market] soften, and it softened quite fast over the last three months. We have seen probably a 10 per cent change although people are still downsizing, moving, upgrading in our area.”



He said there was a low volume of homes for sale in this price range and properties set to come to market now would be among the last to go to auction this year. “It is good to see a strong result in what people are calling a weaker market,” he said. In West Pymble, a young family from the Hills District paid $2.3 million for a full-brick house on a 904-square-metre block. The three-bedroom home at 15 Edenholme Street had a price guide of $2.2 million and drew two registered bidders, both of whom participated.



Bidding began at $2 million and was countered with an offer of $2.05 million. The price then rose in a mix of $10,000 and $50,000 bids. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Grandson of late millionaire Twisties inventor lists $15m Clovelly home The home – a deceased estate – sold under the hammer for $2.3 million, its reserve price, to a family who may knock it and rebuild on the block. The underbidders are a young couple. The Marshall Group RE selling agent Ahmad Basam said there were newer homes on either side. He handled the sale of number 17 a few months ago for $3.9 million. “It is a good street, good quality homes, good pocket, close to the schools,” he said.



He described the market as “segmented”. “The higher price points are struggling. This price point is definitely better – early $2 millions is still a decent price point,” he said. In Homebush, a renovated family home sold under the hammer for $4,151,000 to a young family upgrading from Eastwood. The five-bedroom house at 30 Abbotsford Road on a 940-square-metre block came with a swimming pool, lawn, high ceilings and outdoor dining area and a price guide of $4.1 million. Two parties registered and both competed at auction, starting with a bid of $3.9 million.



Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Point Piper mansion Akuna hits the market for more than $55 million The price rose at first in increments of $50,000, then in a mix of smaller rises including $25,000, $20,000, $10,000 and $5000. A final bid of $1000 won the day. The reserve had been $4.2 million. The vendors were looking for more space for their family and would upsize in the area. McGrath Strathfield selling agent Tarun Sethi described the market as good, adding he sold another home by auction on Saturday at 8 Ravenna Street, Strathfield, with seven registered bidders for $3.88 million. The guide was $3.6 million and the reserve was $3.8 million.



He thought Abbotsford Road appealed because of its renovation, as it did not need any work done. He said the most active part of the market was “turnkey propositions and instant solutions, in terms of a house”. World.title: Trump overload killing Republican midterm chances of victory
World.content:
October 18, 2026 — 2:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The probable fate President Donald Trump faces in the US congressional midterm elections is a consequence of him getting his own way on almost everything his heart desired. Thanks to compliant Republicans not reining him in, Trump has meddled with the judiciary and the media, introduced mad tariffs and started an unresolved war in Iran that has led to soaring fuel prices, among other things. Unsurprisingly, his popularity has plummeted to a record 36 per cent approval rating. President Donald Trump waves as he walks past presidential portraits on Friday. AP He is also taking flak for abusing his position and helping himself and his family to unprecedented wealth, littering Washington with vanity projects and tainting Supreme Court appointments to ensure a conservative majority. Meanwhile, the cost of living in the US continues to rise. The Republicans have resorted to outrageous gerrymandering and unprecedented political donations to stop the Democrats, who are riding high in the polls.



Trump’s support among many groups that changed their spots last election has evaporated, and his former backers are returning to the alternative. Related Article US midterms On the road in Ohio: Why Trump is on the defensive in this crucial state Trump takes a Republican Party into an election that has developed into a referendum on his leadership. He even urged the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, last August, to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important.” The Democrats have taken him at his word. And in the final weeks of the campaign, their election s feature as the fourth-biggest factor voters raise in terms of turning away from the Republicans after healthcare, taxes and accusations of being beholden to special interests. Even though it’s axiomatic that midterm elections are lost by the presidential incumbent and his party, Trump’s role will be seen as central if the Democrats seize control of the House of Representatives on November 3.



Both the House and the Senate are controlled by Republicans, albeit on a narrow margin. The entire House of Representatives is up for election, and about a third of the Senate, which the Democrats could win with a net gain of four seats. It’s highly possible they might control both houses. Despite the weakness of their opponents, the Democrats have found it difficult to articulate what they stand for in the face of Trump’s constant battering. Torn between a left faction that dominates their electoral strongholds and a more nuanced faction creeping into Republican heartlands, voters are confused, and the final outcome may well depend on disillusioned independents who have cooled on the Trump circus. The next two weeks will be crucial. Trump has nothing to lose and his petulant refusal to accept the will of the people raises the spectre of him mounting some phantasmagorical challenge to 250 years of American history. Should the Democrats take control, it will be at least two months before they begin their attempts to stop the rot. It cannot come quick enough for the US. Or the rest of the world. World.content:
SportAthleticsSydney Marathon Sydney Marathon will guarantee local runners a spot. But there’s a catch Frances Howe October 18, 2026 — 1:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Sydney Marathon has introduced guaranteed entry for local runners for the 2027 race under one condition; they have to have completed at least 10 prior Sydney Marathons. While once a measly 3000 or 4000 people ran in the event, popularity has surged, particularly in the past two years after the marathon was granted world major status. Now more than 123,000 people enter the general ballot for 40,000 places, with Australians vying for a spot on the startline against runners from 139 other countries. Viv Kartsounis is a member of the Sydney Marathon Bridge Club. Wolter Peeters The Sydney Marathon has long recognised the group of just under 100 runners who are members of the Bridge Club. That club consists of athletes who have run at least 10 previous Sydney Marathons as members. Before this year, the benefits of being in that club involved little more than some free merchandise and having their names enshrined on the event website. There was no need for a guaranteed entry before the race was afforded major status because there was no risk of missing out on a place at the North Sydney starting line.



But the surge in popularity has meant even Bridge Club members started missing out. In response to their dismay last year, race organisers said they were revising their ballot for 2027 and now, 100 spots have been set aside for Bridge Club members ahead of the general ballot closing on Monday. Because the club’s membership is currently less than 100, all will be guaranteed a spot for the 2027 race, which will be run on Sunday, August 29. It’s a privilege that had previously only been extended to an even more exclusive club of six runners, known as the Blue Line Legends, who have run every race since 2001. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. Getty The guaranteed entry has been years in the making for the race’s most loyal runners. “You would be side by side with your friend at the start until the world major started,” Viv Kartsounis, 62, said. Kartsounis has run 16 Sydney Marathons. “But now you have to understand it’s a world major. It’s a huge event.”



Though Kartsounis has been able to bag a spot in the two years in which the race’s popularity has surged, not everyone has been as lucky. Soonchil Shin, 59, has finished 15 Sydney Marathons but missed out on a place in the 2026 race. Viv Kartsounis has finished 16 previous Sydney Marathons. Wolter Peeters “When I first heard about Sydney Marathon becoming a candidate, I was excited actually because a lot of people [would] come to Australia, and it’s good for business, good for the economy,” Shin said. “This year, I missed out even though I uploaded my application for the ballot. But, I wasn’t chosen, I wasn’t taken. It was surprising.”



Blogger Brian Rock analysed the data from those who finished the 2026 race and found that Australians made up 90 per cent of the field in 2023 but just 39 per cent of the total runners this year. Disappointed, Shin was one of several Bridge Club runners who contacted race organisers about missing out. Kartsounis’ collection of medals from racing in the Sydney Marathon. Wolter Peeters “I sent a private message saying ‘you didn’t look after Bridge Club members’,” he said, adding that he mentioned the New York Marathon in his message, which, along with several schemes to lock in places for local runners, has guaranteed entry for those who have done 15 or more previous editions. Organisers told Shin they were looking into it. Then, last month, club members received an email in the days before the general ballot opened to tell them 100 spots had been set aside for its members, meaning all would get a spot in the 2027 race.



The initiative was introduced alongside a separate ballot for those who have volunteered at the race in previous years. Related Article Sydney Marathon ‘It doesn’t sit right’: Sydney Marathon to change ballot after local runners miss out “We remain grateful to the runners who have shaped this event over so many years, and we look forward to celebrating many more finish lines together,” a spokesperson said. “I was so happy,” Shin said. “And it sounded right because we always love [the] Sydney Marathon and suddenly, we [were] just forgotten. I was surprised they didn’t recognise us as loyal customers, and they just forgot about it. And then finally they looked after us, so I’m happy.” Kartsounis felt similarly.



“After all the loyalty, and not only me, other people … There was still no guarantee that they would get in. So all the people that have been loyal all these years, I think it’s great the Sydney Marathon are recognising them – and it will encourage more people, I think, to do 10,” she said. World.title: Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital
World.content:
NationalImmigration Opinion Before weighing into the immigration debate, spend a night in hospital Brendan Nicholson Writer October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm

October 18, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s time for a serious reality check. Anyone trying to weigh the so-called “immigration debate” should spend some time in an Australian hospital. Anyone who has spent time in an Australian hospital knows that the healthcare system runs on the labour of migrants. Getty Immigration is being used cynically as a political wedge by those harking after a long-gone monoculture without regard for facts or practical consequences. I recently spent several days in hospital where my experience before, during and after an operation demonstrated how deluded and dangerous this low-grade politics is. Any healthcare experience is a reminder that more than half the Australian population was born overseas or has at least one parent born overseas. My blood samples were taken days before by technicians of Nepalese and Indian heritage. The taxi driver who turned up at 5.40am to take me to hospital was a cheerful bloke from Delhi who took me straight to the correct entrance in a sprawl of medical facilities.



Related Article Opinion

Immigration I’m sick of immigration being blamed for problems it doesn’t cause Ross Gittins Economics Editor I was prepared for my operation by a nurse of Nepalese origin. Then I was put under by an alert anaesthetist from India who’d rung me in advance to check on a mistake I’d made in my paperwork. The surgery was carried out by an excellent doctor of Pakistani origin, who explained carefully and clearly before the operation what would be done, and why. Over the next five days I was cared for by nurses whose families were from India, Nepal, the Philippines, Tibet and Ethiopia; a cosmopolitan mix of Muslims, Hindus, Christians and others, along with several we would once have classified as Anglo-Celtics. If the politicians pushing the anti-immigration line could instantly send most of these people “home”, those of us connected to medical devices would have awakened to a largely still and silent building, sadly missing their skills and cheerful approach. The anti-immigration lot will throw up their hands and say that of course they don’t mean to banish “those” immigrants. That’s not the point.



The reality is that with an ageing population and declining birthrate, cynically harking back to the White Australia era risks unleashing racism that can dishearten and discourage people that our workforce badly needs. Loading That lowest common denominator debate and the way it’s being delivered – basically blaming immigrants for everything – is highly offensive, unsophisticated and riddled with misinformation and contradictions. Having a multicultural society brings great benefits and we’ll be in serious trouble if they all go “home”. Certainly, fix any rorts but leave the rest alone. Related Article Opinion

Immigration Why no number of new migrants will ever satisfy Australian-born citizens Parnell Palme McGuinness Columnist and communications adviser



Otherwise, who will fill the huge gaps among highly skilled specialists across many professions, not only in medicine. Who will care for our elderly and those in the NDIS, staff our supermarkets, pick our fruit, build our houses – not to forget providing flair, skill and glamour in our assorted football codes? Just over half the doctors newly registered in Australia in recent years obtained their primary medical qualifications overseas. Well over a third of medical specialists in Australia are internationally trained. At least a third – and probably more – of nurses in Australia were born overseas and about 17 per cent of them obtained their nursing qualifications before coming to Australia. The rest studied nursing in Australia. Well over 40 per cent of Australia’s aged and disability carers and registered nurses were born overseas.



Those in the medical profession who were born abroad are aware of the anti-immigration rhetoric and say it’s not unique to Australia. A willingness to blame migrants for personal or financial difficulties drives such movements in countries including the US, Germany, The Netherlands and Britain. They note that migrants who establish businesses are often very ambitious and entrepreneurial. Many have done so to pursue new ideas, to utilise their skills and experience, to achieve greater financial and professional independence. Others because it took time to have their overseas qualifications recognised, to overcome language barriers, or because they had limited local networks. Some made a strategic decision to establish a business to utilise their cultural knowledge, international experience, professional skills and connections with overseas markets. Over time, these professionals say, self-employment rates among migrants have reached or exceeded those of the broader Australian population and about a third of small businesses in Australia are owned by migrants. Other assumptions made about immigrants are simply wrong, as in the idea that those accepted in Australia as refugees will be a lifelong drain on the rest of us. Related Article Opinion

Immigration nation I am the child of an immigrant. So are 51 per cent of Australians Eryk Bagshaw Investigative reporter



It shouldn’t surprise that some of those brave and enterprising enough to escape horrors in their homelands, also demonstrate significant entrepreneurial skills once they settle in Australia. We benefit enormously from this injection of talent and drive. On the day before my hospital visit, my hair was cut by a man who was born in Iraq and later escaped to Turkey as a refugee. He made it to Australia, runs his own business and speaks Arabic, Turkish and English. A highly skilled immigrant who has prospered in Australia, he observed that there were, of course, some flaws in Australia’s migration system, and the government was working to address them. But, he said, most migrants worked extremely hard and were not dependent on Centrelink payments. “Migrant-owned businesses make an important contribution to Australia’s economy through employment, innovation, investment and economic activity, while also providing migrants with an alternative pathway to professional and financial independence,” he said. Those driving the toxic and superficial immigration debate need to consider the practical realities of our country and the talented and diverse mix of people who make it work.



A big part of this is noticing what our migrant population does for all of us and thinking through what our nation would be like without them. Poorer in every way. Brendan Nicholson is a Sydney writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The intimate photograph that captures Trump’s hunger, just as his bubble bursts
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Opinion The intimate photograph that captures Trump’s hunger, just as his bubble bursts Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist October 18, 2026 — 4:23pm

October 18, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era. It happened when LBJ yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style. Former White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia and Special Assistant Natalie Harp join President Donald Trump in Marine One on Tuesday. NYT It happened when a photographer captured George W. Bush being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle. It happened when Barack Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a Black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.



It happened again when Doug Mills, The New York Times′ dazzling White House photographer, took a picture on Tuesday of President Donald Trump on Marine One with his blonde aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his then press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing. Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy. The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knockoffs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss. It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in America. He desperately craves being the centre of attention and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.



Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetising slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House Why Trump’s new press secretary had to go after just five days In Mills’ photo, Marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble — at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview. Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called Human Printer, who trails — and sometimes sprints — behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies. Zacharia reposted Mills’ photo with the caption, “Best President in U.S. History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”



Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia. But actually, the two women – scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash-talk them – were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet, who told them to hang in there. But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot. They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only. “Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several longtime advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’ daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.



The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared, “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’” Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Natalie Harp has a magnificent obsession with Trump Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’ picture but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap. We can’t see the expression on Wiles’ face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture. Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted – in vain – to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.



Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when the Times’ Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar. “When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump – who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment – snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Why all the president’s women are looksmaxxed, blonde, and more likely to be fired Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard. Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fuelled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.



The past week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Centre, accused by Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the centre; and our ally Volodymyr Zelensky saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution. Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent – and dangerous – court. World.title: So, you’ve been swallowed by a whale. What now?
World.content:
CultureMoviesFilm So, you’ve been swallowed by a whale. What now? Nell Geraets October 18, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For many, Whalefall will unlock a new nightmare. The film follows scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) as he attempts to retrieve his estranged father’s remains, which have fallen to the depths of the Pacific Ocean. But unluckily for him, he gets caught in a struggle between a giant squid and a sperm whale. Despite his best efforts to escape, Jay is sucked into the whale’s mouth, swallowed, and sent on a journey through its innards. Based on Daniel Kraus’ 2023 novel of the same name, the film is ultimately a story of survival. Director Brian Duffield insists they made it as scientifically accurate as possible, even consulting whale experts throughout production. It isn’t untouched territory either – a Venezuelan kayaker survived being swept into the mouth of a humpback whale last year. Austin Abrams’ character is sucked into the belly of the beast – literally. What are his actual chances of survival? Alamy Stock Photo But what are the actual odds of escaping the belly of the Earth’s largest toothed predator? And could you even get gulped by one in the first place? Macquarie University whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta and professor of veterinary anatomy and marine science at The University of Queensland Michael Noad offer some answers.



Are sperm whales capable of swallowing a fully grown human? Michael Noad: [Sperm whales’] oesophagi aren’t very big – maybe 20cm in diameter in a big male. But the oesophagus can stretch when you swallow something, and if they swallow giant squid whole, they might just be able to swallow a person. A big squid is quite a streamlined sort of thing to swallow, though. A person, especially with a scuba tank on their back, is not. It seems highly unlikely. Loading Dr Vanessa Pirotta: Sperm whales don’t munch down on food like we do. There’s no chewing involved. But if this guy’s got a scuba tank on, the sperm whale isn’t dumb. They’re used to eating things that are squishy … the tank would be enough for the whale to be like: “Something’s not quite right here”.



If swallowed, where exactly would you go once past the mouth? VP: You’d go through the oesophagus. There’s no option, like for us, where you can go to the oesophagus or lungs … because the lungs aren’t connected [to its digestive tract]. It’s one way down and usually, one way out. You’d go down to the forestomach – they’ve got a multi-chambered stomach system. That has no gastric acid secretion, it just grinds and crushes the food. Don’t get in the water, Jay. Alamy Stock Photo Could you breathe inside the whale without a diving tank? MN: It’s very unlikely there would be any gas of any kind in there … It [also] looks like the whale might do a deep dive. This would simply kill the diver. The pressure inside the stomach would be the same as the water pressure outside … the scuba gear would keep supplying you with air at ever-increasing pressure so you could still breathe, at least up to a point, but the air would be used up faster and faster. You might only have minutes. The effects of the pressure itself wouldn’t be good for you, and then shooting up again in the other direction would probably cause massive barotrauma and the bends, all of which would almost certainly be fatal, even if you weren’t inside a whale.



What would it be like inside the stomach? MN: The stomach would likely contract tightly around the diver, making it impossible to move. If you were then pushed into the next stomach, there would be acid, but perhaps not enough to burn your skin immediately. It would certainly badly sting and damage your eyes. Related Article Marine life ‘Slimy, wet and rough’: What it’s like inside a whale’s mouth The smell probably wouldn’t be too bad. Things don’t rot in the stomach, especially the forestomach, which is about powerful muscular contraction and grinding things up, not chemical digestion. Even if in the middle stomach, things are digested over hours by the acidic environment. Semi-digested food then passes into the intestines where more digestion takes place. If you get bad-smelling gas, it’s probably further down the intestines rather than in the stomach. Put crudely, farts smell worse than burps.



Could you escape through the blowhole? VP: There’s no option to go from the throat to the nose. It’s anatomically impossible. What’s the most realistic avenue through which to escape a whale? VP: There’s no way you could get out. You’d be dead by the time you go out through the poo chute. There’s no way unless the animal regurgitates you.



Overall, how accurate does Whalefall look regarding whale behaviour and anatomy? VP: There’s definitely been scientific consultation, which is cool. There needs to be high praise for bringing to life what a sperm whale is. But how you watch this movie and how I watch this movie will be very different. What strikes me as cinematic gold is the fact that you have an incredibly deep-diving whale and a deep-diving squid, and somehow the sperm whale has failed to catch that squid at depths and is remaining on the chase up to the surface. Sperm whales use echolocation, biological sonar, and all of that happens in the dark ocean depths. But feeding activity is happening at the surface in this movie. How fabulously convenient. Related Article Whales Do animals grieve? Rare footage of a mother and her calf may hold the answer MN: I don’t think it looks very accurate. But the idea of someone being swallowed by a whale is ancient … it’s part of the history of myths and legends that, in a way, underlie our society [think Book of Jonah, Pinocchio]. So, I’m not going to completely pan this as a movie. Some sort of modern version of this fable isn’t completely off the mark, and the director has “altered” facts to make the impossible possible. Is it scientifically accurate? No. Is it a good story? Sure, and one that’s part of the rich tapestry of our society and relationship with nature.



Finally, how likely is it that someone could survive being swallowed by a sperm whale (on a scale of 1-10, with 1 being absolutely impossible)? MN: One. VP: I would say two because I’m going to give it some cinematic leeway. We need this – anything to get people to connect [with whales]. Thank God we’re getting Hollywood to engage with marine biology. I’m “whale-coming” of this movie. Whalefall is in cinemas now.
